title: Systemic Disinformation: Cannabis and the Inherited Logic of Datafied Prohibition
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Systemic Disinformation: Cannabis and the Inherited Logic of Datafied Prohibition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest
declarations.funderStatement: Self Funded

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the legal cannabis sector provides one of the clearest demonstrations that disinformation can evolve into systemic risk. The twentieth-century propaganda that framed cannabis as dangerous did not disappear with legalization—it was absorbed into the infrastructures that now govern visibility, legitimacy, and value. Through platform moderation, brand-safety classifiers, compliance software, laboratory standards, and financial risk models, inherited bias circulates as code. The result is Datafied Prohibition: the migration of stigma into technology, where fear is automated and profitably sustained. Drawing on the theories of Zuboff, Pasquale, Srnicek, and Harvey—alongside data from the 2025 Cannabis Media Transparency & Advertising Report and market analysis—the paper demonstrates how disinformation embedded in digital and regulatory systems becomes self reinforcing. Advertising restrictions manufacture scarcity; compliance platforms monetize access; and volatility becomes a tradable asset. These mechanisms do not distort a stable system—they are the system. Cannabis exposes disinformation not as a relic of the past but as a living architecture of control. It reveals how inherited falsehoods can destabilize entire domains of governance, economy, and knowledge—proving that when propaganda becomes infrastructure, it produces risk that no institution can diversify away.

title: Asynchronous Mobile Money Integration for Hospital Payments: Technical Architecture and Implementation of the Irembo-OpenClinic GA Integration at a Rwandan Tertiary Hospital
affiliations: University Teaching Hospital of Butare, University Teaching Hospital of Butare, University Teaching Hospital of Butare and

detail.title: Asynchronous Mobile Money Integration for Hospital Payments: Technical Architecture and Implementation of the Irembo-OpenClinic GA Integration at a Rwandan Tertiary Hospital

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Y. Muganga is Chair of Igikumwe Ltd, the system integration developer. All other authors declare no conflicts of interest. The entities named had no role in the design, data collection, analysis, or interpretation of this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The project received ethical approval from the CHUB Research-Ethics Committee (REC/UTHB/158/2024, August 26th 2024). This paper reports only technical implementation details and contains no patient-level data.
declarations.funderStatement: This study received no external funding. The integration was implemented as part of the University Teaching Hospital of Butare’s routine continuous quality improvement program.

detail.abstract:
Background: Patient payment queuing at hospital cashier desks is a persistent operational challenge in resource-limited healthcare settings. The University Teaching Hospital of Butare (CHUB), a 450-bed public tertiary referral centre in Huye, Rwanda, implemented an asynchronous Mobile Money payment module integrated with its OpenClinic GA hospital management information system (HMIS) through the Irembo payment gateway. This paper, the first in a two-part series, provides the full technical description of the integration architecture. The companion paper (Part II) reports the quantitative performance evaluation of the deployed system.

Objectives: To describe: (1) the overall system architecture of the Irembo-OpenClinic GA integration; (2) the dual payment trigger pathway design (patient-initiated SMS and staff-initiated HMIS form); (3) the four-step Irembo Application Programming Interface (API) transaction workflow covering invoice creation, payment initiation, status polling, and callback confirmation; (4) the background processing scheduler and retry mechanism; and (5) the system data model and database design supporting audit and financial reconciliation.

Methods: Technical description is based on direct analysis of the OpenClinic GA source code deployed at University Teaching Hospital of Butare (CHUB), including the Java service layer, the JavaServer Pages (JSP) presentation layer, the background scheduling daemon, and the Irembo Pay Representational State Transfer Application Programming Interface (REST-API) integration (the Irembo mobile money service component). All source artefacts described represent the production code deployed at CHUB in October 2025.

Results: The integration implements a non-blocking, asynchronous payment initiation model using a four-step Irembo API transaction workflow. Two trigger pathways are supported: patient-initiated via a pseudo Unstructured Supplementary Service Data (USSD) Short Message Service (SMS) command (*CODE*1*{patientId}*{payerPhoneNumber}#), and staff-initiated via a modal form within the HMIS patient profile page. A multi-threaded background scheduler (a 10-thread pool with a 20-second base interval) continuously processes pending inquiries and confirms payments without blocking clinical workflows. The data model comprises six database tables capturing the full payment lifecycle from billed item to financial credit, with a dedicated status-history audit log. An exponential-backoff retry mechanism (up to three attempts, 5–60 seconds delay) handles transient API failures. Webhook callback verification uses Hash-based Message Authentication Code with Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (HMAC-SHA256) signature validation.

Conclusions: The described architecture delivers genuine queue elimination by dispatching payment requests asynchronously to patient handsets, enabling payment confirmation without physical cashier attendance. The design is reproducible within any OpenClinic GA deployment and provides a reference model for asynchronous mobile money integration in sub-Saharan African hospital settings.

title: Impact of AI Chatbot Features on Customer Perceptions and Behavioural Intentions in Banking and FinTech Services
affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Rohtak, ICFAI Foundation for Higher Education, ICFAI Foundation for Higher Education, ICFAI Foundation for Higher Education and ICFAI Business School (IBS)

detail.title: Impact of AI Chatbot Features on Customer Perceptions and Behavioural Intentions in Banking and FinTech Services
detail.abstract: AI-powered chatbots are rapidly transforming banking and FinTech services. Yet, limited research explains how specific chatbot features shape customer trust, perceptions of reliability, and adoption behavior in high-risk financial environments. Addressing this gap, the present study integrates chatbot features with the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) alongside social response theory, flow theory, innovation resistance theory, and status quo bias theory. Using data from 342 active FinTech users in India and structural equation modeling, chatbot features were conceptualized as a higher-order construct comprising interaction, information, accessibility, credibility, customization, accuracy, and competence. The findings reveal that chatbot features significantly enhance performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions. Effort expectancy and facilitating conditions strongly influence perceived reliability, whereas all UTAUT dimensions significantly strengthen perceived trust. Trust and reliability subsequently drive behavioral intention and actual use behavior, with trust emerging as the stronger predictor of adoption.

title: Institutional Reform and Generational Sustainability: Corporate Social Responsibility, Financial Governance, and AI Accountability in the Gen Z Era
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Institutional Reform and Generational Sustainability: Corporate Social Responsibility, Financial Governance, and AI Accountability in the Gen Z Era

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest. This research was conducted independently with no external funding or institutional affiliation influencing the findings.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self-funded. No external funding was received.

detail.abstract:
The contemporary global workforce is undergoing a profound structural transformation driven by technological acceleration, Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration, demographic transition, and evolving expectations of corporate accountability (Arora & Sharma, 2025; D'Cruz et al., 2022). Generation Z-widely recognised as the most digitally educated and technologically adaptive workforce cohort in recorded history (Buzzetto-More & Quinn, 2024)-increasingly encounters institutional environments characterised by governance rigidity and inadequate mechanisms for generational inclusion, leading to feelings of disenfranchisement (Bodrick et al., 2025; Zilberstein et al., 2023). 
This paper examines the intersection of institutional reform, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), financial governance, and AI accountability within the context of generational sustainability. Building on the author's foundational policy research ("The System Didn't Break-It Stopped Evolving," 2025), this paper extends the earlier argument with theoretical grounding and a proposed measurement framework. It argues that many contemporary institutions-both public and private-continue to operate under governance structures designed for industrial-era economies, producing systematic barriers to workforce mobility, leadership renewal, and technological adaptation.
Drawing upon Institutional Theory, Stakeholder Theory, Agency Theory, Human Capital Theory, and contemporary ESG governance literature, the study proposes a conceptual framework for "Generational Sustainability" as a new dimension of CSR and corporate governance. The paper further develops the concept of AI-Assisted Competency Masking, explores how artificial intelligence deployment may conceal institutional incompetence where governance systems fail, and proposes three new regulatory bodies — the Institutional Modernisation Authority (IMA), the Corporate Meritocracy Commission (CMC), and the AI Governance and Competency Agency (AIGCA) — alongside a Generational Sustainability Index (GSI) for comparative institutional assessment.
The paper concludes that sustainable institutions in the AI era will not be defined solely by financial performance or environmental compliance, but by their capacity to evolve continuously, integrate technological competence responsibly, and provide equitable pathways for emerging generations to contribute and to lead.

title: Deterministic Formalisation of Large-Scale Rule-Based Knowledge Systems

detail.title: Deterministic Formalisation of Large-Scale Rule-Based Knowledge Systems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and CEO of Smart Astro Ltd, the company that developed and operates the proprietary reference implementation discussed in this paper. This relationship is disclosed for transparency. No external organisation, funder, or third party influenced the research design, analysis, interpretation, or preparation of the manuscript.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study presents a computational architecture and knowledge-engineering methodology. It does not report research involving human participants, patients, animals, clinical interventions, or customer-specific personal data. The worked example is entirely fictional and illustrative. Therefore, ethics approval and informed consent were not required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for conducting this study. The research, development, and preparation of the manuscript were undertaken independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Large-scale rule-based knowledge systems-frameworks encoding domain-specific reasoning across thousands of interdependent rules accumulated over extended periods-present a distinct class of computational formalisation challenge in knowledge engineering. Such systems may be made deterministic where their rules, inputs, conflicts and output boundaries can be specified computationally. In practice, scale, interdependency, and accumulated source heterogeneity have meant that delivery depends on human practitioners who introduce interpretation variability, availability constraints, and non-reproducibility that the underlying rule structures do not require. This paper addresses the following engineering problem: how can a large, historically accumulated, heterogeneous rule-based knowledge system be transformed into a deterministic, reproducible, and auditable computation architecture, while explicitly preserving unresolved ambiguity and excluding rules that depend on non-computable practitioner judgement? The paper presents a formalisation methodology grounded in three explicit ruleselection criteria-computability, consistency, and domain-evidence support-and four deterministic execution properties: input precision, rule determinism, output boundedness, and full reproducibility. The methodology is illustrated through a neutral worked example in a document-classification domain. A proprietary reference implementation of approximately 220,000 lines, spanning multiple decisionclassification domains, provides production-scale implementation context for the methodology. A critical boundary is maintained throughout: deterministic execution guarantees exact replay under fixed inputs and engine version. It does not by itself prove that the encoded rules are substantively correct, complete, or fair. These are separate empirical questions, domain-specific in character, requiring separate domain-specific empirical assessment.

title: Users’ Preferences for AIGC Applications on Social Commerce Platforms: A Best–Worst Scaling Study
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Users’ Preferences for AIGC Applications on Social Commerce Platforms: A Best–Worst Scaling Study
detail.abstract: AI-generated content (AIGC) applications are increasingly integrated into social commerce platforms, supporting content production, personalized recommendations, and interactive user experiences. However, evidence on which applications users prefer and how perceived AI capabilities influence these preferences remains limited. This study investigates users’ relative preferences for ten AIGC applications on social commerce platforms and examines the moderating role of perceived AI capabilities. Data were collected via an online survey of 1,097 valid respondents and analyzed using Best–Worst Scaling (BWS), the entropy weight method, and an alternative-specific conditional logit model with interaction effects. Results indicate that users most prefer Recommendation Systems, followed by Virtual Scenario (AR), Chatbots, and Interactive Media, while Music Composition and Voice Synthesis are least preferred. Applications offering immersive experiences, personalized recommendations, and strong interactivity were valued more highly. Flexibility emerged as the most influential dimension among perceived AI capabilities, and the interaction analysis shows that higher perceived AI capabilities strengthen preferences for several applications, particularly Virtual Scenario (AR), Chatbots, Video Production, Language Translation, and Image Creation. These findings provide empirical insights into user preferences for AIGC applications, highlighting the importance of interactivity and perceived AI competence, and offer practical guidance for optimizing platform design and enhancing user engagement in social commerce.

title: Decision Intelligence in Deterministic Guidance Systems A Boundary Architecture for Computation-Supported Human Judgement

detail.title: Decision Intelligence in Deterministic Guidance Systems A Boundary Architecture for Computation-Supported Human Judgement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and CEO of Smart Astro Ltd, the company that developed and operates the production Deterministic Guidance Systems deployment used as the reference implementation in this paper. No external funding was received for conducting this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper presents a decision-intelligence boundary architecture and does not report experiments involving human participants, patients, animals, or customer-specific personal data. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for conducting this study. The research and development work was independently conducted by the author.

detail.abstract: Deterministic Guidance Systems (DGS) produce structured, reproducible outputs in support of human decision-making. A design question that such systems must resolve is how their outputs should be positioned relative to human action: as automated decisions that assign decision authority to the system, or as bounded decision-support artefacts whose interpretation and application remain outside the system boundary. This paper addresses that question through a decision-intelligence boundary architecture. Decision intelligence, as defined here, is the capacity of a deterministic system to produce structured computation records, present bounded guidance outputs, preserve traceability for review and audit, and enforce a non-substitution requirement that constrains system output scope to decision-support artefacts rather than automated decisions or professional determinations. The paper defines the computation-action boundary, establishes the non-substitution requirement as a structural design property, characterises bounded guidance output components, presents a traceability model linking computation, guidance, and integrity records, and discusses safety boundaries for deployment in consequential contexts. A production DGS deployment is cited as a reference implementation at public-safe level. The contribution is a decision-intelligence boundary architecture for deterministic guidance systems: a model for using deterministic computation to produce bounded guidance that supports human judgement while preserving traceability, auditability, reviewability, and non-substitution.

title: Institutional Inversion: Boundary Governance and the Coordination Bottleneck under Information Abundance

detail.title: Institutional Inversion: Boundary Governance and the Coordination Bottleneck under Information Abundance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or professional interests that could have influenced the preparation of this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a conceptual theoretical paper. No human participants, patients, or personal data were involved in this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

keywords: Institutional Inversion; Boundary Governance; Coordination Bottleneck; Institutional Coherence; Information Abundance; Administrative Complexity; Transboundary Coordination; Metagovernance Failure

detail.abstract: Classical institutional theory posits that organizations exist to mitigate transaction costs and resolve information asymmetries. For over a century, administrative modernization has been predicated on the assumption that expanding an institution's access to decentralized information will proportionally increase its operational capacity and policy effectiveness. This article challenges that linear assumption by introducing the analytical framework of Institutional Inversion. Drawing on the foundational theories of Hayek, Simon, Coase, and North, this paper argues that the fundamental constraint on institutional performance has shifted structurally. Historically, institutions were designed to aggregate scarce information; today, they operate in environments of information abundance where the primary bottleneck is no longer information acquisition, but the capacity to coordinate, filter, arbitrate, and prioritize inputs across organizational boundaries. We define this intermediate condition as the Coordination Bottleneck. Existing paradigms, including State Capacity, Network Governance, Collaborative Governance, and Meta-Governance, explain how to build connections and steer hierarchies, but they fail to adequately explain the administrative paralysis that occurs when extreme connectivity dilutes organizational attention. When organizational perimeters become highly porous, the resulting flood of transboundary information degrades Institutional Coherence, leading to jurisdictional gridlock and policy fragmentation. To survive this structural tendency, institutions require robust Boundary Governance: formal administrative and cultural mechanisms designed to manage the membrane between competing mandates. By repositioning contemporary integration failures across public administration, emergency management, and interoperable data networks as empirical manifestations of this underlying theoretical condition, this paper provides a durable framework for understanding the limits of the administrative state. The defining challenge of governance in the twenty-first century is no longer the production of information, but the generation of institutional coherence under conditions of informational abundance.

title: Building on Rented Land: Platform Dependency, Trust Sequencing, and the Limits of User Agency on Social Media

detail.title: Building on Rented Land: Platform Dependency, Trust Sequencing, and the Limits of User Agency on Social Media
detail.abstract:
Social media platforms have become the primary commercial infrastructure for a generation of entrepreneurs in markets like Nigeria, where the platform serves at once as storefront, customer relationship, social proof, and trust signal. This paper introduces a problem it calls trust sequencing. The standard advice to own your audience by moving people onto email lists and owned channels is incomplete, because trust must first be built on social media platforms before it can be carried anywhere.

Extending Hirschman's (1970) exit, voice, and loyalty framework, it shows that on social media these are not independent alternatives but three responses conditioned by the same underlying dependency, which renders the appearance of choice illusory. Drawing on Zuboff (2019), Van Dijck (2013), and Gillespie (2018), the paper situates account suspension within a system of industrial moderation whose failures fall hardest on those most dependent on the platform for survival. It introduces a distinction between platform dependency and existential platform dependency and argues that the Nigerian context functions as a structural amplifier, where the near-total absence of regulatory recourse turns a wrongful suspension from a setback into the end of a business. Grounded in netnographic observation and first-party referral data from a digital product launch conducted by the author, it concludes that platforms democratise entry while monopolising exit.

title: AI Copilot for Content Creation: Resolving the Quantity-Quality Trade-Off on User-Generated Content Platforms
affiliations: , Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University, Harbin Institute of Technology, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University and Nankai Business School, Nankai University

detail.title: AI Copilot for Content Creation: Resolving the Quantity-Quality Trade-Off on User-Generated Content Platforms
detail.abstract: User-generated content (UGC) platforms face a persistent operational challenge: how to scale content operations and volume without diluting quality. Traditional demand-pull interventions, such as financial and non-financial incentives, stimulate participation but fail to expand creators' underlying, resourceconstrained creative capabilities, leaving this quantity-quality trade-off largely unresolved. This paper investigates whether an augmentation-mode generative AI process innovation-specifically, an AI copilot providing structural and expressive guidance while preserving human agency-can shift the content production frontier. Leveraging the introduction of an AI copilot on a large shopping recommendation platform in China, we study three questions: who adopts the tool, how adoption affects content quantity and quality, and through what mechanisms these effects arise. Using a tree-based machine learning model (CatBoost) paired with Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP), we uncover a dual-logic adoption mechanism spanning the capacity distribution: lower-capability creators adopt for structural compensation, whereas higher-capability creators adopt for process refinement and effort economization. Second, leveraging a synthetic difference-indifferences design integrated with coarsened exact matching, we demonstrate that process augmentation simultaneously increases both operational capacity (+24.9% in posting frequency and 156% in text depth) and downstream market performance (+9.58% in likes and +12.9% in favorites)-bypassing the quantity-quality degradation typical of automation-mode AI. Third, mechanism analyses reveal an asymmetric operational signature: performance gains are driven by a cross-domain exploration mechanism that lowers barriers to entry for unfamiliar product categories, whereas exploitation within established categories is confined to textual refinement. Finally, we document a persistent learning spillover effect in which human-AI collaboration enhances creators' unaided, manual operational capabilities over time. Our findings show that augmentative AI reshapes UGC behaviors by structurally relaxing execution constraints rather than merely manipulating effort incentives, offering novel operational insights for human-AI collaboration design, digital platform governance, and information intermediary performance.

title: PolisAI: Constitutional Orchestration with Structural Validation Gates for Enterprise Multi-AI Adoption -A Comprehensive Architectural Treatment

detail.title: PolisAI: Constitutional Orchestration with Structural Validation Gates for Enterprise Multi-AI Adoption -A Comprehensive Architectural Treatment

It does not report empirical research involving human subjects, animal subjects, patient data, clinical trial participants, or any data collected from individuals. No interviews, surveys, observational studies, or experiments involving people were conducted. Industry statistics cited in the paper (IBM 2025 CEO Study, MIT Project NANDA 2025, McKinsey 2025 State of AI, BCG 2024) are drawn from publicly released industry reports and are cited to their original publishers. No external funding, grant, sponsorship, or institutional support contributed to the research or preparation of this paper. The work was prepared as an academic architectural proposal at the author's own expense and time.

detail.abstract:
Enterprise AI requires constitutional orchestration with structural validation gates. Coordination of multiple AI subcomponents through engineering frameworks alone does not produce reliable enterprise outputs because no architectural mechanism enforces which AI contributions are accepted, how they are bounded, how they are decomposed for accountability, or how cascading failures are contained — a pattern documented by IBM's 2025 CEO study (25% ROI achievement on AI initiatives), MIT NANDA's 2025 "GenAI Divide" (95% of 300 deployments showing no measurable P&L impact), and McKinsey's 2025 State of AI (only about 39% reporting any enterprise-wide EBIT impact).

This paper proposes PolisAI, a constitutional orchestration architecture addressing the gap between policy frameworks (what AI should do) and orchestration frameworks (how AI is coordinated). It rests on three load-bearing mechanisms: (1) an evidence validation gate rejecting AI contributions without grounded references and mandating multi-AI cross-check for action-influencing outputs; (2) bounded propagation limiting any single AI subcomponent's influence to its declared parameter weight, with a conflict rule dampening contributions disagreeing with the curated reference layer; and (3) a decomposition discipline exposing each outcome's contributing workers and weights. A client-local privacy gateway mediates all external AI calls, keeping enterprise data, business logic, and sensitive context inside the client boundary except under explicit governance.

Supporting elements include a three-tier hierarchy, a seven-dimensional resource model, two-methodology governance, identity and separation-of-duties, reference-layer governance, audit-by-construction, a three-dimensional visibility requirement (information confidence, decision, outcome probability), categorical exclusions of high-stakes clinical and physical-control action execution, and six-mode failure-cascade containment.

The framework is mapped to fifty currently-visible enterprise AI challenges with explicit classification: 23 architecturally controlled, 20 structurally mitigated under documented residuals, and 7 out of architectural scope. The paper presents thirty-nine architectural commitments, validation-gate mechanics, orchestration logic, a compliance mapping against NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act, and ISO/IEC 42001, a minimum-conforming-implementation specification, prerequisites for adoption, illustrative mathematical formalization, and worked examples. The framework is a working academic architectural proposal; empirical evaluation of specific implementations is reserved for subsequent work.

title: Seeing the Future: How AI-Generated Future-State Visuals Shape Matching in Two-Sided Markets
affiliations: and The Chinese University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Seeing the Future: How AI-Generated Future-State Visuals Shape Matching in Two-Sided Markets
detail.abstract: Two-sided market platforms are increasingly deploying generative AI tools that transform latent future states into salient decision-relevant information. We study this phenomenon in the context of AI-generated future-state visuals on a large Chinese resale housing platform. Exploiting the platform's staggered rollout of AI Visual across major cities, we examine how this information-design intervention affects matching efficiency, transaction prices, and post-transaction satisfaction. We find that AI Visual significantly improves matching efficiency, reducing days on market by approximately 10% for buyers and 20% for sellers, and increases transaction prices by about 2.7%, consistent with improved seller-side and platform-side outcomes. The effects are more pronounced for poorly renovated properties, listings handled by low-performing agents, and properties in thicker markets. Mechanism analyses suggest that these effects are not explained by observable seller price-adjustment behavior. Instead, they are consistent with demand-side responses in which AI-generated visuals reduce information gaps about post-renovation potential, lower search effort, and facilitate faster convergence in buyers' valuation processes. However, these efficiency gains come with a tradeoff in matching quality: seller satisfaction increases, whereas buyer post-transaction satisfaction declines, consistent with expectation disconfirmation from stylized future-state representations. We further show that high-performing agents' expertise can mitigate this buyer-side backfire while preserving efficiency gains. Our findings highlight generative AI as a powerful information-design tool in two-sided markets: it can reduce demand-side frictions and improve short-run platform outcomes, but platforms must manage expectation formation through targeted deployment and complementary human expertise.

title: The Digital Euro at the Nexus of Payments Sovereignty, Consumer Adoption and Bank Intermediation: Design Requirements and Banking-Sector Implications of a Retail CBDC in the Euro Area
affiliations: Independent and

detail.title: The Digital Euro at the Nexus of Payments Sovereignty, Consumer Adoption and Bank Intermediation: Design Requirements and Banking-Sector Implications of a Retail CBDC in the Euro Area
detail.abstract:
The digital euro is intended to preserve access to public central bank money in an increasingly digital payments landscape while strengthening European payments sovereignty. Its potential success, however, will not depend on institutional legitimacy alone. The decisive question is whether it can offer consumers a discernible advantage over established payment instruments and be embedded in a viable intermediated model. This working paper therefore examines the design requirements under which a digital euro could generate tangible everyday utility while preserving the intermediation role of commercial banks.

Methodologically, the analysis draws on recent primary sources issued by European institutions and central banks, relevant academic literature and selected international CBDC case studies. The findings indicate that user-friendliness, privacy, online and offline functionality, a sufficiently broad acceptance network and robust integration into existing payment infrastructures are particularly important. At the same time, the digital euro gives rise to tensions between attractiveness and financial stability, privacy and regulatory traceability, and public infrastructure and private-sector innovation.

Holding limits, waterfall and reverse-waterfall mechanisms, and an appropriately calibrated remuneration model may help to mitigate these tensions. The digital euro can therefore contribute to European payments sovereignty, provided that it is designed as a user-oriented public infrastructure and underpinned by the functional and economically viable involvement of commercial banks.

title:
Why Emerging Markets Matter in a Multipolar World
Regionalization, Strategic Supply Chains, and the New Global Economy

detail.title:
Why Emerging Markets Matter in a Multipolar World
Regionalization, Strategic Supply Chains, and the New Global Economy
detail.abstract: Instead of a focus on efficiency and integration, globalization is being driven by resilience, localization and national security. Developing markets are consequently rising as key supply partners to developed countries in various sectors including the global supply chain, manufacturing, energy security and geopolitics. This paper analyzes various key factors triggering these global supply chain dynamics: first, the pandemic, which revealed fragility across the supply chain, second, intensifying U. S. -China competition over technology and markets, third, the Russia-Ukraine conflict's impact on supply chains, energy prices and security alliances, the reshaping of global trade through nearshoring and friend-shoring-which redirects investment away from traditional manufacturing hubs and China-and has positioned Latin America ( Mexico, Argentina, Colombia), Southeast Asia ( Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia), Eastern Europe ( Poland, Czech Republic, Romania, Slovakia), India and Africa as major recipients for production hubs and suppliers to developed markets, leveraging demographic advantages, extensive commodity supplies and increasing foreign direct investment, on the downside, several markets are held back by fragile institutions, corruption, limited industrial expertise, infrastructure shortages and the need for reform.
