title: Prepared Remarks of Jill Fisch, Saul A. Fox Distinguished Professor of Business Law University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School Before the Investor Advisory Committee of the Securities and Exchange Commission For a “Panel Discussion: Passive Index Funds and Shareholder Voting”
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School

detail.title: Prepared Remarks of Jill Fisch, Saul A. Fox Distinguished Professor of Business Law University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School Before the Investor Advisory Committee of the Securities and Exchange Commission For a “Panel Discussion: Passive Index Funds and Shareholder Voting”

publicationDetails.detailsText: U of Penn, Inst for Law & Econ Research Paper No. 26-09
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School, Law & Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This written statement reflects and expands on remarks delivered at a panel discussion of the Investor Advisory Committee of the Securities and Exchange Commission - “Passive Index Funds and Shareholder Voting” – on June 4, 2026. The statement focuses primarily on the growing use of voting choice programs by large asset managers as a mechanism for allocating shareholder voting rights in mutual funds and ETFs. While recognizing the practical and political pressures that have motivated asset managers to develop these programs, the statement argues that existing programs are deeply flawed. They offer retail investors a limited menu of proxy advisor-developed voting policies that are difficult to evaluate, potentially misleading in their presentation, and incapable of providing meaningful guidance on many of the most consequential corporate governance matters. As a result, voting choice frequently substitutes delegation to proxy advisory firms for delegation to fund managers without improving investor participation or informed decision-making.

The statement further contends that voting choice raises unresolved fiduciary questions, obscures the role of nonfinancial investor preferences in voting decisions, and fragments the voting power that has enabled institutional investors to engage effectively with portfolio companies. By dispersing votes among competing policies and advisors, voting choice weakens stewardship and reduces the capacity of large asset managers to monitor management and influence corporate governance outcomes. By disenfranchising funds and their investors completely, mirror voting has a similar detrimental effect.

The statement instead advocates greater engagement between fund managers and investors to enable fund managers to understand investor preferences and incorporate those preferences into fund voting policies. It concludes that efforts to constrain index fund voting power through voting choice, mirror voting, or abstention risk diminishing informed institutional stewardship while increasing the relative influence of other market participants, with uncertain consequences for the quality of corporate governance.

reference: International Center for Law & Economics, White Paper 2026-05-14; George Mason Law & Economics Research Paper No. 26-11
title: Regulatory Tripwires: How Arbitrary Thresholds Distort Financial Markets
affiliations: George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School

detail.title: Regulatory Tripwires: How Arbitrary Thresholds Distort Financial Markets

publicationDetails.detailsText: International Center for Law & Economics, White Paper 2026-05-14
George Mason Law & Economics Research Paper No. 26-11
publicationDetails.journalName: Antonin Scalia Law School, George Mason University, Law & Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The use of asset-size thresholds in U.S. financial regulation is widespread. The use of “thresholds” is often promoted for their simplicity, transparency, and administrability. This article examines how thresholds frequently distort firm behavior, undermine competition, and generate unintended consequences that diverge from their stated policy goals.

Dodd-Frank dramatically expanded the use of these “regulatory tripwires.” The law established systemic-risk tiers (originally at $50 billion, later revised to $100 billion and $250 billion), the CFPB’s $10 billion supervisory trigger for depository institutions and “larger participant” rules for nonbanks, and the Durbin Amendment’s $10 billion cutoff imposing price controls on debit-card interchange fees. Rather than aligning oversight with actual risk or consumer harm, these bright-line rules create sharp compliance cliffs. Banks respond rationally by slowing organic growth, fragmenting operations, restructuring balance sheets, and pursuing mergers to spread fixed compliance costs.

The article argues that poorly calibrated thresholds too often substitute for reasoned regulatory analysis, invite political rent-seeking, and expand in scope over time without deliberate policy review due to the absence of inflation indexing or periodic evaluation. It recommends repealing or reforming flawed thresholds—particularly the Durbin Amendment—replacing hard cliffs with graduated approaches, indexing remaining thresholds, and modernizing supervision through risk-based frameworks supported by real-time data analytics and advanced technology.

title: FoodAssist: An AI-Powered Chatbot for Navigating Food Insecurity Services -A Proposed Charitable Technology
affiliations: University of West Attica

detail.title: FoodAssist: An AI-Powered Chatbot for Navigating Food Insecurity Services -A Proposed Charitable Technology
detail.abstract: This paper proposes FoodAssist, an artificial intelligence chatbot designed to support individuals experiencing food insecurity by facilitating access to charitable food services. The system is conceptualized as a multi-platform tool accessible via mobile applications, web browsers, and SMS, enabling users to obtain real-time information about nearby soup kitchens, food banks, and municipal food support programs. Unlike traditional fragmented information systems, FoodAssist integrates service location, eligibility guidance, and emergency escalation into a unified conversational interface. The study is based exclusively on empirical food insecurity data from Eurostat/ELSTAT (2024), HFIAS field research (2025), and a national survey of 187 food support structures in Greece. A structured user flow is presented to demonstrate system functionality, followed by an evaluation of advantages and limitations. The findings suggest that AI-driven conversational systems may significantly reduce information barriers and improve access to food assistance, provided that they are implemented with human oversight and inclusive design principles.

title: The MANKAJ Framework: A Family-Rooted Model for Developing Human_Centered Global AI Governance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The MANKAJ Framework: A Family-Rooted Model for Developing Human_Centered Global AI Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I have independently conducted this study as part of my personal research. I have not received any funding, grants, or financial support from any organization or individual for this work. I declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: No human participants or patient data were involved in this study. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: I have independently conducted this study as part of my personal research. I have not received any funding, grants, or financial support from any organization or individual for this work. I declare no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has intensified global debates concerning ethics, governance, safety, and human alignment. Existing AI governance approaches are often rooted in political, economic, legal, or technological paradigms that vary significantly across cultures and nations, limiting the emergence of a universally accepted human centered framework. This paper proposes the MANKAJ Framework, a family-rooted conceptual model for global AI governance grounded in the shared human institution of the family. The framework argues that while governments, ideologies, and markets differ, the family remains a universal social structure recognized across all civilizations, serving as a unique point of global consensus. Building upon this foundation, the paper identifies 22 “Family Roots” that represent the core conditions of human flourishing, dignity, safety, care, inclusion, and intergenerational continuity. These roots are synthesized through a conceptual governance funnel into five policy pillars: Inclusion & Voice, Protection & Safety, Privacy & Dignity, Agency & Growth, and Justice & Accountability. Furthermore, the paper introduces a three layer governance architecture categorized as Mankind Alignment (The Goal), Networked Knowledge (The Foundation), and Adaptive Judgement (The Mechanism), collectively forming the MANKAJ paradigm. This architecture is designed to connect collective human well being with context sensitive, ethical AI governance. Rather than presenting a finalized technical standard, this paper offers an exploratory conceptual foundation for developing more relational, inclusive, and vulnerability centered approaches to AI governance in the digital age. The framework aligns with broader emerging discussions around human-centered AI, relational ethics, inclusion, and responsible AI governance while proposing the family as a foundational and globally relatable governance unit. MANKAJ: Because the future of intelligence must be as compassionate as the family that created it, serving as the foundation for developing human centered global AI governance.

title: The Weighted Sequence Physical Channels and the Architecture of Pre-Commercial Trust in Complex B2B
affiliations: Fondazione ITS Meccatronica e Avionica

detail.title: The Weighted Sequence Physical Channels and the Architecture of Pre-Commercial Trust in Complex B2B
detail.abstract:
Contemporary B2B marketing has accelerated itself into a structural contradiction. Outreach sequences, automation platforms, and multichannel digital programmes have grown faster and more sophisticated, while purchasing decisions in complex B2B environments have simultaneously slowed, distributed across buying committees of unprecedented size, and moved substantially into the pre-commercial period that precedes any vendor contact. Into this contradiction, most marketing organisations have responded by accelerating further. This paper argues that acceleration is not the answer.

The Weighted Sequence proposes a multi-channel pre-commercial engagement architecture in which the analog touchpoint — a professionally produced, physically delivered piece of thought leadership — functions not as one of seven equivalent exposures prescribed by the Marketing Rule of Seven, but as the neurological anchor to which all other digital touchpoints attach and from which they derive their accumulated commercial weight. The argument rests on three convergent bodies of evidence. The first is neurobiological: fMRI research conducted by Millward Brown and the Centre for Experimental Consumer Psychology at Bangor University, and neuromarketing research conducted by True Impact for Canada Post, document that physical media activate emotional processing circuits — the retrosplenial cortex, the medial prefrontal cortex, the brain's default network — with a depth and durability that digital equivalents do not consistently reach. Physical media require 21% less cognitive effort to process, generate 70% higher brand recall, and produce motivation scores 20% higher than digital equivalents — a gap ten times the threshold researchers define as a reliable predictor of future behavioural change. The second body of evidence is commercial: Bain & Company's research establishing that over 80% of B2B buyers assemble a vendor shortlist before formal evaluation begins, and TrustRadius data showing that 71% of buyers ultimately purchase the first-ranked vendor on that list, define the pre-commercial window in which the Weighted Sequence is designed to operate. The third is strategic: Forrester data documenting that fewer than 20% of B2B marketers currently use physical channels creates a scarcity premium that compounds the neurobiological advantage of physical media with an attentional advantage unavailable in the saturated digital channel.

The paper draws on the neuroscience of trust from Damasio, Zak, and Rizzolatti; Fritjof Capra's systems thinking applied to account intelligence; Marshall McLuhan's theory of the medium as message; and fifteen years of account-based marketing practice in Italian manufacturing and industrial B2B contexts. It is the channel architecture dimension of the Marketing Lento framework, addressing not only what thought leadership to produce for a strategic account, but the medium through which to deliver it and the intelligence-driven timing logic that determines when.

The Weighted Sequence is a companion paper to Marketing Lento: The Art of Winning Only When It Matters (Regis, 2026) and Positioning as the Sole Solver in High-Value Accounts (Regis, 2026), and will be integrated into the forthcoming Marketing Lento volume as its channel architecture chapter.

Keywords: account-based marketing, Marketing Lento, analog channels, physical thought leadership, pre-commercial trust, Rule of Seven, neuromarketing, B2B complex sales, direct mail neuroscience, multichannel sequencing, dark funnel, shortlist formation, Italian manufacturing, buying committee, somatic markers

title: Version-Snapshot Stability of an AI-Presence Consistency Score

detail.title: Version-Snapshot Stability of an AI-Presence Consistency Score

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed by Samsung Electronics America in a corporate brand-creative and governance role. Samsung participates in the automotive sector as a component supplier rather than as a vehicle marque — through Harman International (in-vehicle audio and infotainment), Samsung SDI (battery cells), and Samsung Display (automotive displays) — but does not compete as an automotive brand, and no brand in the v0.22 registry scored here is Samsung-owned or -affiliated; a pre-acquisition conflict-of-interest screen confirmed this. The research is conducted independently through Third System and is self-funded; Samsung Electronics America had no role in the study's design, data, analysis, or reporting. A single pre-registered instrument was applied uniformly across all brands in both arms, and no brand was singled out for differential treatment.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The research uses public LLM APIs and standard prompt batteries; no human subjects, no personal data, no protected populations.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded.

detail.abstract: The AIAS™ (AI Availability Score) program operationalizes AI Availability as a measurable brand-growth layer alongside Mental and Physical Availability. Its Consistency component is presently scored by CPC = 1/(1+CV), the coefficient-of-variation transform locked in methodology version v1.7. v1.7 established that this score is not a mean-independent consistency construct — it is mechanically coupled to recall level (|ρ| with Presence = 0.77) — and did not adopt it; a mean-independent redefinition was escalated to v1.8. The present study sets construct validity aside to ask a logically prior question: is the v1.7 score even version-stable? A measure that moves with the model vintage on which it is taken cannot track a brand across time, whatever its construct status. A pre-registered two-arm design measured CPC on a fixed 24-brand automotive registry under two model-version snapshots — an older vintage and the current frontier — across a six-model panel, holding probe wording, registry, and frame battery identical and varying only the dated model identifier; the contrast was made deliberately maximal across model generations. Brand-mention extraction reused the prior coder verbatim (pre-registered); a pre-scoring spot-check confirmed symmetric extraction across arms. Rank-order stability cleared the registered threshold marginally (Spearman ρ = 0.708) but proved fragile under a pre-registered leave-one-provider-out analysis (ρ ranging 0.48–0.82), with instability concentrated in the gpt-4o→gpt-5.x jump. Magnitude stability was falsified (mean |ΔCPC| = 0.077, exceeding the 0.5·SD tolerance of 0.069), though with no net directional drift — version change reshuffles which brands read as consistent without shifting the overall level. The emerging-brand instability prediction was falsified: no brand crossed the recall floor between arms. The v1.7 CPC score is therefore at best partially and provider-dependently version-stable; version-fragility compounds the recall-coupling already identified in v1.7 as grounds for the v1.8 redefinition. The contribution is a characterization of the interim instrument, not a validation of it.

title: Digital Food Waste Monitoring System in a Ready-Meal Factory
affiliations: University of West Attica

detail.title: Digital Food Waste Monitoring System in a Ready-Meal Factory
detail.abstract: This paper examines a specific digital tool for food waste reduction: a hardware and software monitoring system implemented in a ready-meal factory. The analysis follows the case study material and focuses on how the system works in practice, how it records food waste in real time, how it identifies waste hotspots and how its data support managerial decisions. The theoretical framework connects food waste with food insecurity, sustainability and operations management. The main section then presents the workflow, data use, managerial benefits, limitations and conditions for successful implementation.

title: From Gamified Social Media Health Communication to Authentic Healthy Eating Behavior: Healthy-Eater Identity as a Mediating Pathway

detail.title: From Gamified Social Media Health Communication to Authentic Healthy Eating Behavior: Healthy-Eater Identity as a Mediating Pathway

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential competing interest was reported by the author.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study involved anonymous, non-invasive survey research with adult participants. Participation was voluntary and based on informed consent. Respondents were informed of the study purpose, eligibility criteria, and voluntary nature of participation before beginning the questionnaire. No personally identifying information was collected, and data were analyzed in aggregate form.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Social media health communication increasingly uses gamified cues, including challenges, streaks, badges, progress indicators, and achievement markers, to stimulate user engagement. Yet visible interaction with health content does not necessarily indicate sustained healthy eating behavior beyond the platform. Drawing on the Stimulus-Organism-Response framework, identity theory, and the Identity Activation Loop, this study tests one pathway through which exposure to gamified social media health communication may be associated with self-reported offline healthy eating consistency through healthyeater identity. Survey data were collected from 384 adult social media users in India and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling with bootstrapped mediation testing. Gamified health content exposure was positively associated with healthy-eater identity (β = .479, p < .001), and healthyeater identity was positively associated with self-reported offline healthy eating consistency (β = .478, p < .001). The indirect effect was significant (β = .228, 95% CI [.175, .284]), while the direct effect remained significant, indicating partial mediation. The model explained 23.0% of the variance in healthy-eater identity and 39.4% of the variance in self-reported offline healthy eating consistency. The findings suggest that gamified social media health communication is more strongly associated with offline healthy eating consistency when platform-facing engagement aligns with healthy-eater identity.

title: Provider-Asymmetric Consistency in AI Brand Availability A Pre-Registered Re-Analysis: Modest between-Provider Structure in CV-CPC Recall, and the Limits of a Beyond-Presence Gate under Recognition Saturation

detail.title: Provider-Asymmetric Consistency in AI Brand Availability A Pre-Registered Re-Analysis: Modest between-Provider Structure in CV-CPC Recall, and the Limits of a Beyond-Presence Gate under Recognition Saturation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is Director, Corporate Brand Creative and Governance at Samsung Electronics America. This study is a secondary re-analysis of data assembled in earlier phases (v0.19--v0.23); it introduces no new brand selection or data collection. Two of the five re-analyzed substrates intersect businesses owned by Samsung Electronics: audiophile headphones, a category that includes brands of Harman International (a Samsung subsidiary), and automotive, where Samsung interests include Harman automotive systems and Samsung SDI. The brand registries were fixed under the locked protocol of the original phases, scoring is fully automated against those registries, and the analysis reported here was pre-registered (tag `v0.33-prereg-r1`) before any scoring; the author's affiliation played no role in registry construction, scoring, or the resulting verdicts. Samsung Electronics had no role in the design, conduct, analysis, or reporting of this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable; no human subjects; public APIs and LLM prompts only.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded.

detail.abstract: AI Availability-the discoverability and representation of a brand in the outputs of large language models-has been proposed as a third layer of brand availability, complementing the Mental and Physical Availability of the Ehrenberg-Bass tradition. Within the AIAS TM (AI Availability Score) program, the Consistency component is operationalized as CV-CPC, a coefficient-of-variation statistic over per-model recall; a prior methodology lock found CV-CPC strongly presence-coupled (| = 0.77) and did not adopt it as a validated Consistency instrument. This pre-registered re-analysis tests, across five panel-uniform substrates (112 brands; a fixed six-model panel spanning three providers-Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google), whether the per-model recall structure underlying CV-CPC is systematically organized by provider, and whether any such organization exceeds the provider structure present in Presence (recognition). Between-provider organization of per-model recall is statistically robust but modest: the between-provider variance share exceeds its permutation null (p < 0.001) and survives all five leave-one-substrate-out refits, though its excess over a high small-group chance floor is small. The pre-registered Beyond-Presence gate met its criterion yet does not establish dissociation: binary recognition is saturated among recalled brands-carrying negligible between-provider variance-so the gate collapses onto the recall-asymmetry test rather than contrasting with Presence. This inverts the pre-registered directional prediction and reframes the gate's behavior as the study's principal methodological result: a Beyond-Presence contrast is uninformative wherever recognition is saturated. Provider rank-stability was uninformative as pre-registered, underpowered at five substrates. The study positions provider as a modest organizing factor in CV-CPC recall and bounds the conditions under which the AIAS Beyond-Presence gate can fire.

title: Adverse Selection and Product Variety

detail.title: Adverse Selection and Product Variety
detail.abstract: Most of the empirical adverse selection literature focuses on the impact on insurer pricing incentives. In contrast, this paper examines the impact of adverse selection on insurers' pricing and non-price behavior by exploiting the gradual implementation of risk adjustment from 2004 to 2007 in Medicare Advantage. Under this policy, the government reimburses private insurers proportional to the health risk of their enrollees. Using variation in the distribution of health risks across counties, I find that non-price characteristics respond to adverse selection. I also find that multi-product MA firms adjust the diversity of their portfolio of products in response to selection incentives.

title: Barrier to Import Batteries and Lead Poisoning in Bangladesh
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business, Stanford University and Stanford University

detail.title: Barrier to Import Batteries and Lead Poisoning in Bangladesh
detail.abstract:
Problem definition: This paper explores the public health impact of an import barrier that fosters a domestic circular battery economy in a developing country. 

Methodology/results: Bangladesh increased trade barriers on import of batteries in 2015, which resulted in an increase in domestic manufacturing of lead-acid batteries and recycling of used batteries and smelting of lead. Lead poisoning results in terminated pregnancies due to miscarriages or abnormal pregnancies. Therefore we leverage nationally-representative spatially-detailed data on pregnancies before and after the trade barriers on battery import, combined with geolocation of 276 battery related lead-emitting sites in Bangladesh, i.e., lead-acid battery manufacturers, used battery recyclers, and lead smelters. Our difference-in-differences analysis shows that after implementation of trade barriers on battery import, pregnant women residing within 5 km of a lead-emitting site experienced a 4-5 percentage point higher likelihood of terminated pregnancy than women living farther away. 

Managerial implications: Our results underscore the need to eliminate trade barriers that create a pollution-intensive domestic industry or to regulate the industry to mitigate the pollution. This is particularly important for the battery industry, which is growing in developing countries because of the demand and use of batteries in low carbon technologies such as electric vehicles.

title: Consumer Ethnocentrism on the Market for Local Products: Determinants of Consumer Behaviors
affiliations: University of Life Sciences in Lublin

detail.title: Consumer Ethnocentrism on the Market for Local Products: Determinants of Consumer Behaviors
detail.abstract: The aim of the study was to determine the attitudes and ethnocentric behaviors of consumers on the local food market. The survey also included consumers' purchasing channels, which helped determine the specifics of local product distribution. The criterion for classifying the respondent into the research sample was to indicate the economic motives of consumer ethnocentrism as a factor in the purchase decision. 1,009 correctly completed questionnaires were accepted for analysis. Descriptive statistics and the u Mann-Whitney test were used in the analyses. The results made it possible to determine the products appreciated by respondents, such as eggs, dairy products, and groats. local alcoholic beverages in the categories "local wines" and "craft beers" were appreciated more by men. The respondents had the lowest interest in oils produced locally. among the features with which consumers associate local food are producer identification, freshness, good taste, and affordability. consumers take advantage of short supply chains such as direct sales by the producer or take the opportunity to buy products at local events or thematic trips such as the culinary trail. consumers are able to accept a price increase of 10-15%, with larger increases they start looking for cheaper substitutes. in conclusion it was stated that the market for local products is a source of support for the local economy, therefore the authorities should create conditions for its development through undertaking appropriate measures promoting local products.

title: Vaccination Capacity, Supply-Side Standards, and Pandemic Resilience: Evidence from Brazil
affiliations: Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP and Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP

detail.title: Vaccination Capacity, Supply-Side Standards, and Pandemic Resilience: Evidence from Brazil

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by FGV Cidades.

detail.abstract: We study how heterogeneity in pre-existing vaccination infrastructure shaped immunization outcomes in Brazilian municipalities following a federal regulation that established minimum standards for vaccination rooms (RDC 197/2017). Exploiting cross-municipal variation in pre-regulation capacity in a panel of 5,570 municipalities from 2014 to 2023, we estimate event-study specifications and document three findings. First, the post-regulation period saw measurable convergence in installed capacity, of which a substantial share reflects continuation of pre-existing differential trajectories rather than discrete policy-induced adjustment. Second, pre-pandemic differences in capacity left no detectable footprint on coverage of tracer childhood vaccines. Third, during the COVID-19 pandemic, municipalities with greater pre-regulation capacity experienced significantly smaller declines in coverage-1.5 to 2.0 percentage points per standard deviation-with primary care infrastructure absorbing the acute 2020 shock and hospital networks absorbing the prolonged 2021 disruption. We interpret these state-contingent associations through a capacity-resilience framework: infrastructure with limited average-period returns generates option value under systemic stress. We discuss why this association cannot be attributed to vaccination capacity alone-approximately half of the baseline magnitude reflects state-level variation, while the remaining half operates within states-and what implications follow for the cost-benefit analysis of healthcare standards.

title: Structured Performance Geometry and Observability for Agentic AI: The SOSM-10 Framework

detail.title: Structured Performance Geometry and Observability for Agentic AI: The SOSM-10 Framework
detail.abstract: This paper develops a performance oriented formulation of the Structured Organizational State-Space Model (SOSM), a triadic dynamical framework characterizing organizational behavior across Representation (R), Constraint (C), and Execution (E) manifolds. While SOSM was originally conceived as a structural model of organizational stability, this work reframes it as a computable operator whose residual error yields a unified agent performance score. A single closed form metric is introduced, enabling continuous evaluation of agent effectiveness and efficiency without reliance on governance semantics. The formulation is integrated into a deployable R-C-E control pipeline with real time observability using Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboards. The resulting architecture demonstrates how theoretical constructs can be operationalized into production grade monitoring for agentic AI systems.

title: Financing Justice: Third-Party Funding in Arbitration and Its Implications for Access, Ethics, and Transparency in Global and African ADR Systems

detail.title: Financing Justice: Third-Party Funding in Arbitration and Its Implications for Access, Ethics, and Transparency in Global and African ADR Systems

declarations.funderStatement: This is an independent research made by the author!

detail.abstract: The increasing cost and complexity of arbitration have generated renewed interest in innovative financing mechanisms that enhance access to justice while preserving the integrity of dispute resolution. Third-party funding (TPF) has emerged as one of the most significant developments in this regard, enabling financially constrained parties to pursue meritorious claims through external financing arrangements. Under TPF, an independent funder finances all or part of the costs of arbitration in exchange for a share of the proceeds of a successful award. While this model has gained considerable acceptance in major arbitration jurisdictions such as the United Kingdom, Singapore, and Hong Kong, its implications for emerging arbitration markets, particularly in Africa, remain an evolving area of legal discourse. This article examines TPF through both doctrinal and economic lenses, analyzing its role in enhancing access to justice, facilitating risk allocation, and promoting efficiency in arbitration. It interrogates the ethical and procedural concerns associated with funding arrangements, including conflicts of interest, disclosure obligations, funder influence, and the broader concern regarding the commercialization of dispute resolution. Drawing on comparative regulatory frameworks, leading arbitral decisions, and emerging institutional rules, the article evaluates how different jurisdictions have sought to balance innovation with procedural integrity. Particular attention is given to the Nigerian context, especially the impact of the Arbitration and Mediation Act 2023 (AMA 2023), which recognizes the legality of third-party funding and aligns Nigeria with global arbitration trends. The article argues that while TPF presents significant opportunities for strengthening arbitration in Africa, its long-term effectiveness depends on the development of clear regulatory frameworks that promote transparency, accountability, and fairness.

title: Organisational support for older nurses’ continuation of practice: A qualitative interpretive descriptive study
affiliations: Auckland University of Technology, Auckland University of Technology, Auckland University of Technology and Auckland University of Technology

detail.title: Organisational support for older nurses’ continuation of practice: A qualitative interpretive descriptive study
detail.abstract: Background: Global population ageing is increasing pressure on healthcare systems, contributing to workforce shortages and the loss of experienced practitioners as many approach retirement age. Retaining older nurses is essential because they provide critical clinical expertise, mentorship, workforce stability, and continuity of patient care in increasingly strained healthcare systems. Yet, little is known about how older nurses perceive organisational support for their continuation of practice.Objective: To explore older practising nurses’ perceptions of organisational support, and to understand how organisational representatives perceive organisational support offered to older nurses.Design: A qualitative interpretive descriptive study was conducted using two datasets: older practising nurses and organisational representatives. A convergent design was used.Methods: Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews and analysed using the thematic analysis approach.Results: Thirteen older practising nurses and four organisational representatives participated in semi-structured interviews. All except one of the nurses were female, and most were aged 61–70 years. Organisational representatives recruited were nurse leaders working at frontline, operational or strategic levels within the organisation.Four themes were identified from the nurses: Tensions in continuation of practice, with sub-themes health decline, caring responsibilities, and stigmatisation; Drivers for continuation of practice, with sub-themes passion for care, financial incentives, and positivecollegial relationships; The experience of being an older nurse in practice, with sub-themes feeling valued and cared for, feeling unseen, and navigating technological challenges; and Retirement from a large organisation, with sub-themes support forpart-time practice, pension advice, and fear of leaving an empty spot.Three themes were identified from organisational representatives: Perceived complexities in continuation of practice; Support at interpersonal level; and Support at the organisational level.Conclusion: Challenges at intrapersonal, interpersonal, and organisational levels were identified that may hinder older nurses’ continued practice despite their strong commitment. These included self-internalised ageism, age-based stereotypes perpetuated by managers, and organisational policies and practices that disadvantage older nurses. Additionally, gaps were noted in organisational support for part-time work, pension advice, and succession planning as older practising nurses prepare for retirement. Organisational representatives advocated for organisationally driven interventions that promote wellbeing, support career planning, and foster inclusive workplace cultures. These findings highlight the need for healthcare organisations to move beyond recognising the value of older nurses toward implementing sustained, age-inclusive strategies that actively support their continued participation in the workforce.

title: DSA Risk Assessment -Social Media Mental Harm Automatic Annotation Case Study
affiliations: Jagiellonian University in Krakow, Carnegie Mellon University, Carnegie Mellon University, Jagiellonian University, Jagiellonian University in Krakow, Jagiellonian University in Krakow and Jagiellonian University in Krakow - Faculty of Law and Administration

detail.title: DSA Risk Assessment -Social Media Mental Harm Automatic Annotation Case Study

declarations.funderStatement: The research leading to these results has received funding from the National Science Centre, Poland, project no. 2022/45/B/HS5/01419, titled “Consumer Law and the Attention Economy.”

detail.abstract: The EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) requires Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) to identify and mitigate systemic risks to users' mental well-being through annual risk assessments. However, analyzing these lengthy, heterogeneous reports is labor-intensive for regulators and researchers. This study evaluates the capability of four LLMs (GPT 5.2, GPT5mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Claude Opus 4.5) to automatically annotate mental-healthrelated content in DSA risk reports. Using a human-annotated benchmark of 14 VLOP risk assessments from 2023-2024, we developed a hierarchical annotation schema distinguishing between risk types (internal/external) and mitigation measures (platform-level/external). Our asynchronous, zero-shot annotation pipeline reduced processing time from approximately four hours of human labor per document to under two minutes. Results show Claude Opus achieved the highest sentence-level coverage (56-65%), though all models exhibited systematic biases, such as over-triggering on general risk categories, while under-detecting specific mitigation measures. Although not yet suitable for fully automated compliance assessment, the proposed pipeline establishes a potential foundation for future research on computational oversight and empirical analysis of platform governance under the DSA framework.

title:
Unified Scientific Architecture of the Civilization Engineering Series:
A Computational Governance Framework for Adaptive Engineering Project Intelligence
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
Unified Scientific Architecture of the Civilization Engineering Series:
A Computational Governance Framework for Adaptive Engineering Project Intelligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing financial interests, commercial affiliations, or personal relationships influenced the conceptual development, interpretation, or presentation of this research. The work represents an independent scholarly and theoretical contribution.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research is theoretical and methodological in nature and does not involve human participants, patient data, animal experimentation, or identifiable personal data requiring institutional ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: This article presents the Unified Scientific Architecture of the Civilization Engineering Series as a master research architecture for adaptive engineering project governance. It positions Project Civilization, AEGIS, Beyond Project Management, Engineering Project Governance Intelligence, CIOS, CI-DF, SCIM, and SAYTCO as layers of one research program rather than as disconnected labels. The central problem is that large engineering projects are usually governed through documents, schedules, dashboards, contracts, and reports while their deeper governance state can deteriorate through weak evidence, delayed decisions, propagation pressure, cash-flow stress, interface turbulence, and insufficient adaptive capacity. The article contributes a reviewer-facing architecture that defines the program ontology, formal propositions, construct hierarchy, mathematical grammar, normalization logic, validation pathway, falsifiability gates, publication dependency map, maturity model, claim boundaries, and research roadmap. Its contribution is not universal empirical proof; it is a disciplined theory-building and design-science architecture that makes the series navigable, falsifiable, progressively calibratable, and ready for repository deposit and later journal development. The manuscript serves as the canonical architectural gateway of the Civilization Engineering research series and the foundational reference for derivative construct papers.

title: From Google to Generative AI: A Trend Study on the Digital Visibility of Accommodation Facilities in Foz Do Iguaçu, Brazil (2021-2026)

detail.title: From Google to Generative AI: A Trend Study on the Digital Visibility of Accommodation Facilities in Foz Do Iguaçu, Brazil (2021-2026)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships that could have influenced this study. The research was conducted independently, without consulting or contractual relationships with any of the hospitality businesses analyzed.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study analyzed publicly available AI-generated responses to queries about hospitality businesses in Foz do Iguaçu, Brazil. No human participants were recruited or observed. No personal data was collected. Ethics committee approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. Data collection costs were self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract: This study aims to analyze the digital presence of accommodation facilities in Foz do Iguaçu within generative search engines in 2026, as a continuation of prior research that documented the sector's invisibility in Google organic search in 2021 (Telles & Xavier, 2021). Adopting a trend study design with two parallel experiments, three queries were submitted to three generative AI engines-Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, and OpenAI GPT-in two distinct formulations: structured natural language (E1) and the exact keyword used in Google in 2021 (E2), totaling 108 queries. Results indicate partial convergence in E1: Belmond Hotel das Cataratas was cited in 16 of 18 hotel queries. The E1 vs. E2 comparison revealed the Query Sensitivity Analysis (QSA) phenomenon: citability in generative AI engines is not a stable property-it varies as a function of the engine consulted and the query formulation. GPT demonstrated greater robustness to prompt design; Claude showed high sensitivity, producing establishment sets with minimal overlap between E1 and E2. The study concludes that robust AI presence is rare, observed only in establishments with high cross-source textual footprint across diverse sources. The data additionally revealed a second phenomenon, termed ENDEX (Endorsement Index): models do not list neutrally-they qualify and endorse to varying degrees by engine, the subject of a parallel paper in development.

title: Changes in Purchase Prices and Efficiency vs. Production Profitability in Agriculture: Analytical and Empirical Approach
affiliations: National Research Institute (PIB) - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI) and National Research Institute (PIB) - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI)

detail.title: Changes in Purchase Prices and Efficiency vs. Production Profitability in Agriculture: Analytical and Empirical Approach
detail.abstract: The article discusses the issue of the impact of changes in purchase prices of an agricultural product on production profitability in agriculture, and more precisely with respect to agricultural producers on a given agricultural product market (in a given sector) in an analytical and model approach. The logic of formal deductive reasoning is then illustrated and verified empirically. The authors' own analytical description of the relationship determining changes in the level of production profitability for agricultural producers, with a particular emphasis on the change in the purchase price, is in fact the goal and added value of the article. It enables the identification of dependencies resulting from market laws that affect changes in production profitability. In particular, the authors present the influence of mutual relationships between changes in the purchase price level and the purchase volume on revenue, and thus production profitability. The article has a theoretical and cognitive and, to some extent, methodological message. The reasoning in the article is carried out in terms and at the level of generality appropriate for microeconomics and the theory of agricultural economics as well as a given product market for agricultural producers.

title:
Latent Systemic Fragility: Modeling Technical Debt as Propagating Risk in Financial Infrastructure
 A Conceptual Framework with the Technical Debt Risk Index (TDRI) for Quantifying Systemic Risk in Regulated Enterprise Environments
affiliations: TATA Consultancy Services, Maharshi Dayanand University (MDU) and Visvesvaraya National Institute of Technology (VNIT) - Visvesvaraya National Institute of Technology

detail.title:
Latent Systemic Fragility: Modeling Technical Debt as Propagating Risk in Financial Infrastructure
 A Conceptual Framework with the Technical Debt Risk Index (TDRI) for Quantifying Systemic Risk in Regulated Enterprise Environments

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. All three authors contributed to the conceptualization, methodology, and manuscript preparation as described in the Author Contributions section. No organizational or institutional affiliations have influenced the study design, analysis, or interpretation of results.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or animal subjects. It is a theoretical and computational modeling study based on publicly documented financial infrastructure failures and synthetic simulation data. No ethics approval was required. All data sources used (regulatory reports, published incident analyses, and simulated datasets) are either publicly available or generated by the authors without identifying personal information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not‑for‑profit sectors. The work was conducted as independent research by the authors, without financial or institutional support that could affect its objectivity.

detail.abstract:
Modern financial institutions rely on deeply interconnected digital infrastructures where legacy systems, real-time data platforms, and AI engines support critical operations. While technical debt is often managed as a localized engineering issue, its operational impact propagates through system dependencies. In regulated environments, this debt manifests as cascading failures during periods of high workload or regulatory stress. Current research focuses primarily on the code or component layer, leaving the systemic risks inherent in financial infrastructure largely unaddressed. 

This paper introduces Latent Systemic Fragility (LSF), a framework that models technical debt as a hidden, propagating risk. The LSF framework is built on three core premises: latent accumulation, propagation dynamics, and trigger-induced manifestation. We operationalize this through a three-layer model covering the Component, Dependency, and Regulatory layers. 

To quantify these risks, we propose the Technical Debt Risk Index (TDRI). The TDRI is a composite metric that integrates Criticality (CS), Propagation (PS), and Regulatory Sensitivity (RS), allowing institutions to calibrate risk according to their specific tolerance levels. We validate the LSF framework by applying it to a representative banking ecosystem and analyzing documented failure patterns, including the 2012 Knight Capital incident. Our findings demonstrate that the TDRI effectively identifies high-risk propagation paths before failure occurs. We conclude by discussing the governance implications for financial institutions and proposing a research agenda for large-scale empirical validation.

title: Burnout and Patient Safety Errors in Swedish Healthcare: A Cross-Level Prospective Study
affiliations: Karolinska Institutet, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Linkoping University, University of London - Birkbeck College, Karolinska Institutet, Karolinska Institutet and Karolinska Institutet

detail.title: Burnout and Patient Safety Errors in Swedish Healthcare: A Cross-Level Prospective Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The Longitudinal Occupational Health Survey for Health Care Occupations in Sweden was approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority [Ethical review numbers 2022-03105-01, 2023-04100-02, 2024-00822-02]. All the study participants provided consent to participate and publication when they logged in to the web survey or completed the paper survey.
declarations.funderStatement: This article was funded by the Swedish Research Council [grant number: 2022–00806].

detail.abstract:
Background: Burnout among healthcare professionals has been linked to patient safety risks, yet evidence relies predominantly on self-reported error measures. This study examined associations between self-rated burnout complaints and register-based hospital-level patient safety errors (PSEs).

Methods: Individual-level survey data from the Longitudinal Occupational Health survey for HealthCare Sweden (2023) were linked to hospital-level PSE data from the Swedish National Patient Register (2023–2024), across 2,626 healthcare professionals in 62 hospitals. Burnout complaints were categorized as non-burnout, at-risk, or burned-out. PSEs included misadventures during surgical and medical care, medical device-related adverse incidents, delayed complications, and nosocomial conditions. Negative binomial regression with hospital-cluster-robust standard errors tested direct associations, year-to-year PSE moderation by burnout complaints, and profession-specific differences.  

Findings: At-risk prevalence was 7·2%, and burned-out 4·4%. Burnout complaints were not directly associated with higher PSEs. Individuals classified as burned-out showed a stronger association between their hospital's 2023 and 2024 PSE counts than non-burnout individuals. For medical device-related complications, burned-out individuals showed a 20% stronger year-to-year carryover per 10 prior errors, particularly among physicians (18%). For delayed complications, burned-out nurse assistants showed a 33% stronger carryover.

Interpretation: Burnout complaints have no direct association with increased PSEs but may intensify existing error patterns at the organizational level, with professional variations. Rather than an isolated cause, burnout complaints appear to interact with role-specific responsibilities and organizational routines, suggesting that patient safety requires interventions should address conditions shaping both burnout and error persistence.

title: Resolving Labour Disputes in the Gig Economy: Can Online Dispute Resolution Bridge the Gap Between Platform Workers and Traditional Labour Justice?
affiliations: and Jamia hamdard, Hamdard Institute of Legal Studies and Research

detail.title: Resolving Labour Disputes in the Gig Economy: Can Online Dispute Resolution Bridge the Gap Between Platform Workers and Traditional Labour Justice?
detail.abstract:
The rapid growth of the gig economy has transformed the nature of employment relationships, creating new forms of work that often fall outside the scope of traditional labour protections and dispute resolution mechanisms. Platform-based workers associated with ride-hailing, food delivery, freelance and digital service platforms frequently face issues relating to unfair termination, non-payment of wages, algorithmic penalties, lack of social security, opaque rating systems and arbitrary deactivation of accounts. However, existing labour dispute resolution frameworks in India remain largely designed for conventional employer-employee relationships, leaving gig and platform workers with limited access to timely, affordable and effective remedies.

This paper examines whether Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) can emerge as a practical and accessible mechanism for resolving labour disputes in the gig economy. It analyses the suitability of conciliation, mediation, arbitration and hybrid ADR models in addressing the unique concerns of platform workers, particularly where disputes arise across jurisdictions, involve high-volume low-value claims or require urgent resolution. The paper further studies the limitations of existing labour adjudication under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the Code on Social Security, 2020 and the emerging labour codes in addressing platform-based disputes.

The paper adopts a comparative approach by examining ODR frameworks and gig worker protections in jurisdictions such as the United Kingdom, the European Union and California. Particular attention is paid to recent judicial developments concerning worker classification, platform accountability and digital labour rights. It also explores the role of artificial intelligence, automated decision-making and algorithmic management in creating workplace disputes, while assessing whether ODR mechanisms can provide procedural flexibility without compromising due process, transparency or fairness.

The paper argues that India requires a specialised ODR framework for gig and platform workers that combines mediation, digital conciliation and limited appellate review to ensure quick and affordable justice. It proposes the establishment of sector-specific labour ODR platforms, mandatory pre-litigation mediation for platform disputes, standardised grievance redressal systems and statutory safeguards against biased algorithmic decisions. By situating gig work within the broader future of labour regulation, this paper seeks to contribute to the evolving discourse on ADR, labour rights and digital justice in India.

title: Adaptive Role Identity Alignment (ARIA): A Mechanism Theory of Discretionary Action Under Ambiguity

detail.title: Adaptive Role Identity Alignment (ARIA): A Mechanism Theory of Discretionary Action Under Ambiguity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the development of this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This manuscript is a conceptual theory paper and did not involve human participants, human subjects research, or the collection of identifiable data. Institutional Review Board approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Modern organizations increasingly depend on adaptive performance under conditions of ambiguity, uncertainty, and decentralized decision-making. Yet even highly capable and motivated individuals often hesitate, rigidly comply, diverge, or break down when discretionary action is required. Existing theories of identity, motivation, engagement, and sensemaking explain who individuals are, why they act, and how they interpret situations, but they do not specify the mechanism through which interpreted role demands become psychologically authorized as discretionary action under uncertainty.

This manuscript introduces Adaptive Role Identity Alignment (ARIA), a mechanism-based theory of discretionary role engagement under ambiguity. ARIA proposes that discretionary action emerges through a sequential appraisal process in which Identity Standards and Interpreted Role Meaning are reconciled to produce a state of alignment functioning as a threshold condition for Regulatory Choice. Individuals do not select higher-agency forms of action as a function of motivation or formal authority alone; they do so only when identity-meaning coherence exceeds a critical level of psychological authorization.

ARIA makes seven primary theoretical contributions. First, it identifies the Identity-Meaning Appraisal Process as the missing mechanism that links sensemaking, identity, and discretionary action. Second, it introduces threshold logic as the governing architecture of adaptive regulation, explaining why behavioral change emerges discontinuously rather than proportionally. Third, it distinguishes lag misalignment from forward misalignment, generating different behavioral signatures and organizational risks from structurally similar conditions of identity-role incoherence. Fourth, it identifies the Empowerment Paradox, predicting that increasing structural agency under sub-threshold alignment amplifies divergence rather than Disciplined Initiative, directly falsifying autonomy-based motivational accounts. Fifth, it formalizes Identity Hysteresis as a source of temporal path dependence explaining why recovery from sustained misalignment is structurally asymmetric and slower than deterioration. Sixth, it specifies predictive asymmetry as a central diagnostic principle: superficially similar behavioral outcomes may emerge from fundamentally different appraisal, alignment, agency, or hysteresis pathways requiring different interventions. Seventh, it reframes organizational failure as a problem of degraded discretionary authorization rather than motivational, dispositional, or competence deficit.

ARIA specifies six regulatory modes within an alignment-agency matrix, derives sixteen formal propositions and eighteen discriminating empirical predictions, identifies seven boundary conditions, and develops a diagnostic and intervention architecture for studying adaptive regulation under ambiguity. The theory generates predictions that are distinct from those of self-determination theory, regulatory focus theory, person-environment fit, and proactive behavior frameworks. More broadly, ARIA proposes that organizational deterioration often develops beneath observability, through the latent degradation of authorization conditions, before threshold crossings produce a sudden, visible behavioral collapse. The theory is positioned to inform research across military operations, healthcare, emergency response, leadership development, institutional transformation, and other high-consequence organizational environments where adaptive discretionary action is essential.
