title: Cognitive Amplification and Intergenerational Cooperation in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: Cognitive Amplification and Intergenerational Cooperation in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. The analysis presented in this study reflects the author’s independent research and professional observations regarding artificial intelligence, cognitive systems, and intergenerational knowledge interaction.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human subjects, clinical experimentation, patient data, or personally identifiable information requiring institutional ethics approval. The paper is based exclusively on publicly available data sources, published reports, theoretical literature, and analytical interpretation.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was conducted independently as part of the author’s ongoing research activities in artificial intelligence, cognitive systems, knowledge management, and technological transformation.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the transformative effects of generative artificial intelligence on knowledge creation, professional productivity, and intergenerational collaboration. Drawing on current empirical data-including Microsoft's AI Diffusion Report (2025), ITU global telecommunications statistics, and GSMA Intelligence projections-we identify a fundamental paradox: while AI adoption is numerically dominated by younger cohorts (ages 16-24: over 60% weekly usage rate), the cognitive amplification effect of AI tools appears strongest among professionals with accumulated domain expertise. We argue that AI functions not merely as a productivity instrument but as a cognitive prosthetic that multiplies existing knowledge structures. We further distinguish knowledge from thinking: AI can store and retrieve codified knowledge, but cannot reproduce the tacit dimension-the understanding of exceptions, anomalies, contextual judgment, and long-term consequences that constitutes the deepest value of experienced practitioners. Critically, we also note that AI amplifies errors as readily as it amplifies insight: outdated mental models, when accelerated by AI tools, become more structured and scalable mistakes. We contend that the industrial paradigm of narrow specialization is yielding to interdisciplinary synthesis as the primary value-generating competency. Finally, we propose intergenerational cognitive cooperation-a deliberate alliance between the adaptive speed of younger professionals and the systemic depth of experienced practitioners, mediated by AI as a cross-generational translator-as the organizational form best suited to AI-era complexity. The analysis draws on STS frameworks, tacit knowledge theory (Polanyi; Nonaka and Takeuchi), and the sociology of expertise (Collins and Evans).

title: Polish Finishers from Danish Piglets: Uncontrolled Transformation of Pig Industry in Poland
affiliations: Warsaw School of Economics (SGH)

detail.title: Polish Finishers from Danish Piglets: Uncontrolled Transformation of Pig Industry in Poland
detail.abstract: Only 20 years ago, Poland was self-sufficient in pig production, being one of the key players in the European pig market. Since then a growing specialization of Poland in pig finishing and meat processing has been observed, while the domestic production of piglets has declined. As a consequence, Poland has lost its self-sufficiency in pig production and become strongly dependent on imports of piglets, mainly from Denmark. The aim of this paper is to summarize the evolution of the Polish pig industry and specify the main determinants of the Polish imports of Danish piglets. The results of the estimates using the vector error correction model (VECM) show that the volume of the Polish imports of piglets from Denmark may be explained by a degree of specialization of Poland in pig finishing, the phase of pig cycle, and the competitiveness of Polish pork. The results may be helpful in understanding the evolution of the Polish pig industry and its growing dependence on imports of piglets.

title: Unlocking The Potential of the European Union Quality Schemes for Polish Regional and Traditional Food Products
affiliations: Warsaw University of Life Sciences, Warsaw University of Life Sciences and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Unlocking The Potential of the European Union Quality Schemes for Polish Regional and Traditional Food Products

keywords: Protected Designation of Origin and Protected Geographical Indications

detail.abstract:
The main aim of the study was to identify current problems encountered by the Polish producers of products registered under the PDO, PGI, and TSG labels and develop a set of recommendations that may support the development of the market of FQS products in Poland. The study findings showed that many factors are disrupting the functioning of the Polish market of FQS products and are related to product specificities, market relevance, supply chain governance, legitimacy, and law enforcement. The majority of products is characterized by a low value added, which makes it difficult to distinguish them on the market and therefore protect against counterfeit. There are also products with greater value added, but the lack of farmers' collective action reduces the potential effect that could result from the economy of scale. Furthermore, a limited number of certified producers and small cultivation areas constraint the use of effective marketing strategies, hindering producers' ability to gain more visibility for their produce. Consequently, Polish FQS producers cannot create more profitable market niches, often selling their certified products at regular market prices without the expected price premium. Moreover, FQS labels are also not recognized well by consumers, which indicates a serious problem of information asymmetry in the value chain. In order to improve the FQS sales in Poland, a joint commitment of the public administration agencies and producers is necessary in terms of providing support to producers in the process of developing applications, introducing the
system for monitoring FQS distribution and reporting counterfeits, creating an umbrella association of certified producers acting on behalf of all the participants of the system. Moreover, producers are encouraged to increase the scale of production, introduce common packaging and joint promotional activities, as well as joint sales and distribution in order to avoid producer–producer competition and to strengthen producers bargaining position in the food supply chain

title: Arbitration Risks in Multi-Entity Arrangements: Strategic Implications for Commercial Transactions in Nigeria
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Arbitration Risks in Multi-Entity Arrangements: Strategic Implications for Commercial Transactions in Nigeria
detail.abstract:
In an increasingly interconnected commercial landscape, arbitration has emerged as the dispute resolution mechanism of choice, not only within Nigeria but across cross-border transactions where neutrality, enforceability, and speed are paramount. For investors and multinational actors, arbitration offers a level of predictability that traditional litigation often struggles to provide, particularly in complex, multi-party and multi-jurisdictional arrangements.

However, as commercial structures evolve, often involving layered corporate groups, special purpose vehicles (“SPVs”), and affiliated entities, a recurring and commercially significant question continues to arise: can a party that did not formally sign a contract nonetheless be bound by its arbitration clause and the resulting award?

The Supreme Court’s recent decision in EMERGING MARKETS TELECOMMUNICATIONS SERVICES LIMITED v. AFDIN VENTURES LIMITED & Ors,[1] (the “Emerging Markets Case”) provides important clarity on this issue. In reaffirming key principles of arbitration, the Court adopted a commercially grounded approach that prioritises substance over form in determining the scope of parties bound by arbitral proceedings. Notably, the Court also demonstrated a pragmatic willingness to move beyond strict procedural constraints, recognising that procedural compliance bearing on the Court’s jurisdiction, although critical, should not defeat the resolution of an otherwise substantive and commercially significant dispute where the interests of justice so require, and the impropriety is amenable to be cured by the Court’s inherent powers.

This decision is significant for investors, corporate groups, and contractual counterparties, whether directly bound by the formal contract giving rise to the arbitration, or so intimately intertwined with its performance, as it expands the circumstances under which non-signatories may be bound by arbitral outcomes and reinforces the finality of such awards in Nigeria, subject only to the limited and well-defined statutory grounds for setting them aside.[2]

This article examines the Court’s reasoning, its alignment with international arbitration principles, and the practical implications for structuring high-stake commercial transactions and managing dispute resolution risk in Nigeria.

title: Financing Transformative Search: Runway, Control, and Frontier Innovation
affiliations: University of Minho - Economic Policies Research Unit (NIPE)

detail.title: Financing Transformative Search: Runway, Control, and Frontier Innovation
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of financing and governing transformative search: costly search for a transformative opportunity whose timing, payoff, and implementation are uncertain. The central object is the runway-attainability wedge ∆x , the gap between desired runway and the runway that can be financed while preserving authority over search. The decomposition separates this wedge into financing-frontier and governance shortfalls. Liquidity is valuable because it buys discovery time and, after discovery, implementation capacity. Search raises pledgeable upside by increasing opportunity arrival, but it also burns cash, so fixed claims are compatible with positive runway only over an intermediate range. Debt therefore has no one-sided implication for search: it can create overhang and implementation frictions, but it can also intensify search when higher burn makes delay more costly. When outside ownership is capped, financing changes real policy: controllers may use more debt, underfund runway, or use back-loaded non-voting claims that avoid coupon burn and voting dilution but reduce residual implementation payoff. The decision criterion is whether a financing architecture preserves attainable runway and search incentives, not how much capital it raises. Frontier AI motivates the setting, but the framework applies to difficult-to-pledge transformative opportunities more broadly.

title: Can India Replace China in U.S. Electronics Trade? A Shock Model Analysis of Computer, Electronic, and Optical Equipment Sector (HS-26)
affiliations: University of Tehran, University of Tehran and

detail.title: Can India Replace China in U.S. Electronics Trade? A Shock Model Analysis of Computer, Electronic, and Optical Equipment Sector (HS-26)
detail.abstract: The trade dynamics among the United States, China, and India have become increasingly complex and strategically significant within the global economy, particularly amid intensifying U.S.-China trade tensions. This study employs the Leontief Input-Output model (1936), implemented through the shock simulation framework developed by Dehghani (2023), to assess India's potential to substitute China in U.S. trade relations, focusing on the computer, electronic, and optical equipment sector (HS-26). Three shock scenarios, categorized as low (10-30%), medium (40-60%), and high (70-100%), are simulated to reveal patterns of economic interdependence among the three economies. The results reveal that India cannot fully substitute China in HS-26; however, it could achieve replacement in HS-26 by strongly focusing on IT and other information services sector (HS-62T63), which is closely linked to HS-26. While India's growing presence in global electronics is notable, the United States should pursue a broader diversification strategy, engaging partners such as Mexico, Taiwan, and South Korea alongside India to mitigate trade shocks and enhance supply chain resilience.

title: Cost Minimisation and Conditional Factor Demand in Ghanaian Commercial Banking: A Transcendental Logarithmic (Translog) Cost Function Approach

detail.title: Cost Minimisation and Conditional Factor Demand in Ghanaian Commercial Banking: A Transcendental Logarithmic (Translog) Cost Function Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The Author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses only aggregate and publicly available secondary data. No human subjects, personal data, or confidential supervisory information were used. Institutional ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: In this paper, a translog cost function is estimated simultaneously with factor cost share equations using equation-by-equation OLS based on data of ten Ghanaian commercial banks for 2013-2023 (105 firmyears observations). Using the intermediation model framework and Shephard's lemma, the analysis identifies the conditional factor demand functions, Allen-Uzawa substitution elasticities, and Ray scale economies index. Four main empirical findings merge. First, Ghanaian banks show significant economies of scale: the RSE index of 0.399 indicates that double-output expansion will lead to only 39.9 percent increase in costs. Second, there's a monotonic relationship between scale economics and size, as RSE decreases from 0.448 for the asset-size smallest quartile to 0.353 for the largest; this trend intensified following the reforms of Bank of Ghana in 2017-2018 (from 0.415 before reform to 0.387 after reform; χ² = 13.949, p<0.001). Third, capital and labor are Allen substitutes (σ₁₂ = 0.943), indicating that technological development results in digital labor replacement, typical for Sub-Saharan Africa. Fourth, there's 2.1 percent growth per year in unit costs controlling for output and prices effects, which is related to the higher costs of regulatory compliance without technical progress. The cost of loanable funds is 81.2 percent of the total cost level.

title: Critical Mineral Supply Risks in the Expanding Electric Vehicle Industry
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Critical Mineral Supply Risks in the Expanding Electric Vehicle Industry
detail.abstract: The global electric vehicle (EV) market has been growing in the past decade as the climate crisis, government policymaking on decarbonization initiatives, and battery manufacturing technologies are driving proliferation. As a result, the demand for critical minerals like lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite and rare earth elements, which are used in the production of lithium-ion batteries and electric vehicles, has risen significantly. As the world becomes more reliant on small clusters of mineral-rich areas, however, there are significant issues of supply security, geopolitical control, and sustainability (Ballinger et al. 113844). The study presented here aims to investigate the link between EV growth and critical mineral dependency by synthesizing the literature, analyzing the policies and performing a supply chain assessment and SWOT analysis. The results show that the global EV supply chains are still very sensitive to disruption of trade restrictions, political uncertainty, and market concentration in countries that dominate mineral extraction and processing. Furthermore, the ethical underpinnings of clean-energy transitions remain under threat from environmental damage, carbon-heavy extraction methods and labor rights issues (Jones, Nguyen-Tien, and Elliott 5). Meanwhile, the study uncovers areas of opportunity for battery recycling, material replacements, and circular economy approaches that could help decrease reliance on virgin mineral usage (Nygaard 1102). The study identifies the need for more diverse sources of minerals, technological advancement, increased international collaboration and policy resiliency that will facilitate sustainable EV expansion.

title: Leveraging Inter-Organizational Agility for Innovation
affiliations: University of Zurich and UBS AG

detail.title: Leveraging Inter-Organizational Agility for Innovation
detail.abstract:
Today, companies face significant challenges from economic and social trends and external events and shocks. Rapid and radical changes in consumer behavior can occur within a short span, necessitating swift responses from goods and services suppliers to ensure business’s survival and success. 
Traditional planning, which depends on deliberate strategies, may be inadequate in dynamic and fast changing environments. Organizations should embrace continual change and evolution, rather than relying on a single competitive advantage. To achieve this, leaders must rethink strategy and innovation, focusing on creating short-term or transient advantages[1] by identifying and capitalizing opportunities before returning to core business activities once these opportunities are exhausted. 
Current management literature explains why companies should adopt agility. Correspondingly, our study focuses on how this might be accomplished in practice, assuming that a manager’s understanding of agility leads to improved communication, collaboration, and consequently, innovative solutions.

title: The Advancement of Digitalization Processes in Food Industry Enterprises in the European Union
affiliations: National Research Institute (PIB) - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI)

detail.title: The Advancement of Digitalization Processes in Food Industry Enterprises in the European Union
detail.abstract: The aim of the article is to assess the directions, pace, and advancement of digital transformation in food industry enterprises in the European Union (EU). The analysis uses statistical data collected in public databases as well as secondary data from the state-of-the-art literature and surveys carried out in enterprises in the sector. Moreover, the Digital Intensity Index developed by Eurostat was used. The progress made by food industry enterprises in terms of digitalization was assessed in terms of their relevance to the prospects of building a more sustainable food system in the EU. The conducted analysis allows to conclude that even though the pace of digitalization in the sector's enterprises has accelerated in recent years, the level and scope of digital changes is still limited. What is more, large inequalities in the level of digitalization, visible both within the sector itself and between EU Member States, remain a problem. The directions of using digital solutions show that digitalization is seen mainly to increase production efficiency and attract new customers and sales channels. Parallel possibilities to support environmental and climate protection are not yet sufficiently exploited. Given the challenges related to the implementation of the European Green Deal, it is necessary to accelerate and expand the scope of digitalization in EU food industry enterprises.

title: Anchored to the Dot Plot: Central Bank Projections and Interest Rate Expectations
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Anchored to the Dot Plot: Central Bank Projections and Interest Rate Expectations
detail.abstract: Central bank projections shape private expectations but may also inefficiently anchor them. Using federal funds rate forecasts from 2012-2026, I document that the Federal Reserve's Summary of Economic Projections creates predictable forecast errors in private-sector forecasts through anchoring. Both survey-based and, to a lesser extent, market-based forecasts anchor to prior SEP releases, generating systematic under-adjustment even after controlling for prior consensus and macro-financial predictors. This anchoring is distinct from other forms of information rigidity documented in the literature such as anchoring to the previous consensus forecasts. The findings reveal a communication tradeoff: frequent central bank projections enhance transparency but create reference points that impede expectation adjustment during turning points, with implications for the speed and effectiveness of monetary policy transmission.

title: When Machines Think Fast: A Behavioral Economics Test of AI
affiliations: and Lincoln Memorial University

detail.title: When Machines Think Fast: A Behavioral Economics Test of AI
detail.abstract: We test whether large language models reproduce or correct for fourteen well-documented human behavioral biases. We administer each canonical experiment to ChatGPT and construct a pseudo-panel of responses from each iteration. The biases we examine span belief-formation tasks (anchoring, conjunction fallacy), preference-based tasks (framing effects, prospect-theoretic risk attitudes, present bias, mental accounting, sunk-cost reasoning, the endowment effect, the disposition effect, and naïve diversification), and intertemporal and social-choice problems (myopic loss aversion, save-more-tomorrow commitments, the house money effect, and the ultimatum game). On eight of fourteen tasks, the model behaves in a manner consistent with the rational benchmark. On the remaining six tasks (framing of the Asian disease problem, the conjunction fallacy, mental accounting, the house money effect, naïve diversification, and the endowment effect), the model exhibits a directional bias that mirrors the human pattern, but in every case, the magnitude of the deviation is smaller than the human benchmark. We interpret these results as evidence that large language models can serve as effective debiasing decision aids in many settings. We show that residual biases inherited from training on human-generated text concentrate predictably in tasks involving valuation, framing, and intuitive judgments about likelihood.

title: Optimal Cohort Partitions
affiliations: and Yale School of Management

detail.title: Optimal Cohort Partitions
detail.abstract: The optimal cohort partition problem involves the partition of a heterogeneous population of individuals into distinct groups to optimize the objective of a social planner. Through the lens of majorization theory, we provide an optimization framework that characterizes optimal partitions under part-additive objectives, in both fractional and integral settings. Our technical approach geometrically characterizes the feasible partition polytope and identifies new structural classes of optimal policies. Our main result shows that under the broader class of asymmetric Schur-convex objectives, optimal fractional partitions are locally uniform---mixing adjacent types within a segment and then redistributing them evenly across consecutive sections---while optimal integral partitions, for $K \leq 3$ sections, are strongly locally balanced, a discrete extension of locally uniform partitions. Under Schur-convex objectives, the assortative partition is optimal in both settings; under Schur-concave objectives, the uniform partition is optimal among fractional policies and a nested partition among integral policies. We apply our framework to a range of applications. We mainly focus on education, where we study how to optimally partition students into sections in the presence of peer effects. Using the workhorse linear-in-means (LIM) model from the empirical literature, we characterize the optimal partitions for four distinct objectives (performance, inequality, welfare, and diversity), and further identify a class of sorting-neutral models that, despite being potentially non-linear, mirror the LIM benchmark. We also extend our analysis to two non-linear peer-effects models, as well as to non-educational applications by characterizing the optimal assignment of experts to teams and the design of Tullock contests. Finally, we complement our theoretical findings with an empirical exercise using a novel dataset of quasi-random student assignments in Greek public high schools.

title: Managing Spillovers in Supplier Decarbonization under Competition
affiliations: Renmin University of China, School of Business, University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business, University of Western Ontario - Ivey Business School and Renmin University of China

detail.title: Managing Spillovers in Supplier Decarbonization under Competition
detail.abstract: Consumer-facing firms increasingly invest in suppliers' carbon-reduction technologies to lower product carbon footprints. When suppliers serve competing downstream firms, however, such investments may spill over to rivals, creating a supplier decarbonization dilemma: buyer-led investment can reduce emissions but also erode the investor's competitive advantage. We develop a game-theoretical model of two firms in quantity competition in which a focal firm invests in a supplier's carbon-reduction technology and a rival may benefit through shared-supplier spillovers. We show that spillovers reduce the focal firm's investment and profit, and may also increase total emissions. The environmental outcome is governed by three forces: spillovers spread cleaner technology to the rival, weaken the focal firm's investment incentive, and change total production. Although spillovers diffuse cleaner technology, total emissions can rise when reduced investment and output-scale effects dominate the diffusion benefit, especially under intermediate competition. We then compare two spillover-management schemes: carbon offsets and royalty fees. Contrary to common intuition, offsets always increase supplier technology investment by expanding the focal firm's green demand and production scale. Royalty fees increase investment only when the fee is sufficiently low; a high fee can shrink the rival's use of the shared technology, reducing the royalty base and the focal firm's marginal return from investment. Both schemes can achieve an all-win outcome---higher profits for both firms and lower emissions---only when initial emission intensity is low. Offsets additionally require low investment cost and not-too-intense competition, whereas royalty fees require a sufficiently low fee. When initial emission intensity is high, only royalty fees can deliver a second-best outcome, raising total profit and reducing emissions by disciplining output expansion. Our results provide an operational guide for managing green technology spillovers in competitive supply chains.

title: Dynamic Pricing and Learning with Censored Demand
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Department of Industrial & Systems Engineering, University of Science and Technology of China (USTC), Dalian Maritime University and

detail.title: Dynamic Pricing and Learning with Censored Demand
detail.abstract: We study a single-product pricing problem where lost sales are unobservable, and prices are discrete. The demand is price-dependent, but the seller lacks prior knowledge of the demand-price relationship and demand distributions. The objective is to dynamically experiment with prices and learn from censored sales data to identify the optimal price that maximizes revenue. We propose two revenue distribution estimation methods: one is suitable for general and nonparametric demand, and the other is specifically designed for Gaussian demand. For nonparametric demand, we develop a machine learning model using artificially generated uncensored data to approximate revenue distributions. For Gaussian demand, we derive closed-form expressions for the mean and variance of censored revenue, allowing for the estimation of unknown parameters. Using the large deviations theory, we establish optimality conditions under infinite testing periods and develop a dynamic price-testing policy. Under mild assumptions, we show that the asymptotic allocation obtained by the proposed policy converges to the optimal allocation. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our algorithms outperform traditional methods, providing robust solutions under a variety of demand distributions, including Gaussian, Gamma, Weibull, and mixed distributions. Our findings reveal significant interactions between inventory levels and the number of learning rounds, offering valuable managerial insights for price optimization with censored demand.

title: From AI Risk Taxonomies to Recursive Cybernetics The A3 Model as a Category and Order Shift in Systemic AI Governance
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: From AI Risk Taxonomies to Recursive Cybernetics The A3 Model as a Category and Order Shift in Systemic AI Governance
detail.abstract: Contemporary AI governance has become increasingly rich in risk taxonomies, safety frameworks, ethics principles, and responsibility mappings. The MIT FutureTech Delphi study of 272 international experts-one of the most systematic prioritisation exercises conducted to date-demonstrates that AI risks are no longer marginal concerns but systemic, cross-sector, and potentially catastrophic challenges (Saeri et al., 2026). Experts judge 18 of 24 AI risk domains to carry at least a ten per cent probability of catastrophic outcomes under business-as-usual assumptions over the next five years, and identify a structural responsibility-vulnerability asymmetry: those most exposed to AI harms are often ordinary users and affected stakeholders, while primary responsibility lies with frontier AI developers and governance actors. This paper argues that such studies provide a necessary but incomplete risk surface. They identify what is dangerous, where vulnerability lies, and who appears responsible, but they do not by themselves provide a deeper recursive grammar for diagnosing why these risks cluster, persist, and intensify across technical, institutional, epistemic, and ethical domains. The A3 Model, developed by Vendan Ananda Kumararajah, is presented here as a category and order shift in cybernetics and systemic AI governance. Rather than treating ethics as a compliance layer, risk as a probability-severity matrix, or governance as post-hoc control, A3 re-architects the foundations of governance around three co-temporal primitives: Aram, Aanavam, and Adhikaram. Aram provides the test of ethical coherence and legitimacy. Aanavam diagnoses systemic distortionincluding egoic competition, incentive corruption, epistemic manipulation, institutional defensiveness, opacity, and false certainty. Adhikaram evaluates legitimate agency: whether an actor, institution, or AI system has the knowledge, action capacity, experience, absorption, and governance maturity required to act under consequence. Together, these primitives allow A3 to function both as a problem-space scanner and as a recursive solution architecture. A3 is not simply another AI ethics or risk-management framework. It is a cybernetic intervention that shifts the field from risk enumeration to recursive ethical agency governance.

title: Advancing Risk Management in Swiss Banking: AI-driven Client Documentation, Identity Matching, and Fraud Detection
affiliations: University of Zurich - Department Finance and University of Zurich

detail.title: Advancing Risk Management in Swiss Banking: AI-driven Client Documentation, Identity Matching, and Fraud Detection
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming financial services, driven by rising regulatory expectations, digital client engagement, and increasingly sophisticated financial crime. Swiss banks face persistent challenges in documentation quality, identity verification across fragmented data sources, and the detection of evolving fraud typologies. Traditional control frameworks are often insufficient to manage these risks at scale and in real time, creating the need for more continuous, data driven, and intelligence-based approaches to risk management. 
This white paper from the Department of Finance at the University of Zurich examines how AI can address these industry gaps, drawing on the outcomes of RiskON 2025, an initiative that connects academic research with real world banking challenges. Multidisciplinary teams developed solutions across three core domains: client documentation, adverse media identity matching, and AI driven fraud detection. The proposed approaches demonstrate how advanced analytics can strengthen documentation standards, improve identity assurance, enhance fraud detection, and support more scalable and transparent compliance processes. 
The findings underline the strategic importance of close collaboration between academia, financial institutions, regulators, and technology partners. Structured experimentation and practical solution development within open innovation frameworks are critical to accelerating the integration of advanced analytics into operational risk and compliance processes. Looking ahead, this collaborative model can strengthen the global competitiveness of the Swiss financial center, reinforce trust, and position Switzerland as a leading hub for responsible and resilient AI enabled financial services.

title: Writing Code vs. Shipping Code: Productivity Effects Across Generations of AI Coding Tools
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, University of Pennsylvania - Business & Public Policy Department and

detail.title: Writing Code vs. Shipping Code: Productivity Effects Across Generations of AI Coding Tools

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Leon Musolff and Mert Demirer both previously held postdoctoral research positions at Microsoft and now work as paid research consultants for the company.
declarations.funderStatement: This project was funded in part by the Mack Institute For Innovation Management at Wharton and the Chicago AI Incubator.

detail.abstract: How do the productivity effects of AI evolve across successive generations of tools, and to what extent do task-level gains ultimately translate into final output? We study these questions in the context of software development, using data on more than 100,000 GitHub developers combined with their AI usage telemetry. In a matched event study design, we find that autocomplete, interactive coding agents, and autonomous coding agents each significantly increase coding activity ("commits"), with respective cumulative effects of 40%, 140%, and 180%. These gains, however, attenuate sharply across the production hierarchy: the 180% cumulative effect falls to 50% for the number of projects, and to 30% for actual releases. This pattern is consistent with the weak-link hypothesis: the strong productivity gains from AI are attenuated by human bottlenecks in the production chain, with an estimated elasticity of substitution of 0.25 between AI and human effort, which indicates strong complementarities. We further confirm these results across four major app marketplaces, finding a moderate increase in the number of new apps but no increase in total usage. Large task-level AI productivity gains have therefore translated only partially into shipped and used software thus far.

title: Land Grabbing and Food Security in Developing Countries
affiliations: Land Grabbing and Food Security in Developing Countries

detail.title: Land Grabbing and Food Security in Developing Countries
detail.abstract:
The aim of the article is to present the phenomenon of land grabbing and its impact on ensuring food
security in africa between 2000 and 2020. The analysis used data on large-scale land acquisitions
from the Land Matrix database and legal acts from the online contracts repository, i.e., the open Land
Contracts (oLC) kept at Columbia University. In the article non-reactive research methods were used,
i.e., the analysis of the literature on the subject as well as statistical and descriptive methods. Between
2000 and 2020, africa recorded the highest number of large-scale land acquisitions on a global scale.
Transactions were concluded throughout the period, although most of them were concluded from 2007
to 2011, i.e., during the periods of higher prices of agricultural products. In terms of specific objectives, agricultural transactions were dominated by food crops (182 transactions and over 1 million ha
of contracted land) and crop production for biofuels (55 transactions and almost 1.5 million ha of land).
64.3% of agricultural land purchase transactions were in the operational phase, i.e., in production.
The conducted research allowed for drawing the following conclusions: some of the agreements omitted the issue of food security of local communities altogether, which contradicts the declarations
of national governments, whose aim was to guarantee it as a result of the defectiveness of the contracts (vide the methods of their conclusion and enforcement), they are unilaterally invalidated by
the national courts in the host country or are sued by investors; land grabbing contributes to the loss
or reduction of food security in developing countries that seek to obtain investments in arable land.

title: Redesigning Policies for Lasting Impact with Causal Graphs: Evidence from Uganda's Youth Opportunities Program
affiliations: Cornell University - SC Johnson Graduate School of Business,  and Cornell University - SC Johnson Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Redesigning Policies for Lasting Impact with Causal Graphs: Evidence from Uganda's Youth Opportunities Program
detail.abstract: Problem definition. Anti-poverty programs-cash transfers, vocational training, asset grants-aim to produce durable gains in income, health, and education for poor and underemployed populations. These gains take years, often a decade, to materialize, while the operational decisions that shape them are made on much shorter cycles. To iterate effectively, policymakers need methods that estimate long-term impact from short-term data and identify which short-term changes carry that impact, so the program can be redesigned around the mechanisms that drive durable gains. Methodology/results. We develop a framework that combines short-term experimental data with long-term observational data to estimate the long-term effect of a program and rank design modifications by their predicted long-term gain. We learn the causal mechanisms linking the treatment, intermediate (surrogate) outcomes, and long-term outcomes. These mechanisms are encoded in a causal graph, recovered using our COMB-PC algorithm. Using the learned graph, we identify a valid surrogate set, yielding a consistent estimator for the long-term effect. We then decompose the longterm effect into directed pathways using a graph-constrained structural model in an interpretable way, and rank design modifications by their predicted long-term gain. Applied to the Uganda Youth Opportunities Program (YOP), our method identifies the welfare effects that persist and those that fade, recovering the nine-year impact from only two-year surrogates which are based on two years of post-disbursement data. We find that most of the lasting effect operates through a single mechanism: enrollment in vocational training. Counterfactual analysis on the learned graph shows that strengthening this channel is expected to produce the largest long-term gains. Managerial implications. For policymakers designing the next pilot or scaleup, our framework converts short-horizon experimental evidence into actionable guidance on both whether a program's gains will persist and what design changes improve the next iteration. For YOP, the decomposition isolates a single high-leverage channel-early enrollment in vocational training-and points to a redesign built around raising enrollment: bundling the cash grant with enrollment vouchers, transportation support, or direct connections to training providers.

title: Hidden Costs, Biased Decisions: Predicting and Optimizing E-Retailer Shipping Charges Under Information Asymmetry
affiliations: ,  and Texas A&M University - Department of Information & Operations Management

detail.title: Hidden Costs, Biased Decisions: Predicting and Optimizing E-Retailer Shipping Charges Under Information Asymmetry
detail.abstract: When e-retailers outsource order fulfillment, the packing and shipping decisions made by third-party logistics (3PL) providers are largely opaque, making actual shipping charges difficult to predict at the point of sale. Within the 3PL itself, a further information asymmetry arises: base charges are calculable from published common carrier rate tables, but accessorial charges, surcharges assessed after delivery, remain hidden until the carrier invoices the fulfillment 3PL, and the 3PL passes it on to the e-retailer. This paper investigates how this partial observability distorts operational decisions and how machine learning (ML) can mitigate the resulting inefficiency. We develop sequential learning ML models that capture the cascading structure of 3PL fulfillment decisions (packing → carrier selection → charges), outperforming standard ML benchmarks for both base and accessorial charge prediction. We then integrate these predictions into a predict-then-optimize approach for shipping method selection, yielding meaningful expected cost savings relative to actual 3PL decisions. Finally, leveraging a regression discontinuity analysis at the base-charge indifference boundary, we provide causal evidence that the hidden accessorial charge component systematically distorts carrier selection. These three stages-prediction, optimization, and causation-form a methodological framework for diagnosing and correcting decision bias under partial observability.

title: Elite Participation as a Measure of Global Development
affiliations: Lund University - Department of Economics, Research Institute of Industrial Economics (IFN)

detail.title: Elite Participation as a Measure of Global Development

declarations.funderStatement: Financial support from Jan Wallanders och Tom Hedelius Stiftelse (grant P23-0186) is gratefully acknowledged.

publicationDetails.journalName: Research Institute of Industrial Economics (IFN) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Treating development as the ability to participate in complex, non-subsistence, globally comparable activities, this paper proposes participation in elite activities as an indicator of global development. Using standardized rankings from 1970 to 2025 across domains, including sports, chess, supercomputing, and fine dining, adjusted Shannon diversity and Herfindahl concentration indices are calculated. Results show that global elite diversity has increased and concentration has decreased across all studied areas. Global convergence is nearly complete for the measure with the lowest bar (having a national football team). These trends provide a development perspective less sensitive to purchasing power parity distortions.

title: Leading Through the Supply Chain: Customer CEO Industry Tournament Incentives, Leadership Capital, and Supplier Innovation
affiliations: Soochow University, Lehigh University - College of Business, School of Business Administration, South China University of Technology and East China University of Political Science and Law (ECUPL)

detail.title: Leading Through the Supply Chain: Customer CEO Industry Tournament Incentives, Leadership Capital, and Supplier Innovation
detail.abstract: We examine whether and how customer CEO industry tournament incentives influence supplier innovation. Customer CEO industry tournament incentives (CITIs) arise from external compensation gaps between a focal customer CEO and higher-paid industry peers, creating careerbased motivation to pursue visible strategic outcomes. We propose that stronger customer CITIs motivate CEOs to exercise boundary-spanning leadership for innovation, thereby improving interfirm coordination with suppliers and the suppliers' innovation performance. We further suggest that these effects depend on leadership capital: CEO power strengthens the credibility and persistence of customer innovation priorities, whereas domain-relevant experience improves the CEO's ability to translate strategic ambition into supplier-relevant operational guidance. Using 13,953 customer-supplier-year observations involving U.S. public firms from 1992 to 2018, we find that stronger customer CITIs are associated with greater supplier innovation quantity and quality. Furthermore, customer CITIs are linked to interfirm innovation coordination mechanisms, specifically resource synchronization, relationship-specific knowledge creation, and knowledgeflow integration and innovation-pipeline alignment. The effects of CITIs on supplier innovation performance are stronger when customer CEOs have longer tenure, CEO duality, supply-chain experience, or R&D experience. Our study contributes to operations management research by identifying customer CEO leadership incentives and leadership capital as customer-side antecedents of supplier innovation and by showing how leadership can affect innovation coordination across firm boundaries.

title: Deep Fractile Newsvendor Optimization Enhanced by LLM-Based Feature Discovery from Semantic Labels
affiliations: City Univ. of Hong Kong - College of Business, Dept of Management Sciences, The University of Hong Kong - Department of Data and Systems Engineering, City University of Hong Kong, Sichuan University and City University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Deep Fractile Newsvendor Optimization Enhanced by LLM-Based Feature Discovery from Semantic Labels

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA

detail.abstract: Retail datasets often contain both numerical features and semantic labels, such as store locations, product names, and dates of sales, that implicitly encode external demand drivers but are typically treated as opaque categorical codes. We propose a Deep Fractile Newsvendor framework that combines decision-focused neural learning with LLM-based feature discovery. On the decision side, rather than training a neural network to predict order quantities directly, we use the empirical mixture distribution (EMD) as a distribution-side prior and the cost-implied critical ratio (fractile) as a decision-side prior. The network with feature input learns only a bounded, dimensionless adjustment around the cost-implied critical fractile, and the resulting adjusted fractile is mapped back through the EMD to obtain the order quantity. This formulation constrains decisions within the historical demand range, reduces scale sensitivity, and discourages large deviations, and is stabilized by Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) regularization in limited-sample settings. On the feature side, an LLM serves as a semantic-to-source mapper: it interprets semantic labels and identifies verifiable external data sources (e.g., a meteorological API), from which numerical features are retrieved. A profit-based selection loop retains only features that improve profit. Across four datasets spanning three countries and three languages, adding quality-checked LLM-discovered external candidates followed by profitbased selection improves validation-period profit significantly when informative semantic labels, such as store locations, dates of sales, and product names, are present. In synthetic-data experiments, our fractile adjustment approach yields lower regret than the tested benchmarks when sample sizes are limited.

title: Electoral Democracy in India (1947–2025): A Data-Driven Analysis of Fragmentation, Volatility, and Coalition Networks
affiliations: and Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna (HNB) Garhwal University

detail.title: Electoral Democracy in India (1947–2025): A Data-Driven Analysis of Fragmentation, Volatility, and Coalition Networks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: This study presents a comprehensive, multi-decade quantitative analysis of Indian parliamentary elections from 1951 to 2024. By constructing a harmonized constituency-level panel dataset integrating official Election Commission records with socio-economic indicators, we evaluate the structural drivers of electoral outcomes using statistical modeling, machine learning, and network analysis. Our findings reveal a highly robust constituency-level incumbency premium alongside an accelerating reliance on pre-poll coalition networks as institutional power multipliers. Computational change-point detection and unsupervised clustering of index vectors mathematically validate the historical transition of India's party system from single-party hegemony to fragmented coalition dynamics, and ultimately to a polarized, multi-party equilibrium.

title: The promise and pitfalls of adaptive conservation for farmers and biodiversity: a climate-ecological-economic modelling approach
affiliations: Brandenburg University of Technology Cottbus-Senftenberg and Brandenburg University of Technology Cottbus-Senftenberg

detail.title: The promise and pitfalls of adaptive conservation for farmers and biodiversity: a climate-ecological-economic modelling approach
detail.abstract: Conservation measures need to be adapted to continue to protect biodiversity cost-effectively when climatic conditions change. We suggest that adaptive agri-environment schemes (AES), in which timing restrictions for land use are specified relative to the phenological beginning of spring, might be a simple but valuable alternative to typical fixed AES, in which timing restrictions are fixed calendarial dates. We systematically analyse the promise and pitfalls of adaptive AES. Specifically, we predict that adaptive measures should maintain the attractiveness of the scheme for farmers and stabilise ecological impacts in times of gradual warming. However, the fixed AES may outperform the adaptive AES in some years. Finally, adaptive measures are unlikely to solve the problems associated with extreme climatic events. We then develop a climate-ecological-economic model to examine adaptive and fixed measures for conserving a meadow bird in Schleswig-Holstein, Germany, focusing both on impacts on the species and farmers. We find evidence of all three predicted effects: Adaptive measures stabilise outcomes in comparison to fixed AES, but fixed AES outperform adaptive AES in some years of a late start of phenological spring. In years of extreme events, we see no difference between the two policies. Overall, we find evidence that adaptive measures can maintain the effectiveness and attractiveness of AES in times of moderate climate change, but other solutions are needed for increasing extreme climatic events.

title: Agile Regulation: Experiments in Flexible Governance

detail.title: Agile Regulation: Experiments in Flexible Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced their study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This article is not based on data collected from patients/participants.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for the research reported in this article.

detail.abstract: The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and national policymakers are increasingly embracing agile regulation. They see it as a response to the new patterns of scientific and technological innovation often referred to as the Fourth Industrial Revolution. Agile regulation uses instruments, such as anticipatory regulation, outcome-focused regulation, data-driven regulation, and experimental regulation to support fast-paced, cross-sectoral innovation while mitigating the potential harms of such rapid change. These methods are seen as complements and possibly substitutes to traditional regulation, which is perceived as comparatively rigid and slow. Despite the heightened interest in agility, the notion that regulation sometimes needs to adapt quickly is not entirely new. With a focus on network infrastructure policy, this chapter examines the past and future roles of agile forms of regulation in the digital economy. In a broader historical arc, agile regulation is but the latest adaptation of governance in the co-evolution of sector conditions and policy approaches. It is primarily a practical response to improve the procedural rationality of governance but is built on weaker theoretical foundations than traditional regulation. It will therefore be important to establish appropriate learning-and knowledge-sharing frameworks that will contribute to a gradual refinement of the approach.

title: How to Bid and Allocate Cloud Resources to Computation Tasks
affiliations: Shanghai University, , Shanghai University and Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: How to Bid and Allocate Cloud Resources to Computation Tasks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: The number of resource units acquired under a given bidding price is governed by an initially unknown acquisition relationship, referred to as the resource acquisition curve, which needs to be learned from observed bidding outcomes. To address this problem, we develop an integrated modelling and algorithmic framework for joint bidding-price determination and cloud-resource allocation. We formulate a mixed-integer optimization model that jointly determines bidding prices and resource allocation decisions based on the learned acquisition curves. To handle the unknown curves, we embed nonparametric curve estimation into an exploration-exploitation procedure. In each cycle, exploration batches update the estimated acquisition curves, whereas exploitation batches solve the resulting mixed-integer bidding-and-allocation model using an integer L-shaped decomposition method. We further establish the validity of the clairvoyant benchmark under true acquisition curves and provide a conditional performance analysis for the learning policy under explicit regularity conditions. Computational experiments based on real and synthetic data show that the proposed method improves cost performance relative to benchmark policies and obtains computational speedups over commercial solvers on the tested instances. Sensitivity analyses show that moderate batch sizes and balanced exploration-exploitation schedules improve solution stability and cost efficiency, and that jointly determining bidding prices and resource allocation outperforms decoupled decision approaches.

title: Circular Ecosystems 2.0: The Systems-Change Gap Between Resource Circularity and Financial Extraction
affiliations: University of Hamburg - Faculty of Business, Economics, and Social Sciences, University of Hamburg and Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB)

detail.title: Circular Ecosystems 2.0: The Systems-Change Gap Between Resource Circularity and Financial Extraction
detail.abstract: The transition to a circular economy (CE) has largely focused on the reconfiguration of material flows through strategies such as recycling, remanufacturing, and reuse. However, these efforts are frequently undermined by a financial system structurally oriented toward financial linearity and extraction. This paper argues that a viable CE requires radically expanding circularity from the material layer to the financial layer. Drawing on fundamental principles from network science, complexity theory, and the emerging field of ergodicity economics, we demonstrate that mainstream financial models commit a fundamental "ergodicity error" by ignoring time- and path-dependent nature of complex adaptive systems. This error drives investors and business managers to implement "default strategies" of linear extraction to correct for the losses inherent in non-ergodic dynamics, destabilizing the very circular ecosystems they seek to build. We expand the two-dimensional window of viability framework into a three-dimensional model by introducing the degree of non-ergodicity as a critical context-dependent variable. From this we show that finance-as-usual remains structurally distant from the window of viability as long as complementary circularity in both the financial and material layers is missing, and clarify the consequences for building a new economic paradigm. We translate these insights into finance and governance implications, distinguishing between strong circular finance and weak circular finance. We argue that strong circular finance is necessary to enable strong circular ecosystems—resource-pooling networks governed polycentrically—which are best realized through the Phi strategy, a context-sensitive approach for navigating volatile, unpredictable, complex and ambiguous (VUCA) conditions.

title: Financing Investment in Electricity
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance,  and University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Financing Investment in Electricity
detail.abstract: Meeting rising global electricity demand requires financing large-scale investment in power generation. Despite producing the same electricity output, renewable and fossil fuel plants are financed very differently: renewables typically rely on "project finance" and offtake agreements like Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) that lock in electricity prices and quantities over the long term. We develop and calibrate an NPV framework that explains these differences by linking production technologies to financing choices under financial frictions. We show how PPAs can help mobilize private funds through a capital structure channel. Because renewables have near-zero marginal costs, price certainty under PPAs can significantly reduce cash-flow risk, enabling greater use of bank debt relative to costly equity. This lowers discount rates and increases investment in renewables. In contrast, we show that PPAs are much less attractive for fossil fuel projects with volatile input costs. The framework also highlights a downside of PPAs for renewables: the amplification of macroeconomic shocks, leading to higher investment volatility over the business cycle. We use our framework to explain the slowdown of renewable investment following the 2021-2022 inflationary episode and show that state-dependent investment subsidies indexed to cost shocks can help stabilize private investment.

title: Trade-offs between protection and extraction in Chilean kelp forests
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Chile

detail.title: Trade-offs between protection and extraction in Chilean kelp forests
detail.abstract: Kelp forests dominated by Lessonia trabeculata and Macrocystis pyrifera are foundational ecosystems along the Chilean coast, sustaining biodiversity, ecosystem functioning, and valuable artisanal fisheries. However, Chile’s dependence on wild kelp harvesting intensifies the trade-off between short-term economic extraction and the long-term ecological processes that support coastal productivity. Here, we integrate trophic network analysis with economic valuation to assess the ecological-economic consequences of kelp exploitation. Using a diffusion-based model applied to a subtidal food web comprising 147 taxa, we quantified how energy and trophic influence from kelp species propagate through harvested components of the ecosystem. Macrocystis pyrifera generated broader and more efficient trophic diffusion toward commercially important species, whereas Lessonia trabeculata provided stronger localized support to benthic assemblages. We then linked these ecological dynamics to a dynamic opportunity-cost framework comparing direct kelp extraction with the indirect value maintained through ecosystem services and fisheries productivity. Across most simulated conditions, conserving standing kelp forests generated greater cumulative ecological-economic value than direct harvesting, with ecosystem value substantially exceeding the market value of extracted biomass. Results demonstrate that current market incentives systematically undervalue the trophic and ecosystem-support functions of kelp forests. By explicitly modelling these trade-offs, our framework provides a basis for emerging governance instruments, including biodiversity certification and payment for ecosystem services schemes, helping align economic incentives with long-term ecosystem resilience and coastal wellbeing.

title: Money Can’t Buy Me Fish: Lessons from an Incentivized Harvest Program
affiliations: Mississippi State University, Arizona State University (ASU), affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Money Can’t Buy Me Fish: Lessons from an Incentivized Harvest Program
detail.abstract: Recreational incentivized harvest programs (IHPs) are an increasingly popular tool for invasive species management in public lands and waters. We use trip-level recreational fishing data from anglers at northern Arizona’s Lees Ferry, Colorado River fishery to perform the first full counterfactual analysis of how the average harvester responds to an invasive species IHP. We separately estimate the effect of an IHP for invasive brown trout (Salmo trutta) on three behavioral margins which multiplicatively comprise harvest. This approach allows us to more accurately assess the IHP’s effects on the general fishery population using margin-specific counterfactuals, and to identify which behavioral margins were activated by several program design choices. We also leverage program-specific angler data cards to show that much of the additional brown trout harvest induced by the IHP can be attributed to a small group of mostly local anglers who were incentivized to learn by doing to become specialized brown trout anglers. We determine that the IHP was effective at increasing brown trout removals and that the program as designed was likely becoming a cost effective method of controlling the brown trout population relative to other proposed approaches. We make suggestions for designing and administering effective and economically efficient IHPs based on our findings.

title: Shrinking Families: How Does Demographic Decline Shape Investors?
affiliations: Florida State University - College of Business, , Xiamen University - School of Management and Xiamen University - School of Management

detail.title: Shrinking Families: How Does Demographic Decline Shape Investors?
detail.abstract: Fertility rates are declining worldwide, producing a growing share of only children. Exploiting China's One-Child Policy in a regression discontinuity design, we show that only children are significantly more risk-averse, less trusting, and less socially engaged than individuals with siblings. These trait differences reduce participation in FinTech (online lending, digital wealth management, and mobile payments) but not traditional finance. The effects are economically large, persist after accounting for differences in economic resources and digital access, and concentrate among less educated individuals and in regions with weaker investor protection. Only children also retreat more sharply from digital platforms following scandals, confirming trust as an operative mechanism. As the financial system becomes increasingly digital, demographic decline may impose a psychological constraint on financial modernization.

title: Reversal of Great Gatsby: Is Educational Great Gatsby Curve U-Shaped in Developing Countries?
affiliations: Radford University - Department of Economics, Columbia University, Johns Hopkins University and World Bank - Development Research Group (DECRG)

detail.title: Reversal of Great Gatsby: Is Educational Great Gatsby Curve U-Shaped in Developing Countries?
detail.abstract: We study educational Great Gatsby Curve (GGC) that posits a negative association between parental education inequality and children's relative educational mobility, with a focus on possible reversal beyond a threshold level of inequality (a U-shaped GGC). Our analysis addresses major methodological concerns: mechanical association between inequality and relative mobility, coresidency bias in measures of mobility, (non)comparability of data across sources, and robustness to alternative measures of inequality. We use sibling correlation (SC) and intergenerational correlation (IGC) as measures of relative mobility because they do not capture mechanical associations and are robust to coresidency bias. Gini coefficient and Atkinson index are used as measures of inequality. Our empirical analysis utilizes both crosscountry (66 developing countries) and sub-national panel data (2,694 districts and four 5-year birth cohorts in 25 Sub Saharan African countries). The crosscountry data comes from 277 waves of Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), and the sub-national data from 10% samples of censuses in IPUMS International. We report three major findings. First, the linear specification yields misleading conclusions, suggesting no robust evidence of a educational GGC. Second, linearity is rejected (1% level) across the board irrespective of data sets and measures of mobility and inequality in favor of a convex GGC. In sub-national IPUMS panel, district and cohort fixed effects strengthen the convexity: the squared-Gini coefficient on sibling correlation is-2.064 (s.e. 0.219) with fixed effects versus-0.267 (s.e. 0.089) without. Third, the Lind and Mehlum (2010) U-test rejects monotonicity in favor of a U-shaped GGC in most specifications. In IPUMS panel with fixed effects, 49-51 percent of districts fall in the "wrong" part of the U-curve beyond the minimum point. The standard educational GGC therefore reverses at the upper tail of inequality for roughly half the districts in our SSA panel. In the 66-country DHS data, the share of countries in the inverse-GGC segment of the U-curve rises across cohorts, from about 29-41 percent in the 1970s to 45-54 percent in the 1990s.

title: The Habenular Nexus: Reframing Addiction As Natural Adaptation and Exposing the Categorical Fallacy of the “Addictive Agent”
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Habenular Nexus: Reframing Addiction As Natural Adaptation and Exposing the Categorical Fallacy of the “Addictive Agent”
