detail.abstract: This paper is part of a series of preprints integrating Silvan Tomkins' affect theory, Donald Nathanson's Compass of Shame, and lateral habenula (LHb) neurophysiology into a unified theoretical framework. The author acknowledges Claude (Anthropic) and Google Gemini as a collaborative intellectual partners in the development of these arguments. The ideas, clinical experience, and theoretical synthesis are the author's own.

title: Inflation and Economic Growth in Vietnam, 2000-2024: Exploratory Evidence From Annual Data and Commodity Price Interactions

detail.title: Inflation and Economic Growth in Vietnam, 2000-2024: Exploratory Evidence From Annual Data and Commodity Price Interactions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing personal or financial interests that could have influenced the research reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available aggregate macroeconomic data and does not involve human participants, patients, or personal data. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper examines unconditional annual associations between Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation and real GDP growth in Vietnam from 2000 to 2024 using annual World Bank data and international commodity-price data. Because the annual sample contains only 25 observations, the study is framed as an exploratory empirical exercise rather than a causal assessment. The analysis begins with an unconditional bivariate ordinary least squares (OLS) model and then examines lagged specifications, non-linear and threshold specifications, commodity price interactions, illustrative Granger predictability checks, stationarity diagnostics, regression diagnostics, a sensitivity power analysis, and robustness checks. Across specifications, no statistically significant association is detected. A sensitivity power analysis indicates that the design has 80% power only for correlations of approximately |r| = .52 or larger, so nonsignificant findings should not be interpreted as evidence that no economically meaningful relationship exists. The commodity price interaction terms are also statistically insignificant, suggesting that annual aggregate data and a broad commodity-price proxy are insufficient to identify a systematic supply-side channel. The paper concludes that stronger evidence on Vietnam's inflation-growth relationship would require higher-frequency data, additional macroeconomic controls, and identification strategies capable of distinguishing demand-side from supply-side inflationary pressures.

title: Globalization, Entry Strategies, and Performance: An Empirical Analysis of the Mexican Gasoline Retail
affiliations: Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI)

detail.title: Globalization, Entry Strategies, and Performance: An Empirical Analysis of the Mexican Gasoline Retail
detail.abstract: The 2013 Energy Reform introduced radical changes to Mexico's energy markets. It opened markets to global companies across the entire value chain and ended a strict policy of price controls. We leverage detailed station-level data to analyse foreign firms' strategic behaviour and the effects that their entry had on local gasoline retail markets. Despite Mexico’s low station density and rising retail margins, entry into the gasoline market decreased after liberalisation. We show that the most important change has been the horizontal restructuring of the market. Instead of investing in new markets, firms have found it more profitable to develop their own brand or to adopt a foreign commercial image. Our evidence suggests that incumbents are more likely to differentiate when competition is fiercer. Foreign branded stations are larger, specializing in some complementary services. Results show that foreign stations, especially vertically integrated ones, charge higher prices and derive larger markups. Evidence from TWFE models with differential timing and heterogeneous effects suggest that the entry of a foreign competitor decreases local prices by up to 0.3 per cent, and markups by 4.5 per cent. However, results from event study analysis and robustness checks cast serious doubts on the causality of the static model estimates. We find no robust evidence of a competitive price effect of foreign entry.

title: Health Regulation and Dialysis Outcomes: Evidence from Brazil's RDC 11/2014
affiliations: Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP and Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP

detail.title: Health Regulation and Dialysis Outcomes: Evidence from Brazil's RDC 11/2014

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by FGV Cidades.

detail.abstract: We study the effects of Brazil's RDC 11/2014, a national sanitary regulation for dialysis services issued by the National Health Surveillance Agency (Anvisa) in March 2014. Using administrative microdata for the universe of public-system hospitalizations and registered dialysis facilities between 2010 and 2019, we estimate a continuous-intensity differencein-differences specification that exploits the pre-reform composition of the local dialysis market. Health regions with a larger 2013 share of for-profit private clinics-providers operating under the structural conditions most affected by the new rules-experienced a 7.9 percent reduction in hospitalizations for dialysis complications after 2014 (β =-0.051, p = 0.057). The result is robust to alternative clusterings, intensity definitions, state-specific trends, and falsified-reform-year placebos (all three pre-2014 placebo years null). A tripledifference design produces effects between-0.087 and-0.094 in log specification across five non-renal control groups, with the post-surgical-complications comparison reaching-0.091 (p = 0.043). Pre-trends are flat (F (3, 356) = 0.51, p = 0.68). The effect concentrates in regions with pre-existing peritoneal dialysis activity (-9.5%, p = 0.024), in self-sufficient regional dialysis networks (-9.6%, p = 0.085), and in the late stages of regulatory implementation (2018-19:-11.8%, p = 0.030). Facility-level data show that the for-profit share of clinics falls sharply, surviving facilities expand staffing and PD equipment, and total treatment volume is preserved-a pattern consistent with regulation operating through market consolidation rather than through universal facility upgrades.

title: NICU Designation and Neonatal Mortality in Brazil: Evidence from Hospital Designations, 2007-2023
affiliations: Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP and Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP

detail.title: NICU Designation and Neonatal Mortality in Brazil: Evidence from Hospital Designations, 2007-2023

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by FGV Cidades.

detail.abstract: We exploit staggered NICU designation across Brazilian public hospitals between 2007 and 2023 to estimate effects on neonatal mortality. Linking birth and death administrative records to hospital designation status, we find that NICU designation reduces very low birth weight mortality by a statistically significant 21.6 deaths per 1,000 live births, an 18 percent reduction. The effect is concentrated in lower-tier Type II hospitals, where mortality falls by 50.2 per 1,000, while higher-tier Type III designation shows no detectable effect. Type II hospitals serve larger and sicker populations, indicating that scope for improvement, rather than baseline quality, drives the result. A dose-response gradient across birth-weight strata and a sharp concentration of the effect in the neonatal window both point to a mechanism operating through neonatal intensive care rather than broad hospital improvement. The estimate is robust to the Sun-Abraham, Callaway-Sant'Anna, and Borusyak estimators, to a Goodman-Bacon decomposition, and to permutation placebo tests. Over the period, designation averted roughly 2,150 neonatal deaths at an estimated cost of R$1.9 to 3.9 million per life saved.

title: Beyond HbA1c: Continuous Glycaemic Pharmacovigilance (CGPV) in the Era of CGM and Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: Beyond HbA1c: Continuous Glycaemic Pharmacovigilance (CGPV) in the Era of CGM and Artificial Intelligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of MyCliniLedger (an electronic medical record platform) and MyMediLedger (a personal health record platform), and provides independent medical consulting — including pharmacovigilance and HealthTech advisory — through MedClariva. None of these ventures manufactures continuous glucose monitoring devices, automated insulin delivery systems, or glucose-lowering therapies, and none provided funding for this work. The author declares no other competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for the conceptualisation, drafting, or preparation of this manuscript.

detail.abstract: Background. Pharmacovigilance of glucose-lowering therapy still rests on HbA1c. This biomarker integrates glucose exposure over 90 days. It cannot detect transient excursions, varies by ancestry, and is silent on algorithmic harms from automated insulin delivery and AI decision-support. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) is now widely deployed [6]. Pharmacovigilance has not absorbed it. Objective. We propose Continuous Glycaemic Pharmacovigilance (CGPV) as an operational framework. CGPV uses CGM-derived data as a continuous signal substrate for drug safety surveillance. It addresses three convergent gaps: temporal blindness, population miscalibration, and algorithmic opacity. Framework. CGPV rests on five pillars: (1) Signal Detection through CGM metrics as adverse-drugr-eaction triggers; (2) Causality Attribution by adapting Bradford Hill criteria to continuous signals, integrated with WHO-UMC categories; (3) Population Calibration through ancestry-aware reference ranges; (4) Algorithmic Accountability through a structured audit protocol for software-as-medical-device; (5) Equity-Embedded Implementation through a tiered architecture across the global resource gradient. Worked example. We apply CGPV to glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) surveillance in South Asians. The framework detects gastroparesis-pattern adverse effects, combination-therapy hypoglycaemia, and population-stratified efficacy attenuation that conventional pharmacovigilance misses. Conclusion. CGPV requires expansion of MedDRA terminology, extension of ICH E2B(R3) data standards, ancestry-stratified trial reporting, and SaMD training-cohort disclosure. The framework is feasible on a 3-5 year horizon for early-adopting jurisdictions. It commits pharmacovigilance to three priorities: continuous-signal infrastructure, surveillance equity, and algorithmic accountability.

title: Annotation-Efficient Adaptation of SAM3 for Thyroid Ultrasound Segmentation: A Comparative Analysis of LoRA and Full Fine-Tuning Across Label Regimes
affiliations: Fayetteville State University and National School of Applied Sciences Agadir

detail.title: Annotation-Efficient Adaptation of SAM3 for Thyroid Ultrasound Segmentation: A Comparative Analysis of LoRA and Full Fine-Tuning Across Label Regimes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Background: Thyroid nodule segmentation in ultrasound imaging is clinically important but typically requires large volumes of expert annotations. Foundation models offer a promising approach to reducing labeled data requirements, yet the relationship between annotation budget and segmentation performance across adaptation strategies remains insufficiently characterized.

Methods: We evaluated four SAM3-based adaptation strategies on TN5000 (5,000 biopsy-confirmed thyroid ultrasound images): full fine-tuning (MedSAM3), zero-shot inference (SAM3-Zero), and Low-Rank Adaptation at ranks 8 and 16 (SAM3-LoRA8, SAM3-LoRA16). All models were initialized via Masked Autoencoder pretraining on the unlabeled corpus and evaluated under four annotation regimes (10%, 25%, 50%, and 100% of labeled data) using Dice, IoU, AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and F1-score, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and Bonferroni-corrected significance testing. External validation was conducted on the independent DDTI dataset.

Results: At full annotation budget, MedSAM3 achieved the highest internal performance (Dice = 0.815, AUC = 0.989), significantly outperforming the zero-shot baseline (Dice = 0.097, p < 0.001 across Wilcoxon, DeLong, and McNemar tests). At 25% label availability, SAM3-LoRA8 matched or exceeded MedSAM3 (Dice = 0.736 vs 0.726) while updating only 1.85% of model parameters, identifying 25% as the annotation-efficiency crossover threshold. No statistically significant difference was observed between LoRA ranks 8 and 16 on per-image Dice (Wilcoxon p = 0.704), indicating that increasing rank beyond 8 yields no measurable performance benefit for this task. External validation on the DDTI dataset preserved model ranking (MedSAM3 AUC = 0.911); a dissociation between AUC and Dice under domain shift was observed across all fine-tuned models, with implications for cross-site deployment.

Conclusions: Full fine-tuning with domain-adapted initialization provides the best segmentation performance at large annotation budgets. LoRA adaptation with rank 8 offers a more annotation-efficient and parameter-efficient alternative, matching full fine-tuning at 25% label availability and requiring approximately half the training time. These findings provide a concrete decision framework for selecting adaptation strategies in annotation-constrained clinical deployments of thyroid ultrasound segmentation.

title: Permission without Adoption: A Pharmacy Diagnostic-Access Reform and Dengue Surveillance in Brazil
affiliations: Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP, Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP and Sao Paulo School of Economics FGV EESP

detail.title: Permission without Adoption: A Pharmacy Diagnostic-Access Reform and Dengue Surveillance in Brazil

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by FGV Cidades.

detail.abstract: We provide the first population-scale, quasi-experimental evaluation of an at-scale liberalization of pharmacy diagnostics: Brazil's RDC 786/2023, which from August 2023 authorized retail pharmacies to perform screening clinical exams, including rapid tests. Using a triple-difference design that exploits cross-municipal variation in pre-reform pharmacy density and laboratory scarcity on a monthly panel of all 5,570 municipalities (2014-2024), we estimate the reform's effect on dengue, a hyperendemic and compulsorily notified disease whose rapid tests fit the authorized technology. We find a precisely estimated null across every pre-specified outcome-notifications, time-tonotification, hospitalizations, intensive care, and deaths-in two independent data systems, robust to Poisson estimation, a continuous dose-response specification, outcome and date placebos, and state-level inference. Apparent reductions in severity under a naive difference-indifferences do not survive pre-trend tests or the continuous specification and track the 2024 epidemic. The null is consistent with a missing first stage: the authorized service is registered by only a handful of pharmacies nationwide and did not grow after the reform. Permitting a service is not the same as delivering it.

title: Rural Electricity Consumption: Reality and Prospects in the Opinion of the Inhabitants of Podkarpackie and Lubelskie Voivodships
affiliations: Rzeszow University of Technology and Rzeszow University of Technology

detail.title: Rural Electricity Consumption: Reality and Prospects in the Opinion of the Inhabitants of Podkarpackie and Lubelskie Voivodships
detail.abstract: The aim of the research is to present electricity consumption in rural areas and the preferred directions of development of the energy sector in Poland in the opinion of the rural population of the Podkarpackie and Lubelskie Voivodships. Due to the extensive scope of the analysis, the part showing the actual energy consumption was based on the data from statistical offices, whereas the part concerning the prospects was based on the survey conducted in 2021 among 516 inhabitants of rural areas of the Podkarpackie and Lubelskie Voivodships, which are typically agricultural regions. The study was partial and was carried out using the diagnostic survey method and the CaWi technique. The study was not probabilistic. The study shows that the surveyed inhabitants of rural areas positively assessed the consequences of the European Union climate policy for the natural environment and expect greater state support to increase the share of renewable energy sources in Poland's energy mix and to apply the requirements for the energy efficiency of devices. The respondents were convinced of the possibility of covering and replacing energy from conventional sources. They positively assessed energy from renewable sources, perceiving renewable energy, mainly photovoltaics, as the main source of energy in Poland's energy mix.

title: Indebtedness: Field Notes on Farmers from Haryana, India
affiliations: Chaudhary Devi Lal University, Chaudhary Devi Lal University and Chaudhary Devi Lal University

detail.title: Indebtedness: Field Notes on Farmers from Haryana, India
detail.abstract: The aim of the paper was to assess the debt burden on farmers and suggest policy solutions. The study is based on a field survey of six hundred indebted farmers. It showed that the average amount of debt per sampled farmer was INR 563,960 (USD 6,945.24). 1 The study found a skewed debt access to semi-medium and medium farmers. The largest debt share is mostly observed among semi-medium, medium, and large farmers, as the top 33% of farmers account for 71.8% of the debt share. By contrast, the bottom 48% (marginal farmers) are left to struggle with only 14.8% of the debt share. The source-wise distribution shows that one-third of debt share is still acquired from non-institutional sources. It depicts that non-institutional sources are also engaged in the disbursement of loans to agriculture sector at higher and compound interest rates. Furthermore, commission agents' or arhtiyas' 2 role is dominant among the farmers. Nearly half of the debt amount is still used for non-productive activities. This is one of the major challenges for policymakers to resolve the problem of indebtedness.

title: Impact of Legalization of Recreational Marijuana on Drug Law Violations: Evidence from US Colleges and Universities
affiliations: Indiana University Bloomington and Western Carolina University

detail.title: Impact of Legalization of Recreational Marijuana on Drug Law Violations: Evidence from US Colleges and Universities
detail.abstract: The use of various controlled and illegal substances, especially by young adults, has been a cause of much concern among policymakers, law enforcement officials, educators, and parents. State-level legalization of recreational marijuana in the United States raised concerns about potential adverse impacts on campus drug use and drug law violations. This paper combines data from three sources for 2001-02 to 2023-24, including college campus drug law violations that are collected under the Clery Act of 1990. We find that state legalization of recreational marijuana substantially reduced the arrests and disciplinary incidents for drug law violations.

title: Global and European Climate Policy
affiliations: National Research Institute (PIB) - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI)

detail.title: Global and European Climate Policy
detail.abstract: In 2022, thirty years have passed since the adoption of the United nations Framework convention on climate change. This period is long enough to evaluate the effectiveness of this policy. The aim of this paper is to determine the achievements of climate policy so far and the most likely directions for further actions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Particular attention was paid to agricultural emissions, which results from the significant share of agriculture in global emissions and the specific structure of emissions, i.e., the significant role of the sector in methane and nitrous oxide emissions. The paper uses statistical analysis based on the World Bank data. it was supplemented by a critical analysis of the literature on climate policy. The presented results show that the current policy does not bring the expected results. There are, however, some examples (the european Union), where the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions is visible. as a result, the share of community emissions in global emissions tends to decrease. This applies to both total and agricultural emissions, i.e., methane and nitrous oxide. Based on the presented data and global trends, it seems most likely that the current direction of changes will be continued, i.e., poor care for climate on a global scale and increasing emission restrictions in selected regions of the world. nevertheless, this solution will be ineffective, since climate change is a global problem and must be solved globally.

title: Community, State, and Capital: Guidelines for a General Psycho-Socioeconomic Model
affiliations: and Universidad Nacional del Litoral - Instituto de Humanidades y Ciencias Sociales del Litoral (IHuCSo-Litoral UNL|CONICET)

detail.title: Community, State, and Capital: Guidelines for a General Psycho-Socioeconomic Model
detail.abstract: The text proposes a reconceptualization of economic action from a psychosocial perspective that integrates relational, historical, and subjective dimensions. It challenges the centrality of the utilitarian paradigm and proposes, instead, a plurality of forms of social integration: mercantile-capitalist, bureaucratic-state, and gift-based-community. These do not operate in isolation, but rather in dynamic tension, shaped by a historical specificity unique to modernity, characterized by the hierarchization of capital and the state and the subordination of the community. The model is structured around the tension between the autonomization of these spheres and the development of mutual mediations. It also incorporates the role of the unconscious, whose functionality is expressed in a dialectic between linkage and overflow. No dimension can be eliminated without affecting the vitality of the social system. This complexity constitutes a hermeneutic key to understanding modern economic action.

title:
Blockchain Technology, BRICS Pay Consortium and the Private International Law Challenges of Decentralized Autonomous
Organizations (DAOs)
affiliations: University of Detroit Mercy School of Law

detail.title:
Blockchain Technology, BRICS Pay Consortium and the Private International Law Challenges of Decentralized Autonomous
Organizations (DAOs)
detail.abstract: The emergence of Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) represents a paradigm shift in organizational governance, replacing traditional corporate structures with algorithmically governed models on blockchain networks. This article provides an analysis of the private international law (PIL) challenges posed by the BRICS Pay Consortium, a proposed decentralized payment messaging system for BRICS member states, modeled on DAO principles. The BRICS Pay Consortium DAO highlights a fundamental tension between the transnational and often decentralized nature of blockchain and conventional territorial legal frameworks. The Consortium is designed to operate without a central headquarters or legal personality, thus undermining traditional PIL connecting factors-such as domicile, registered office, and principal place of business-used to determine jurisdiction and applicable law. The article examines divergent global framework for the regulation of DAOs. By evaluating current responses-including statutory legal wrappers and on-chain dispute resolution-this article demonstrates that existing doctrines are inadequate for decentralized entities. It concludes that existing frameworks on jurisdiction and choice of law are currently inadequate for the complexities of the BRICS Pay Consortium DAO. Ultimately, the article argues that resolving these challenges requires a transition from traditional territorial models toward regulatory innovation, contractual best practices, and cross-border cooperation.

title: De-biasing or Backlash? Confronting Prejudice Among Police Officers in India
affiliations: World Bank, , affiliation not provided to SSRN, Northeastern University (USA) and World Bank Group

detail.title: De-biasing or Backlash? Confronting Prejudice Among Police Officers in India

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Police officers' discretionary handling of gender-based violence (GBV) complaints is a critical and largely neglected barrier to justice in developing countries. We collaborate with the Madhya Pradesh Police in India, the second largest state, to conduct a lab-in-the-field randomized experiment in which 323 male and female officers participate, and study the effect of randomly confronting officers with evidence of their biased handling of a fictitious GBV case on officer behavior and attitudes towards GBV. We find no statistically significant average effect, but sharply divergent and robust responses by officer gender. Confronted female officers prioritize the victim's statement by 23 percentage points more than controls, a 27 percent increase relative to the control mean. Male officers exhibit a backlash: they deprioritize the victim's statement, elevate the offender's statement, and on a computerized stereotyping task assign significantly more negative stereotypes to GBV victims one week after confrontation. We find no effects on deeper attitudinal outcomes such as beliefs in the truthfulness of rape complaints. A likely explanation for the heterogeneous response is the stark difference in baseline bias: 72 percent of female officers display only mild bias, while 51 percent of male officers are strongly biased. Because policing is male-dominated, the average female officer perceives a work environment more biased than her own, and women are thus willing to de-bias their case handling while men are not. Interventions targeting officer bias must account for these gender-differentiated responses to avoid unintended consequences.

title: Real-time Acquisition-to-display Panoramic Super-resolution Microscopy
affiliations: Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Institute of Technology, Georgia Institute of Technology and Georgia Institute of Technology

detail.title: Real-time Acquisition-to-display Panoramic Super-resolution Microscopy
detail.abstract: Practical super-resolution microscopy for biomedicine requires scaling nanoscale resolving power to large-area coverage, high throughput, and immediate final-quality display within standard fluorescence workflows. Here, we introduce A2D-SPI, an end-to-end optical–computational platform for acquisition-to-display panoramic super-resolution microscopy. A2D-SPI integrates optical photon reassignment, synchronized time-delay integration detection, and optics-aware neural restoration into a unified streaming pipeline, enabling image acquisition, reconstruction, and display to proceed concurrently during continuous stage scanning. The platform delivers real-time, fully restored super-resolution panoramas with twofold resolution enhancement, uninterrupted streaming, compatibility with epi-fluorescence settings, and scalable field coverage, without sequential image acquisition or offline reconstruction. We validate A2D-SPI across phantom, single-cell, multicellular, and tissue specimens, demonstrating acquisition-time super-resolution visualization from subcellular structures to population- and tissue-scale contexts. We anticipate A2D-SPI as a generalizable platform for real-time, high-throughput super-resolution microscopy, with broad potential for biological discovery and large-scale biomedical diagnostics.

title: Navigating the Amazon: The Incidence of Digital Service Taxes
affiliations: Catholic University of Eichstaett-Ingolstadt and WU Vienna University of Economics and Business

detail.title: Navigating the Amazon: The Incidence of Digital Service Taxes

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Firms in the digital economy often pay little tax in the countries where their customers are based. In response, market countries have introduced digital service taxes on the revenue of these firms to indirectly tax their profits. We study the incidence of these taxes using data on Amazon, the largest online retailer. We find that in most countries, Amazon increased its fees by roughly the amount of the digital service tax. Firms using Amazon as a platform have largely passed these increased fees on to consumers. Large digital firms thus bear only a small part of the tax burden, but the tax may nevertheless succeed in making them less competitive relative to brick-and-mortar retailers.

title: From Census to Sensors: The Bureaucratic Regime and the Data Revolution
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Department of Sociology, University of Washington, University of Washington and

detail.title: From Census to Sensors: The Bureaucratic Regime and the Data Revolution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: We examine a profound transformation in the relationship between statistical knowledge and state governance through the lens of two "data regimes." In the earlier bureaucratic regime, government agencies produced expensive, theory-driven data through representative surveys and official reporting mechanisms. These techniques are no longer hegemonic. In the emerging brokerage regime, data production is cheap, decentralized, and dominated by private actors. Passive collection of digital traces is displacing representative sampling; algorithmic pattern detection is supplanting theory-guided analysis; and sensitive administrative data is being recast as raw material for AI systems. In the process, a new, paradoxical, political rationality emerges. The private sector encroaches on critical public functions while supplying the state with precise "truths" about people and collective entities that enhance its capacity to manage them.

title: The Code of Deletion: A Forensic Audit of a 116-Year Administrative Omission in the United States Census Bureau Data Architecture

detail.title: The Code of Deletion: A Forensic Audit of a 116-Year Administrative Omission in the United States Census Bureau Data Architecture

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no financial relationships with any organizations that could be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper is a documentary and archival analysis of publicly available federal data variables and published academic literature. No human subjects research was conducted. No ethics approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. Self-funded independent research.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a forensic data audit of a 116-year structural gap within the United States Census Bureau data architecture. Utilizing the IPUMS USA variable matrix, we track the historical lifecycle of companion variables CHBORN (fertility) and CHSURV (survival). Following the census of 1910, the Census Bureau exercised its administrative discretion under its broad statutory framework to retire CHSURV from active decennial tabulation. While legally permissible under 13 U.S.C. § 141, this operational choice dismantled the relational household ledger system originally designed to index family well-being. This paper analyzes the structural boundaries of this data gap, specifically its focus on ever-married women aged 12 and over, and frames its reactivation as a zero-marginal-cost opportunity for the 2030 Census window to provide baseline demographic tracking for an uncounted populace experiencing documented long-term effects on parental adjustment (PMCID: PMC2841012).

title: Paternalism and Autonomy
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: Paternalism and Autonomy
detail.abstract: Some of the most intuitive and deeply held objections to paternalism point to autonomy. A central claim is that paternalism is objectionable even if it improves people's lives, because it does not treat people as adults or with respect. To know whether paternalism violates autonomy, we need to specify what kind of paternalism is involved; identify the right conception of autonomy; and understand how and why paternalism works. Coercive paternalism tends to violate autonomy as it is standardly conceived. Libertarian paternalism does not violate autonomy as it is often conceived, but certain forms of libertarian paternalism do violate some intelligible conceptions of autonomy. The question is whether those conceptions should operate as (1) trump cards, (2) cautionary notes, or (3) intelligible understandings of autonomy that do not have a great deal of normative force. In the end, (3) is probably correct.

title: Agentic AI in Law and Finance: Navigating a New Era of Autonomous Systems
affiliations: 273 Ventures, Illinois Tech - Chicago Kent College of Law and 273 Ventures

detail.title: Agentic AI in Law and Finance: Navigating a New Era of Autonomous Systems

publicationDetails.detailsText: Open Source Textbook Licensed Under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (CC BY 4.0)
publicationDetails.journalName: Stanford Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Agentic AI systems, meaning software capable of autonomous goal pursuit, environmental perception, and iterative action, are rapidly entering legal and financial services. Yet widespread definitional confusion, architectural opacity, and governance gaps leave professionals ill-equipped to deploy them responsibly. We offer a comprehensive treatment of agentic AI for high-stakes professional domains, proceeding in three movements: definition, design, and governance.

We begin by establishing definitional clarity. Drawing on nearly a century of scholarship across eight disciplines, from Anscombe's philosophy of intention to recent advances in large language models, we propose a three-level hierarchy of agency: Level 1 (Agent), defined by the minimal properties of Goal, Perception, and Action; Level 2 (Agentic System), which adds Iteration, Adaptation, and Termination implemented through traditional algorithms; and Level 3 (Agentic AI), which fulfills these six properties using AI for planning and orchestration. A practical evaluation rubric helps practitioners distinguish genuine agentic systems from sophisticated tools and single-shot chatbots.

We then turn to architecture, because agents are not magic; they are architecture. Organizing the analysis around ten fundamental design questions spanning inputs (triggers, intent, perception, memory), execution (planning, delegation, action tools), and safety (termination conditions, human escalation, governance), we show how each design decision carries real tradeoffs that determine what a system can do, how reliably it performs, and how it fails.

Finally, we propose a governance framework that scales oversight to each system's risk profile, situating agentic AI within a five-layer regulatory stack spanning foundational law, professional ethics, sector-specific regulation, emerging AI-specific rules such as the EU AI Act, and voluntary assurance standards. In industries built on trust and non-delegable professional duties, we argue, human-in-the-loop and human-in-command architectures are not merely best practices but critical designs for satisfying fiduciary and regulatory obligations. We conclude with organizational models, responsibility-assignment tools, and a maturity-based adoption path that enable legal and financial institutions to capture the benefits of agentic AI while managing liability exposure and reputational risk. Throughout, we argue that responsible adoption requires architectural literacy, the necessary bridge between technical implementation and professional obligation.

title: Equilibrium Effects in Complementary Markets: Electric Vehicle Adoption and Electricity Pricing
affiliations: University of Toulouse 1 - Toulouse School of Economics (TSE), University of Mannheim and University of Toulouse 1 - Toulouse School of Economics (TSE)

detail.title: Equilibrium Effects in Complementary Markets: Electric Vehicle Adoption and Electricity Pricing

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Electric vehicles shift passenger transport from oil to electricity, linking vehicle adoption to hourly power-market conditions. We develop and estimate a joint equilibrium model of German vehicle demand and electricity supply in which driver-specific charging decisions map travel profiles and electricity prices into EV operating costs and load. A 10% EV stock raises wholesale prices by 3.3%, creating sizable cost spillovers on non-EV electricity users, but reduces EV adoption by less than 1%. Time-varying tariffs lower charging costs and shift load to cheaper hours; in equilibrium, EV adoption offsets much of the system-cost relief while redirecting generator profits toward renewables.

title: Trust Law's Beneficiary Problem: Trusts for Purposes, Pets, and Artificial Intelligence Companions
affiliations: Pace University - School of Law

detail.title: Trust Law's Beneficiary Problem: Trusts for Purposes, Pets, and Artificial Intelligence Companions
detail.abstract: The classical trust doctrine holds that every trust must have identifiable beneficiaries with standing to enforce its terms. Yet contemporary law permits trusts for animals, cryopreserved remains, non-charitable purposes, and, most likely, the perpetual maintenance of artificial intelligence companions. This Article argues that the beneficiary principle was never a unified theory of human flourishing but rather an enforcement institution that ensured that someone with a legal claim could monitor trustee behavior. Reframing the principle in these terms reveals that the proliferation of purpose trusts is a systematic institutional response to the genuine limitations of the classical rule. Trusts for artificial intelligence companions are a limiting case. Drawing on law-and-political-economy and feminist legal theory traditions, the Article demonstrates that the transformation in trust law from an emphasis on beneficiary protection to settlor autonomy displaces rights-holders, concentrates discretionary power in trustees, and raises distributional concerns. Purpose trusts should be reclassified and renamed, subject to heightened fiduciary duties, increased oversight, temporal limitations, and resource-dedication caps.

title: Stockpiling or Recycling? Country-Specific Strategies for EV Battery Mineral Security
affiliations: Monash Business School, University of Tasmania - School of Economics and Finance and Monash University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Stockpiling or Recycling? Country-Specific Strategies for EV Battery Mineral Security
detail.abstract: Accelerating transport electrification is vital for net-zero goals, yet remains hindered by slow, uncertain development of battery minerals. We show how non-technical risk, such as policy, regulatory, social, and geopolitical risk, increase capital costs, delay greenfield supply, and heighten price volatility for lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, graphite, and copper. Combining Fraser Institute investment scores with reserve shares of these critical minerals, we construct dynamic, mineral-specific risk premiums, derive an optimal stockpiling rule balancing risk and storage costs, and introduce a distance-to-iso-cost map, which provides a way to compare recycling and stockpiling as strategies to mitigate non-technical risk in battery mineral markets. Our framework suggests that stockpiling will remain the most cost-effective strategy in 2030 across all countries. However, by 2040, recycling will become relatively more cost-effective in Japan and Korea, whereas stockpiling will continue to be relatively more cost effective in China, the United States, and the European Union, albeit with noticeably smaller differentials. The method that we propose provides a tractable and updateable toolkit for deciding optimal stockpiles and prioritising recycling where it is most cost-effective

title: Spatial Spillover Effects of Cooking Fuel Deprivation on Household Health Vulnerability in Ghana: A Spatial Durbin Modelling Approach
affiliations: University for Development Studies, University for Development Studies and University for Development Studies

detail.title: Spatial Spillover Effects of Cooking Fuel Deprivation on Household Health Vulnerability in Ghana: A Spatial Durbin Modelling Approach
detail.abstract: The lack of cooking fuel continues to be a major public health and sustainable development issue in sub-Saharan Africa, especially in Ghana where many households are still using biomass fuels for cooking, including firewood and charcoal. The aim of this study is to explore the spatial spillover effects of cooking fuel deprivation on household health vulnerability in Ghana in the context of nationally representative using Afrobarometer Round 10 data. Using Principal Component Analysis, a multidimensional Household Health Vulnerability Index and Cooking Fuel Deprivation Index were created. Spatial autocorrelation was evaluated by Moran's I statistics and the Spatial Durbin Model (SDM) was used to account for direct and indirect neighbourhood effects. The results show a high regional variation in cooking fuel deprivation and household vulnerability to health in Ghana. The findings of the SDM show that deprivation in cooking fuels has a significant impact on health vulnerability of households in communities and that it also has spillover effects in the surrounding areas. Having access to health facilities, access to education, improved water sources, and income were identified as having negative association with vulnerability, whereas staying in the rural area had a positive association. The study finds that cooking fuel deprivation is not just a household problem, but a public health and sustainable development problem, connected with space. The study identifies cooking fuel deprivation as a spatial public health and sustainable development problem, not an isolated household problem. The results point towards the need for spatially specific clean energy policies and integrated interventions in the context of Ghana to enhance health outcomes and support sustainable development.

title: CFOs Meet LLMs
affiliations: Duke University - Fuqua School of Business,  and Georgia State University - Department of Finance

detail.title: CFOs Meet LLMs
detail.abstract: Business sentiment is a closely watched economic signal, but measuring it is slow and costly: surveys reach only a few hundred firms, arrive periodically, and take time to compile. We show that large language models hold the potential to address these shortcomings. We prompt an LLM to role-play as the CFO of a specific company at a specific date and focus on the economic-optimism question on the Duke-Federal Reserve CFO Survey over 2002-2025. We find that the LLM reproduces individual human responses: the predicted optimism score significantly forecasts the CFO's actual answer, surviving firm and year-quarter fixed effects and a control for the most recent prior response. Predictive accuracy increases with the amount of information supplied, as both respondent history and firm characteristics improve fit, and the relationship persists under quarterly aggregation. With appropriate conditioning, LLMs may be able to serve as credible digital twins of executives, offering scalable, high-frequency expectations data for financial research and policy.

title: Mergers and Emissions
affiliations: Imperial College London and

detail.title: Mergers and Emissions
detail.abstract: We provide systematic evidence on the environmental consequences of corporate mergers. We model two competing channels: a market power channel that contracts output and a technology adoption channel that internalizes the returns to abatement. We test their distinct predictions by linking European mergers to facility-level pollution, firm financials, and patent records, and applying a Sun-Abraham staggered difference-indifferences design, exploiting the differential timing of merger completion across treated firms and using canceled deals as a quasi-experimental control. We show that completed mergers reduce facility-level CO2 emissions and emission intensity (CO2 per unit of revenue), while turnover and employment are unchanged. The reductions are concentrated in high carbon intensity firms that also raise intangible fixed assets, consistent with the green technology channel. Patenting increases post-merger across all firms. In carbon-priced industries, mergers thus reduce emissions through efficiency rather than output contraction. Our analysis identifies within-facility decarbonization and the faster diffusion of cleaner production technologies as the main channels, rather than system-wide CO2 abatement.

title: American Banking Law as a Species of Public Utility Law
affiliations: Columbia University - Law School

detail.title: American Banking Law as a Species of Public Utility Law

publicationDetails.journalName: Columbia Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This chapter argues that American banking law is a species of public utility law. It’s core building blocks are public utility law tools and include industry structure rules (entry restrictions, ownership controls, and structural separations); geographic and service regulations; and administrative oversight to enhance service quality and ensure service continuity. The government also regulates rates through the Federal Reserve, and indirectly regulates industry profits through deposit insurance premiums. Although these public utility tools sometimes take distinctive forms in banking, they are similar conceptually to their correlates in other sectors such as energy and transportation. And although, beginning in 1980, U.S. legislators deregulated aspects of banking, Congress retained most of the utility law framework that it had built up over the preceding 150 years.

title: Difference-In-Difference Impact Evaluation Of Health System Strengthening Intervention On the Uptake of Selected Maternal and Child Health Services in Ghana: A Quasi-Experimental Study
affiliations: University of Ghana, University of Ghana, University of Ghana, University of Ghana, University of Ghana, Mailman School of Public Health, University of Ghana, University of Ghana, Columbia University - Mailman School of Public Health, Ministry of Health, Ghana and University of Ghana

detail.title: Difference-In-Difference Impact Evaluation Of Health System Strengthening Intervention On the Uptake of Selected Maternal and Child Health Services in Ghana: A Quasi-Experimental Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors declare that they have no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was conducted in accordance with ethical approval granted by the Ghana Health Service Ethics Review Committee (GHS-ERC 04/01/2017) and the Research and Compliance Administration System of Columbia University (IRB-AAAR0315). All study participants were provided with written informed consent forms, which they signed to indicate willingness to participate in the study. For mothers below 16 years of age, informed consent/assent was obtained from their parents or legal guardians. Furthermore, the since the endline survey was conducted some months after strict Coronavirus Disease (COVID-19) pandemic restrictions in Ghana had been relaxed, all COVID-19 preventive measures were followed. The study abided by all the dictates of the Helsinki Declaration.
declarations.funderStatement: The work was fully funded by the Doris Duke Foundation.

detail.abstract:
Background: This study evaluates the impact of a community-based primary healthcare system strengthening program on the uptake of selected maternal and child health services in two rural regions of Ghana. 

Methods: This study evaluates the health system strengthening (HSS) innovations, known as CHPS+, instituted in eight non-randomly selected districts and six comparison districts. We used repeated cross-sectional cluster surveys to collected data from women of reproductive age (15-49 years) at baseline (April to October 2017) and follow-up endline (August to December 2020).  Samples were collected in the Northern and Volta Regions where poverty and health adversity is pervasive. A difference-in-differences (DiD) analytical framework was used to estimate CHPS+ impact by estimating logistic regression models for maternal and child healthcare services outcomes (antenatal care, skilled birth and childhood immunization), utilizing weighting procedures to adjust for unequal probabilities of sample selection.

Findings: The results show that women in the CHPS+ saw significantly higher likelihood of completing the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended minimum number of ANC visits between baseline and endline compared with their counterpart in the comparison areas (0R: 1.624, 95% CI: 1.044-2.525). Likewise, the odds that children were receiving diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (DPT) (OR: 1.292, 95% CI: 0.790 - 2.111) and measles (OR: 1.536, 95% CI: 0.986 - 2.393) immunization were elevated among the intervention group relative to children resident in comparison areas.

Interpretation: HSS using the CHPS+ model will accelerate Ghana’s effort to achieve SDG 3.2 and improve prospects that Ghana will progress toward universal health care.

title: Policy Spillovers and Boom-Bust Cycles in Housing Markets
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - School of Economics

detail.title: Policy Spillovers and Boom-Bust Cycles in Housing Markets
detail.abstract: This paper studies how cross-region capital reallocation generates boom-bust cycles in housing markets. We first document two empirical patterns using evidence from China. First, housing purchase restrictions in large cities significantly raise real estate investment in nearby unregulated cities. Second, spillover-driven investment booms are associated with a higher probability of subsequent housing price crashes. To interpret these facts, we develop a two-region model with heterogeneous housing projects and credit market frictions. We show that tighter regulation in one region reallocates capital toward neighboring unregulated regions. These inflows affect not only the volume of housing investment, but also the average quality of financed assets by inducing the financing of more low-quality projects. Sufficiently large capital inflows can freeze the credit market and generate fragility in the housing market of receiving regions.  In a dynamic extension with endogenous housing demand and house prices, this mechanism produces boom-bust dynamics even without changes in local fundamentals. Further simulations suggest that macroprudential restrictions on non-local housing investment are more effective at stabilizing the housing market than demand-side support alone.

title: AI 시대의 디지털 통상규범 연구(Digital Trade Rules in the Age of AI: Global Regulatory Trends and Korea's Strategic Direction)
affiliations: Korea Institute for International Economic Policy

detail.title: AI 시대의 디지털 통상규범 연구(Digital Trade Rules in the Age of AI: Global Regulatory Trends and Korea's Strategic Direction)

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: While WTO-level discussions on digital trade rules have been delayed, rule-making at the bilateral and regional levels—through e-commerce chapters in free trade agreements (FTAs) and stand-alone digital trade agreements (DTAs)—has advanced rapidly. However, because these agreements differ substantially across countries and over time in both the depth and scope of their provisions, regulatory fragmentation has intensified. At the same time, the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is introducing new challenges to the emerging digital trade order. Issues such as privacy and copyright infringement arising from large-scale data collection and use, data dominance by digital platforms, the spread of misinformation, and heightened cyber security risks fall outside what traditional trade rules anticipated. AI technologies now generate multidimensional implications across data governance, intellectual property rights, competition policy, and ethical and safety standards, thereby heightening the need for domestic regulatory preparedness as well as international cooperation and institutionalization.

title:
Too Good To Go : 
A Digital Platform for Reducing Food Waste
affiliations: University of West Attica

detail.title:
Too Good To Go : 
A Digital Platform for Reducing Food Waste
detail.abstract: Food waste is one of the biggest environmental and economic problems in modern society. Millions of tons of food are discarded every year by restaurants, supermarkets, bakeries, and cafes. Digital technologies can help businesses reduce this problem through innovative applications and online platforms. This paper examines the digital platform "Too Good To Go" and explains how it contributes to reducing food waste. The study analyzes how the application works, its business model, its advantages, and its impact on businesses and consumers. In addition, the paper discusses the role of digital platforms in supporting sustainability and responsible consumption. Finally, the paper evaluates the challenges and future prospects of food redistribution applications.

title: 지속가능한 소버린 AI 확보전략을 위한 정책연구(Policy Research for Securing Sustainable Sovereign AI)
affiliations: Korea University, Korea University and Korea University

detail.title: 지속가능한 소버린 AI 확보전략을 위한 정책연구(Policy Research for Securing Sustainable Sovereign AI)

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Amid the intensifying U.S.–China semiconductor conflict and the Russia–Ukraine war, the vulnerabilities of global value chains (GVCs) have deepened, elevating technology from a mere industrial asset to a strategic lever shaping national trade, diplomacy, security, and politics. The United States has pursued an innovation-based economic security strategy that integrates R&D, supply chains, and emerging industries through the CHIPS and Science Act and the IRA, while Europe has responded by advancing the concept of technology sovereignty. Technology sovereignty emphasizes a nation’s ability to independently develop and procure critical technologies essential for national prosperity and competitiveness, thereby mitigating unilateral dependencies.

Against this backdrop, escalating U.S.–China technological rivalry has driven countries to pursue Sovereign AI strategies aimed at designing data, computing, models, cloud, and regulatory ecosystems in ways that are controllable within their own borders. Sovereign AI can be defined by applying the four pillars of technology sovereignty to the AI domain: (1) identification of strategic technologies, (2) dependency management, (3) governance design, and (4) social and democratic context.

title: Fit for Purpose: Modernizing OSFI’s Governance
affiliations: C.D. Howe Institute and C.D. Howe Institute

detail.title: Fit for Purpose: Modernizing OSFI’s Governance
detail.abstract:
• Since its creation in 1987, the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) has served as Canada’s federal micro-prudential regulator, operating under a single-head governance model that was suitable at the time but has not undergone a major review in nearly three decades.
  • Particularly following the 2008 financial crisis, OSFI’s activities have expanded in response to a more complex and rapidly evolving environment in which Canadian financial institutions operate. Meanwhile, governance practices across the financial sector have modernized, leaving OSFI’s structure increasingly out of step with its domestic and international peers.
  • To modernize OSFI’s governance, policymakers should mandate regular parliamentary oversight and introduce a multi-member model, such as a board of directors supported by advisory committees. These changes would strengthen transparency, accountability, and diversity of perspectives, ensuring that OSFI remains a credible and responsive regulator.
  • OSFI would also benefit from a periodic review of its governance framework. A formal review cycle, at least once every decade, would help keep its governance model current, effective, and aligned with its expanding responsibilities.

title: 개도국의 공급망실사 대응과제와 국제협력에 대한 시사점(Supply Chain Due Diligence and Developing Countries: Challenges and Implications for International Cooperation)
affiliations: Korea Institute for International Economic Policy and Korea Institute for International Economic Policy

detail.title: 개도국의 공급망실사 대응과제와 국제협력에 대한 시사점(Supply Chain Due Diligence and Developing Countries: Challenges and Implications for International Cooperation)

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Supply chain due diligence emerged in the 1990s, during the rapid advancement of global division of labour, as part of ESG implementation and efforts to create a level playing field. It became institutionalised, primarily in Europe, evolving into a substantive obligation for companies. Furthermore, recent geopolitical factors have led to supply chain due diligence being utilised as a means of supply chain blockading. Supply chain due diligence regulations impact not only the companies subject to the due diligence obligation but also their suppliers within the supply chain, thereby placing a burden on companies in developing countries, too. As most Korean industries rely on developing countries’ production networks for intermediate goods and raw material procurement, strengthening developing countries’ capacity to respond to supply chain due diligence is a critical issue for Korea.

title: 경제안보 관점에서 본 日·中의 글로벌 사우스 전략과 시사점(Japan’s and China’s Global South Strategies from an Economic Security Perspective and Their Implications)
affiliations: Korea Institute for International Economic Policy

detail.title: 경제안보 관점에서 본 日·中의 글로벌 사우스 전략과 시사점(Japan’s and China’s Global South Strategies from an Economic Security Perspective and Their Implications)

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Against the backdrop of growing political, diplomatic, and military- security significance, the strategic value of the Global South has been steadily increasing. The Global South is not an entirely new concept; rather, it constitutes a meta-category encompassing what were previously referred to as the Third World or developing countries, as well as regions sharing geographical commonalities in the Southern Hemisphere and historical experiences of discrimination and structural inequality.

Alongside the rising prominence of the Global South, another critical issue has recently drawn considerable attention in the international community: economic security. This reflects how the economy and security are once again becoming closely linked amid intensifying U.S.–China strategic competition and escalating rivalry over leadership in advanced science and technology. Contemporary discussions of economic security primarily focus on key areas such as supply chain resilience; the enhancement of industrial competitiveness, including the protection of advanced technologies; the prevention of excessive dependence on specific countries through the diversification of trade and investment; and responses to economic coercion (or economic statecraft).

reference: University at Buffalo School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2025-029; In John D. Haskell, Research Handbook on Law and Political Economy, Second Edition (2025).
title: Beyond Personal Responsibility:  Government Support for the Substantive Human Condition
affiliations: University at Buffalo Law School

detail.title: Beyond Personal Responsibility:  Government Support for the Substantive Human Condition

publicationDetails.detailsText: University at Buffalo School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2025-029
publicationDetails.journalName: University at Buffalo School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: In John D. Haskell, Research Handbook on Law and Political Economy, Second Edition (2025).

detail.abstract: Government protection against systemic harm to human well-being is stymied by the liberal idea that power is most legitimately wielded by autonomous individuals taking personal responsibility for their substantive well-being. Instead, a robust vision of democracy and socioeconomic justice requires grounding legitimate power in institutional responsibility, replacing the formal individual actor of liberal theory with the universally embodied, embedded human subject developed in Martha Fineman’s Vulnerability Theory. This chapter connects the message of personal responsibility in neoliberal US welfare reform policies to rationales defending the government’s failure to alleviate systemic human harm in the 2008 financial crisis and the accelerating climate crisis. For each of these issues, public authorities restrained their power for institutional change by presenting widespread human harm as a problem best addressed by neutrally mediating individualized decisions about substantive priorities. Yet without actively structuring political economic power in favor of distinctly human subjects, government will appear more responsible the more it yields power to institutional structures that undermine the substantive conditions necessary for effective human agency and value.

reference: 12 International Labor Rights Case Law 77-83.; University of Georgia School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper
title: Commentary - Modern Slavery Thriving in the Shadows of West Africa: Why Coubaly v. Cargill Furthers Legal Barriers to Labor Rights Accountability
affiliations: University of Georgia School of Law and

detail.title: Commentary - Modern Slavery Thriving in the Shadows of West Africa: Why Coubaly v. Cargill Furthers Legal Barriers to Labor Rights Accountability

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Georgia School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Georgia School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This article examines how the D.C. Court of Appeals decision in Coubaly v. Cargill Inc. (2025) erects new legal barriers to corporate accountability for global supply chain slavery. While traditional avenues like the Alien Tort Statute (ATS) and International Organizations Immunities Act (IOIA) have been severely restricted by the Supreme Court, the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA) initially offered a promising private right of action for victims of forced labor. However, the Coubaly ruling denied relief to former child laborers enslaved on Côte d'Ivoire cocoa farms. The court held that the plaintiffs failed to adequately define the supply chain venture or meet a high threshold for causation linking multinational cocoa importers to specific plantations. By contrasting this outcome with Doe 1 v. Apple Inc., this article illustrates how Coubaly imposes unrealistic evidentiary burdens on vulnerable plaintiffs. This decision reinforces severe informational asymmetries between multinational corporations and workers, signaling a troubling trend that may force human rights advocates to abandon U.S. federal courts in favor of alternative market and reputational leverage strategies.

title: Strategic Collaboration of Defense Industry between India and South Korea: Toward a Matured Economic Partnership
affiliations: Chung-Ang University and Berhampur University

detail.title: Strategic Collaboration of Defense Industry between India and South Korea: Toward a Matured Economic Partnership

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This study is based on the hypothesis that defense industry cooperation between India and South Korea (ROK) goes beyond the technical dimensions of defense and technology transfer. Instead, it serves as a strategic pathway to foster deeper mutual trust, enhance economic interdependence in trade and investment, and strengthen both countries’ positions as credible middle powers in an increasingly fragmented and volatile international order.

Building upon decades of export-driven growth that underpinned the “East Asian Miracle,” South Korea—now the world’s tenth-largest economy—seeks to transition into a sustainable, high-technology economy with the goal of joining the “higher high-income” group, by exceeding a per capita income of USD 40,000. Simultaneously, it is developing a modern and diversified defense portfolio to deter persistent security challenges from North Korea and its ongoing efforts to attain international recognition as a nuclear state. Confronted with external security threats and a protectionist trade environment under US President Donald Trump’s “America First” agenda, Seoul has adopted a dual-track innovation strategy. It aims to become one of the world’s top three artificial intelligence (AI) powers and among the top four global arms exporters in the near future.

reference: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 26/IER/31/2/2; KIET Industrial Economic Review Vol. 31, No. 2, pp. 19-31
title: South Korea's Economic and Geopolitical Challenges
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: South Korea's Economic and Geopolitical Challenges

publicationDetails.detailsText: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 26/IER/31/2/2
publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics & Trade Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: KIET Industrial Economic Review Vol. 31, No. 2, pp. 19-31

detail.abstract: South Korea faces multiple economic and geopolitical challenges: threats to globalization, fissures between the United States and China, global financial volatility, demographic headwinds, and disruptive changes in technology. The country's model of export-led growth based on manufacturing investment will have to change to meet these challenges. No single reform offers a magic bullet to solve these problems. Rather, reform will have to proceed on multiple fronts, something that is a challenge for any country but especially for one as politically divided as Korea.

title: 크루즈 산업 협력을 통한 동북아시아 다자협력 방안 연구(Strategies for Multilateral Cooperation in Northeast Asia through the Cruise Industry)
affiliations: Korea Institute for International Economic Policy, Korea Institute for International Economic Policy and  Liaoning University

detail.title: 크루즈 산업 협력을 통한 동북아시아 다자협력 방안 연구(Strategies for Multilateral Cooperation in Northeast Asia through the Cruise Industry)

publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for International Economic Policy (KIEP) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Although Northeast Asia functions as a core axis of the global economy, it faces a structural dilemma where economic cooperation is restricted due to political and security tensions between regional states. This study focuses on the cruise industry as a strategic alternative to break through this rigid environment. Due to its nature as a tourism sector, the cruise industry carries a relatively low political burden. However, it generates significant economic ripple effects across both upstream and downstream industries, ranging from port infrastructure development to the advancement of service sectors. Consequently, the industry can serve as a strategic medium for strengthening economic cooperation between nations.

The primary objective of this study is to establish a multilateral cooperation model for Northeast Asia by leveraging the cruise industry and to evaluate its practical feasibility. To do this, cruise trends in global and Northeast Asian markets and policy environments were analyzed, alongside a review of North Korea’s tourism strategies and relevant cases. Furthermore, by analyzing the limitations of existing shipping routes and regional consultative bodies, improvement tasks were derived. Ultimately, by establishing South Korea as a core hub and mediator of the Northeast Asian cruise network, this study proposes a phased policy roadmap to entice North Korea into a multilateral cooperation framework and achieve the advancement of the regional cruise industry.

reference: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 26/IER/31/2/3; KIET Industrial Economic Review Vol. 31 No. 2, pp. 34-47
title: Trading in Turbulence: Korea and Japan’s Responses to Trump’s Tariffs
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Trading in Turbulence: Korea and Japan’s Responses to Trump’s Tariffs

publicationDetails.detailsText: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 26/IER/31/2/3
publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics & Trade Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: KIET Industrial Economic Review Vol. 31 No. 2, pp. 34-47

detail.abstract:
This article by Troy Stangarone is part of a series of contributions to Industrial Economic Review celebrating KIET's 50th anniversary. Stangarone is a Non-Resident Fellow at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology and the former head of the Hyundai Motor-Korea Foundation Center for Korean History and Public Policy. He is an expert on economic and foreign policy on the Korean peninsula.

The return of Donald Trump to the White House in 2025 resulted in a significant departure in US trade policy. Since the end of the Second World War, the United States has been the leading advocate for trade liberalization, but under the Trump administration Washington has pulled back from economic openness, erecting new trade barriers and reinforcing existing ones, with the Trump tariffs being the signature policy of this new approach. The administration has also sought to leverage the large US market to extract concessions from trading partners. This pivot away from economic openness has necessitated that US allies such as South Korea and Japan recalibrate their approach to trade and economic engagement with the United States.

title: Federated Artificial Intelligence for Cross-Border Epidemic Forecasting: A Critical Examination of Privacy Preserving Data Sharing in Fragmented Health Systems Author

detail.title: Federated Artificial Intelligence for Cross-Border Epidemic Forecasting: A Critical Examination of Privacy Preserving Data Sharing in Fragmented Health Systems Author
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed a persistent vulnerability in global health security: the inability to share patient level clinical and epidemiological data across national borders without compromising privacy or violating regulatory frameworks. This paper critically examines federated artificial intelligence as a methodological and governance solution to cross-border epidemic forecasting. Unlike centralized data pooling, federated learning enables distributed machine learning models to train on local data sources while exchanging only parameter updates, thereby preserving data locality and reducing privacy risks. Drawing on a synthesis of peerreviewed literature from public health informatics, privacy preserving machine learning, and global health governance, the study evaluates the technical feasibility, legal interoperability, and ethical viability of federated systems for real time outbreak prediction. The analysis reveals that while federated architectures address key barriers to cross-border data sharing, including the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation and national health data sovereignty laws, they introduce new challenges related to statistical heterogeneity across jurisdictions, incentive alignment, and adversarial vulnerabilities. The paper advances a hybrid governance technical framework that pairs differential privacy with secure multi-party computation within federated infrastructures. Findings suggest that federated AI is not a panacea but a necessary evolutionary step toward privacy conscious pandemic intelligence. The discussion concludes with recommendations for transnational regulatory harmonization and infrastructural investment.

title: Does Credential Information Generate Uniform Returns in Teaching Evaluations? Experimental Evidence from India
affiliations: Management Development Institute Gurgaon

detail.title: Does Credential Information Generate Uniform Returns in Teaching Evaluations? Experimental Evidence from India
detail.abstract: Credential information is widely proposed as a remedy for gender bias in student evaluations of teaching, yet its effects may not be uniform across professor and student gender. We test this using a randomized controlled trial at a leading Indian business school, where 493 MBA students were randomly assigned to view either only a professor's name or a standardized credential slide before completing evaluations of one of their current professors. While credential information raises average evaluations by 0.22 standard deviations, this conceals sharp heterogeneity: female students reward credentialed female professors but penalize credentialed male professors, while male students respond positively regardless of professor gender. Belief-based analyses identify three channels through which female students discount credential signals from male professors: perceived structural advantage, effort attribution, and disclosure framing. These channels are largely absent for female professors. The findings suggest that credential transparency is not a neutral policy instrument: while it improves evaluations for female professors across evaluator groups, its effects for male professors depend critically on the prior beliefs students bring to the evaluation.

title: Bounded Rationality, Monetary Policy, and the Scars of Supply Shocks
affiliations: Sapienza University of Rome - Department of Economics and Law, Czech National Bank, Sapienza University of Rome and Sapienza University of Rome

detail.title: Bounded Rationality, Monetary Policy, and the Scars of Supply Shocks
detail.abstract: Bounded rationality reshapes monetary-policy trade-offs in response to supply shocks in a New Keynesian model with endogenous growth. A negative supply shock depresses innovation and future productivity, which gives rise to long-run scarring and persistent inflationary pressures. Under rational expectations, tighter monetary policy eases the initial rise in inflation but amplifies the fall in demand, innovation, and productivity. Under bounded rationality, households underreact to future income losses. This weakens the negative wealth effect and mitigates the decline in demand and growth. As a result, tighter monetary policy can contain inflation without generating large scarring effects.

title: Lifecycle Confounding in Estimates of Adult-Child Labor Responses to Parental Dementia
affiliations: University of Hawaii at Manoa - Department of Quantitative Health Sciences

detail.title: Lifecycle Confounding in Estimates of Adult-Child Labor Responses to Parental Dementia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no competing financial or personal interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study analyzes secondary, de-identified data from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) accessed under a data-use agreement; it involves no new data collection from or interaction with human subjects. Secondary analysis of these de-identified records does not constitute human-subjects research requiring ethics-board approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The Health and Retirement Study (HRS) data used are sponsored by the National Institute on Aging (grant NIA U01AG009740) and conducted by the University of Michigan.

detail.abstract: A literature estimates that parental dementia reduces adult children's labor supply and reads this as a caregiving cost. I argue the estimate is substantially a lifecycle confound. Because dementia is an aging disease, affected parents are about six years older at baseline (78.9 versus 72.7 years for cognitively normal parents), so their adult children are correspondingly older and nearer their own retirement. Using Health and Retirement Study panels linked to the HCAP-2016 assessment and the Langa-Weir dementia classification, I estimate a child-level period difference-indifferences for full-time work. The naive dementia-versus-normal effect of-0.045 is not robust to independent age-discipline tests-age-matched controls (-0.008), prime-age children who cannot yet retire (-0.007), and within-family post-onset comparisons (-0.004)-and heterogeneity-robust estimators (Callaway-Sant'Anna, Sun-Abraham) concur, with clean pre-trends and no anticipation. Minimum-detectable-effect calculations rule out the published-scale effect but not a modest one, so I bound the labor response rather than nullify it. The most consistently detectable family adjustment is residential-a modest rise in co-residence (≈ +0.02 to +0.03), robust to attrition and survivorship checks but borderline after multiple-comparison adjustment (Romano-Wolf p ≈ .06-.07). Gendering and pandemic-surge effects do not survive placebo and duration controls. Lifecycle position must be addressed before attributing labor responses to caregiving.

title: Sweden's Rare Disease HTA Reform 2022-2026: Operational Patterns from Six TLV Decisions

detail.title: Sweden's Rare Disease HTA Reform 2022-2026: Operational Patterns from Six TLV Decisions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no financial relationships with pharmaceutical companies, the Dental and Pharmaceutical Benefits Agency (TLV), or other organizations involved in Swedish health technology assessment. The author is employed as a data analyst in the financial sector at a Nordic bank; this employment is unrelated to the subject matter of this paper.
