The research presented here was conducted independently as part of the author's private intellectual work and received no external funding or institutional sponsorship.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Between 2022 and 2026, Sweden's Dental and Pharmaceutical Benefits Agency (TLV) developed and implemented a substantial reform of how subsidy decisions are made for medicines targeting rare diseases. The reform introduced a quantitative patient count formula, a graduated willingness-to-pay scale calibrated to condition rarity, codified principles for handling structural uncertainty, rules for delineating populations, and a systematic role for confidential side agreements. This paper analyzes how the reform operates in practice through examination of the official documents that established the framework and structured analysis of six TLV decisions issued between January 2025 and April 2026: Lamzede, Fabhalta, Ayvakyt, Imbruvica, Alyftrek, and Terrosa. The analysis identifies five operational patterns that emerge consistently across the cases: the rarity staircase functions mechanically once upstream parameters are set; subpopulation delimitation operates as a bidirectional discretionary instrument; uncertainty handling drives calculated ICERs upward systematically, in some cases through direct invocation of ethical principles; side agreements function as structural components rather than transitional tools; and the reform's ethical reflection concentrates on threshold-setting while the methodological production of ICERs and the calibration of threshold levels proceed without comparable scrutiny. The paper finds that the reform addresses two interconnected concerns — infrastructure for systematic handling of rare disease cases within a defined cost trajectory, and methodological structure that enables cost-utility methodology to produce approvals for very small populations — and shows that these concerns apply to different segments: the rarity staircase reaches only the ultra-rare end of the orphan medicines spectrum (conditions affecting fewer than approximately 100 patients in Sweden), while the larger segment of orphan medicines within the EU definition is handled through the standard framework supplemented by price negotiation. The analysis positions the Swedish approach against the United Kingdom's institutionally separated Highly Specialised Technologies programme and Germany's automatic added-benefit presumption for orphan drugs below the budget impact threshold under the AMNOG framework. The paper provides documentary reference material for ongoing analysis of Swedish HTA practice without evaluating whether the reform's outcomes are normatively justified. AI-assisted tools were used for document extraction, drafting, and editorial review; all analytical claims and final formulations are the author's own (see Acknowledgments and AI Disclosure).

title: The Decline Of Household Savings In India: Causes, Consequences, And Policy Pathways

detail.title: The Decline Of Household Savings In India: Causes, Consequences, And Policy Pathways
detail.abstract: India's household savings rate has undergone a dramatic decline over the past decade, reaching a five-decade low of 5.1% of GDP in Financial Year 2022-23, a sharp fall from 8.8% during the pandemic peak of 2020-21. This paper provides a comprehensive, data-driven examination of the structural and cyclical determinants of this decline, drawing on the latest data from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), the National Statistical Office (NSO), ICRA Research, and international sources. The study identifies rising household financial liabilities, post-pandemic consumption normalization, inflationary pressures, the expansion of consumer credit, and shifting savings composition as key drivers. It also analyzes the macroeconomic consequences, including reduced domestic capital formation, increased household financial fragility, and potential long-term growth risks. The paper concludes with evidence-based policy recommendations spanning monetary policy, financial inclusion, regulatory reform, and financial literacy, drawing on best practices from India and comparable economies. A partial rebound to 5.1% was observed in FY 2023-24, signaling cautious optimism, though structural vulnerabilities persist.

title: The Asset-Side Blind Spot: Why ESG Scores Cannot Capture Sustainability Exposure in Financial Intermediation
affiliations: Université de Sherbrooke

detail.title: The Asset-Side Blind Spot: Why ESG Scores Cannot Capture Sustainability Exposure in Financial Intermediation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Observatoire BMO en gestion du développement durable and the Chaire Desjardins en finance responsable de l’Université de Sherbrooke.

detail.abstract: ESG scores have become central tools for integrating sustainability considerations into financial decision-making. Yet these scores are constructed at the level of the firm, while sustainability exposure in financial intermediation often arises through asset structures, financing relationships, and system-level dynamics. This paper argues that the resulting mismatch is structural rather than methodological: it cannot be resolved through improved disclosure, methodological refinement, or expanded scope under double materiality. To clarify this limitation, the paper develops a three-level framework distinguishing entity, relational, and system levels of sustainability exposure. The framework identifies what ESG-based instruments capture, what they miss, and where complementary tools are required. A stylized illustration based on syndicated lending shows how institutions with similar ESG profiles may nonetheless occupy materially different sustainability positions once asset-side structures and relational exposures are considered. The paper highlights the limits of entity-level ESG assessment in finance.

title: Analysis of Volatility Strangles Via Normalizing Volatility Transforms
affiliations: Imperial College London,  and Marex

detail.title: Analysis of Volatility Strangles Via Normalizing Volatility Transforms
detail.abstract: We revisit the problem of determining implied volatilities from European option prices quoted in the FX markets. Depending on the quoting convention, this procedure involves solving nonlinear equations of varying complexities, entailing the questions of existence and uniqueness of solutions, as well as optimal computational procedures. For some conventions these questions have been adequately addressed, but a complete picture is still missing. We fill this gap by proving monotonicity of strangle premium for both the regular and premium-adjusted delta conventions, which so far has been taken for granted by FX practitioners. We also show that in the premium-adjusted case the monotonicity is lost if the conversion from delta to strike uses the smaller root. We also present some new interval bounds for the location of strikes for premium-adjusted convention, but leave it to future work to investigate their full use in numerical algorithms.

title: The Tragedy of the Asses: Stock Liquidation and Inverted Lemon Markets mould Medicinal "Bottom Up" Deglobalisation

detail.title: The Tragedy of the Asses: Stock Liquidation and Inverted Lemon Markets mould Medicinal "Bottom Up" Deglobalisation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All interests declared. Ie, no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Relevant and necessary ethics approvals were sought in original interviews undertaken for this research.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding.

detail.abstract: The paper traces China's extraordinary U-shaped demand for donkeys and the related emergence of a donkey skin global supply chain that prices a donkey hide at rates higher than the annual per capita income in donkey-dependent parts of rural low-income country environments. Three economics frameworks are drawn from to explain contested resulting donkey depletion and welfare dynamics: Clark (1973) and Dercon (1996) on poverty-driven livestock asset liquidation; an inversion of Akerlof's (1970) "Market for Lemons," in which unobservable hide provenance produces a pooled price that subsidises illicit sourcing and externalises depletion costs; and Kremer and Morcom (2000) on how the storability of hides and ejiao, combined with inconsistent regulation, risk accelerating rather than arresting donkey stock depletion. Together these dynamics constitute a "tragedy of the asses"compound depletion mechanisms the cost of which fall both on donkey stocks and disproportionately on the world's poorest women and girls. The cumulative result is an historically unprecedented response: the African Union's 2024 fifteen-year continent-wide moratorium on donkey slaughter-a very rare but perhaps foreboding act of bottom-up deglobalisation and African trade unity. Failure of the moratorium risks accelerating these dynamics, and success may generate its own political economy consequence. This forms a unique contribution to the modern high-income country-anchored de-globalisation literature, helps to correct for the absence of study of the donkey in economics, and also sets out suggestions for the directions for future research.

title: Women's Rights as Human Rights: The Enforcement Deficit, Compelled Marriage and the Case for Domestic Reform and International Accountability in India

detail.title: Women's Rights as Human Rights: The Enforcement Deficit, Compelled Marriage and the Case for Domestic Reform and International Accountability in India

declarations.funderStatement: Bhagwani consultancy

detail.abstract: Gender-based violence against women in India persists at a high level despite a statutory framework that is, on its face, among the most protective in the world. This article argues that the deficit lies not in the law on paper but in its enforcement, and that the failure must be understood as a human-rights failure affecting half the population rather than a private or domestic misfortune. Drawing on the feminist critique of the public/private distinction developed by Charlesworth and Chinkin and on Fareda Banda's comparative analysis of the interaction of human-rights norms with custom in the regulation of family life, and situating the analysis within the principle that women's rights are human rights, affirmed at Vienna in 1993 and given content by CEDAW and its General Recommendations, it reads the Indian constitutional guarantees of equality and personal liberty against the criminal and matrimonial law of dowry, cruelty and marital sexual autonomy. It then develops a structural claim: that the constitutionally protected right to choose whether and whom to marry has become, for most women, practically unavailable, because social ostracisation, physical insecurity and financial dependence rooted in unequal inheritance practice render marriage effectively compulsory. That compulsion is what exposes half the population to the risk of dowry violence. Because that dependence is in turn rooted in women's constrained economic agency, the article argues that financial independence, and the statistical recognition of women's paid and unpaid labour, is the precondition that makes the formal rights real. The article contends that India should accede to the Optional Protocol to CEDAW, restoring mechanisms available to women in States such as Mexico, and that the gravity of the situation warrants exploring complementary external avenues, provided any such scrutiny is participatory, intersectional and oriented to reform rather than spectacle. It engages directly with the principal objections raised against this position, the alleged misuse of protective laws and the claim that women's empowerment threatens the family, and argues that the evidence commonly cited for misuse in fact reflects the same enforcement failure the article diagnoses.

title: Removing Barriers to Girls' Education in LMICs: A Review of Recent Evidence
affiliations: Population Council, United States, Population Council, United States and The Population Council

detail.title: Removing Barriers to Girls' Education in LMICs: A Review of Recent Evidence

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported in part by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (INV-005386), Echidna Giving through the Evidence for Gender and Education Resource (EGER) and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (300849-104).

detail.abstract: This scoping review synthesizes new causal evidence released between 2019 and 2025 on policies and interventions addressing gender-based barriers to girls' education in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs). Building on Psaki et al. (2022), which classified interventions addressing eighteen barriers according to strength of evidence, we identify new randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies and assess whether the evidence has shifted. Evidence has grown most in categories already classified as e ective or promising, including tuition and fee elimination, school feeding, academic support, and school access, where long-term follow-up studies, scalability evidence, and mechanism studies reinforce these classifications. Several previously understudied categories, including safe spaces with complementary components, community support for girls' education, and female role models, show promising evidence of e ectiveness. Evidence gaps persist for interventions targeting school-related gender-based violence, sports programs, school-based childcare, life skills, and gender-insensitive school environments. Recent evidence on menstrual hygiene management is more tempering than earlier work suggested, with null e ects on attendance and achievement in most contexts but promising e ects in other domains. Across barriers, three themes recur: context and complementarities determine success; bundled multi-component interventions outperform single-component ones but obscure mechanisms; and many interventions benefit girls and boys similarly, without narrowing gender gaps.

title: Digital Public Infrastructure and Bayesian Nowcasting of India's GDP
affiliations: and

detail.title: Digital Public Infrastructure and Bayesian Nowcasting of India's GDP
detail.abstract: India's post-2017 digital public infrastructure-GST, UPI, electricity, and bank creditprovides high-frequency administrative data weeks ahead of the 45-to-60-day quarterly GDP release. We build a 26-quarter panel of thirteen indicators (2019Q3-2025Q4) and evaluate seven nested specifications under a Ridge-Gradient-Boosting-Bayesian state-space ensemble. Adding UPI transaction volume yields the lowest out-of-sample RMSE (0.75 vs. 0.80 for the official-only baseline) over an eleven-quarter post-COVID window; the Clark-West gain is in the predicted direction but not conventionally significant (p = 0.18). A variance decomposition attributes 84 percent of forecast uncertainty to reducible components, indicating a power-limited rather than noise-dominated framework.

title: Do Crises Increase Parochial Behavior? Evidence from Donations during Covid
affiliations: , University of Bristol and University of Turin

detail.title: Do Crises Increase Parochial Behavior? Evidence from Donations during Covid
detail.abstract: Do people behave more favorably towards their in-group during a crisis? Defining in/out-groups by geography, we study donations to local versus non-local charities during the Covid pandemic. The evidence points to increased parochialism: We document a relative increase in donations to local charities and show that donors in high-Covid areas increased their local giving and became less responsive to international disasters. Increased local giving was most pronounced during the first year of the pandemic. Our interpretation is that greater parochialism in donations was due to heightened concern about the immediate impact of Covid at a time when localities were salient.

title: LLM Meets Job Advertisements: Unmasking Skill Premia in the UK

detail.title: LLM Meets Job Advertisements: Unmasking Skill Premia in the UK

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I would like to thank the Department of Economics at Royal Holloway, University of London (RHUL), as well as Prof. Arnaud Chevalier, Prof. Melanie L¨uhrmann, Dr. Stijn Broecke, Prof. Ija Trapeznikova, and other colleagues at RHUL for their valuable guidance and support. I am also grateful to Prof. Andy Dickerson and Prof. Sandra McNally for helpful comments and guidance.
declarations.funderStatement: I gratefully acknowledge the Urban Big Data Centre for providing access to the Adzuna data. This research was supported by the Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC) through the South East Network for Social Sciences (SeNSS) Doctoral Training Partnership. The views expressed are my own and do not necessarily reflect those of Adzuna, the UBDC, or the ESRC.

detail.abstract: Rapid advances in technology and events such as COVID-19 have significantly transformed the modern workplace, potentially altering the skills demanded in jobs. This study examines the evolving demand and posted-wage premia for Information and Communication Technology (ICT), interpersonal, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) skills in the UK labour market. Using a comprehensive dataset of online job advertisements (2016 to 2022), skills are extracted and categorised via GPT-4 zero-shot learning. Cross-sectional log-wage regressions, incorporating occupation and regional fixed effects with three-way Cameron-Gelbach-Miller clustered standard errors, reveal divergent trends in skill compensation. While interpersonal skills are ubiquitously demanded (approximately 90% of listings), they yield no significant posted-wage premium, likely reflecting their near-universal baseline requirement across postings. In contrast, ICT skills, demanded in approximately 55% of postings, carry a postedwage premium of approximately 7%. AI skills, mentioned in approximately 3% of postings, carry a posted-wage premium of approximately 9% within the ICT-mentioning subsample. These findings document robust associational posted-wage premia for technical competencies amidst recent pandemic-induced and technological labour market shifts.

title: Will the Agentic AI Boom Become a Financial Crisis?

detail.title: Will the Agentic AI Boom Become a Financial Crisis?

keywords: and the Attestation Bottleneck agentic AI

detail.abstract: This article asks whether the current agentic-AI investment boom is more likely to end as a publicequity correction, an infrastructure-financing hangover, or a broader financial crisis. The analysis combines Perez's installation/deployment paradigm, Kondratieff long-wave vocabulary, boom-bust theory, historical comparators, public market concentration evidence, issuer filing denominators, official private-credit and financial-stability reports, AI adoption and productivity evidence, and public evidence on delegated-action controls. The central finding is conditional. AI appears technologically real and financially exuberant, and the financing edge of the buildout is becoming more credit-sensitive. Present public evidence supports a dotcom-like equity correction or telecom-like capex-credit hangover more strongly than a 2008-style systemic crisis. Four findings drive that conclusion. First, AI/data-center credit is no longer merely hypothetical: public ABS, delayed-draw term-loan, project-finance, and infrastructure-fund materials show a visible financing channel with both concentrated and diversified collateral pools. Second, realized loss and recovery evidence exists at the data-center/mining/HPC edge and protective loss-allocation terms are visible in utility and project-finance documents. Third, fund-by-fund exposure is dollar-valued in public schedules, while bank-by-bank evidence is strongest as public role mapping rather than retained loss exposure. Fourth, filing-grade revenue validation is material at hyperscaler, supplier, and selected neocloud layers, but capex payback is uneven and not proven across the full stack. The unresolved mechanism is the attestation bottleneck: high-value agentic-AI revenue remains less bankable where delegated action is not publicly shown to be attributable, authorized, provenance-bound, replayable, statusaware, and meaningfully reviewed. A transparent 500,000-run synthetic sensitivity lab is used only to rank evidence priorities; it is not a market-probability forecast.

title: Impacts Of Covid-19 And The Economic Crisis On Shrimp Prices In Sri Lanka

detail.title: Impacts Of Covid-19 And The Economic Crisis On Shrimp Prices In Sri Lanka

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funds, grant or any other financial support to assist with the preparation of this manuscript.

detail.abstract: This study examines the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2022 economic crisis on retail and wholesale shrimp prices in Sri Lanka from January 2017 to December 2025. The monthly average shrimp price data were extracted from the Fisheries Statistics published by the Ministry of Fisheries and analysed using descriptive statistics, one-way ANOVA and Games-Howell post-hoc tests using SPSS version 23. The dataset was categorised into four periods in order to recognise the effect of the COVID-19 and 2022 economic crisis on shrimp prices as pre-COVID, COVID, economic crisis, and post-crisis. The results revealed that COVID-19 pandemic had no significant effect on shrimp prices (p = 0.297), while the 2022 economic crisis produced highly significant price increases (p < 0.001). The 2022 economic crisis permanently shifted shrimp prices from a baseline of 1,137 LKR/kg to a plateau of 2,046 LKR/kg, simultaneously reducing consumer welfare. The findings demonstrate that macroeconomic crises affect shrimp prices fundamentally different than supply-chain disruptions like COVID-19 pandemics. No previous study has empirically analysed shrimp price dynamics in Sri Lanka across COVID-19 and economic crisis in 2022. Thus, this study addresses the gap by providing empirical evidence, structural price disruptions and macroeconomic shocks impacts during 2017 to 2025. Recommendations include real-time price monitoring systems to alleviate market inefficiencies and increase consumer welfare.

title: Greening the Deal: Can Mergers Redirect Innovation?
affiliations: ETH Zürich - CER-ETH - Center of Economic Research at ETH Zurich, Zurich University of Applied Sciences and ZHAW School of Management and Law

detail.title: Greening the Deal: Can Mergers Redirect Innovation?

declarations.funderStatement: This research has been funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) under Grant Agreement No. 221149.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how mergers and acquisitions (M&As) affect the direction of corporate innovation. Using data on U.S. M&A transactions from 1988-2015 matched with detailed patent data, we construct novel measures of changes in the technological orientation of acquirers based on patent text embeddings. We estimate dynamic treatment effects in a staggered difference-in-differences framework that compares merging firms to matched controls over a 17-year period, centered on the deal announcement year. We find a large and statistically significant shift in the acquirer's innovation direction toward the target's knowledge base post-deal. This positive effect is driven by deals between acquirers and targets that operate in technologically distinct domains. Using a subsample of deals involving targets that hold clean patents, we find that "dirty" acquirers - firms whose patent portfolios are concentrated in dirty technologies - show particularly strong post-deal shifts toward their target's clean technologies, accompanied by increased citations to the target's clean patents and increased clean patent filings by the acquirer. Overall, our results point to the potential for M&A to reshape innovation trajectories and mitigate against path dependencies.

title: Distributional Dynamics in Atal Pension Yojana (APY) Enrolments: A multi-method analysis across States and Zones of India-Period 2015-16 to 2024-25
affiliations: and Motilal Nehru National Institute of Technology (MNNIT)

detail.title: Distributional Dynamics in Atal Pension Yojana (APY) Enrolments: A multi-method analysis across States and Zones of India-Period 2015-16 to 2024-25
detail.abstract: This study presents the first comprehensive multi-method distributional analysis of Atal Pension Yojana (APY) enrolment across 29 Indian states over the complete first decade of the scheme's operation i.e. from its launch in FY 2015-16 to FY 2024-25. The study employs APY enrolments per 1,000 eligible population as the analytical metric. The approximate eligible population has been derived from Population Projections for India and states 2011-2036 report issued by National Commission on Population, MoHFW, with linear interpolation for intermediate years. The study deploys seven complementary analytical frameworks- Gini coefficient Lorenz curves, Theil T decomposition, σ-convergence, β-convergence via OLS, heteroskedasticity-consistent (HC3) robust standard errors & Fixed Effects panel regression, non-parametric rank correlation tests (Spearman ρ and Kendall’s τ), Wilcoxon rank-sum test, quartile mobility matrix and Gender Parity Index (GPI) analysis. The national Gini coefficient for APY total enrolment penetration rose from 0.210 in 2015-16 to a peak of 0.359 in 2021-22 before moderating to 0.280 in 2024-25, indicating a net increase in inequality over the decade. Female enrolment penetration inequality is consistently and substantially higher than its male counterpart, peaking at 0.444. Theil T decomposition reveals a decisive structural transformation- inter-zone inequality collapsed from 31.7% to 3.3% of total inequality, while intra-zone state-level divergence now accounts for 96.7%. Sigma-convergence confirms divergence, with the national standard deviation rising from 1.72 to a staggering peak of 38.87 (during Covid years), before partially recovering to 13.60. Although cross-sectional OLS β-convergence was found to be non-significant, due to small sample constraints, the panel Fixed Effects regression using the entire year-state observations confirmed highly significant β-convergence for Total (β = -0.233, p < 0.001), Male (β = -0.271, p < 0.001) and Female (β = -0.210, p < 0.001). The Male convergence was independently confirmed through Spearman ρ = -0.387 (p = 0.039) and HC3-corrected OLS (p = 0.041). The national Gender Parity Index, defined as the ratio of Female enrolments per 1000 population to Male enrolments per 1000 population, rose from 0.689 to 1.339 over the decade, with parity crossed in 2022-23. However, substantial state-level disparities persist. These findings collectively indicate that APY inequality has increased, shifted from inter-zonal to intra-zonal and requires state-specific rather than zone-level policy interventions.

title: This is Not My Turn: The Hidden Costs of Centralized Environmental Campaigns
affiliations: ,  and Peking University - Guanghua School of Management

detail.title: This is Not My Turn: The Hidden Costs of Centralized Environmental Campaigns

declarations.funderStatement: Huang gratefully acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grant number 72403012) and the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities, Peking University.

detail.abstract: Central governments often use rotating inspections to correct local implementation failures, but the same rotation may change behavior outside inspected jurisdictions. This paper studies this possibility in China's Central Environmental Protection Inspections, a high-stakes campaign that sends central teams to selected provinces in batches. Using a regression discontinuity design in time around inspection events and high-frequency pollution data, we show that inspections reduce PM 10 by 8 to 11 micrograms per cubic meter in target provinces when teams arrive on site. At the same time, PM 10 rises by 6 to 8 micrograms per cubic meter in non-target provinces at the start of the short preparation window before a new inspection batch enters its target provinces. Evidence from monitoring-station pollutants, firm emissions, production proxies, enforcement records, and heterogeneity by personnel scarcity and political incentives suggests that this "not-my-turn" effect reflects both weakened routine oversight and strategic responses to lower immediate central scrutiny. Rotating campaigns can therefore generate substantial spillovers beyond treated jurisdictions.

title:
Measuring What Moves
A Dynamic Metrics Framework for Identity Governance Responsiveness
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
Measuring What Moves
A Dynamic Metrics Framework for Identity Governance Responsiveness
detail.abstract: Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) programs are designed to ensure that appropriate access is maintained across organizational resources. However, the operational metrics used to evaluate these programs remain overwhelmingly static and activity-based: certification completion rates, provisioning speed, and policy violation counts. These metrics measure whether governance work was performed, not whether the governance program is keeping pace with the rate at which access states change. This paper examines the gap between the continuously evolving nature of access environments and the periodic, checkpoint-based governance models that most organizations rely on. Drawing on a review of current IGA literature, industry frameworks, vendor approaches, and standards-body publications, we identify the absence of a formalized, vendor-neutral measurement vocabulary for access dynamics at the governance program level. We propose four named metrics to address this gap: Entitlement Drift Rate (decomposed into gross, net, and unreviewed variants), Governance Lag, Justification Half-Life, and Trust Gradient. These metrics are designed to function as program-level indicators of governance responsiveness, analogous to the role that DORA metrics play in measuring software delivery performance. The framework is applied to both human and non-human identity (NHI) governance contexts, with analysis of how each metric behaves differently across identity types. We position this framework not as a replacement for existing IGA measurement approaches but as a complementary layer that captures the dynamic properties current metrics do not address.

title: Liquidity Before Information: Why Transparency Fails Upstream and What Actually Breaks Monopsony in the Myanmar Jade Supply Chain
affiliations: VNU-HCM High School for the Gifted (PTNK)

detail.title: Liquidity Before Information: Why Transparency Fails Upstream and What Actually Breaks Monopsony in the Myanmar Jade Supply Chain

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an active mid-to-high segment jade market practitioner. Analytical judgments have been formalized into model structure to permit independent evaluation.

detail.abstract: Standard information asymmetry models predict that market exploitation persists because sellers know more than buyers. This paper argues that in the Myanmar jade supply chain, this framing misidentifies the operative constraint. Drawing on a formal oligopsony model with survival-level time horizons and practitioner field observation, I demonstrate that upstream miners are not primarily constrained by lacking price information; they are constrained by lacking liquidity and time. Under quasi-hyperbolic discounting with a survival-level planning horizon, when a broker is the only cash-holding agent in a conflict zone, price knowledge becomes formally irrelevant: the seller's outside option is zero regardless of what they know. This reframing has direct policy implications. Upstream information provision (the standard development economics prescription) cannot shift the exploitation equilibrium. The equilibrium breaks only when downstream margin compression removes the economic incentive to maintain upstream opacity. I propose two mechanisms through which this compression may occur: (1) behavioral transparency tools targeting downstream buyers, reducing the inflated margins that sustain upstream coercion; and (2) the structural pressure posed by synthetic jadeite on the provenance premium. The paper concludes with a proposed empirical methodology for testing the first mechanism, offered as a framework for future research.

title: Repair Explanations are Not Canonical under Clause-Equivalent Encodings: Evidence from the Sen24 Base Case

detail.title: Repair Explanations are Not Canonical under Clause-Equivalent Encodings: Evidence from the Sen24 Base Case
detail.abstract: A finite impossibility witness can certify that a boundary between axiom combinations is real, but does it also determine how the resulting repairs should be presented? We show that it does not, even under a strong comparison notion. Two lever-structured encodings of the same impossibility boundary in the Sen24 base case (n, m) = (2, 4) are shown to be clause-multiset equivalent (≡ CM): they produce identical CNF clause multisets up to variable renaming. Both are UNSAT. Yet their raw lever-level minimal repair families differ. Under the natural lever correspondence that transports bundled repairs to the split lever family, the bundled singleton repair becomes a two-element set that is not inclusion-minimal on the split side, where finer person-specific singleton repairs are available instead. The transported and actual repair families therefore do not coincide. This is an existence theorem: clausemultiset equivalence does not guarantee canonical raw repair explanation. The normative implication is that finite witness legitimization alone-even backed by ≡ CM-does not settle repair presentation. Audit-oriented repair reporting requires an explicit abstraction contract specifying how repairs are to be compared or grouped across encodings.

title: Cognitive Convergence and Systemic Fragility in AI-Driven Financial Markets An Exploratory Framework
affiliations: Institute For Egronitive Intelligence

detail.title: Cognitive Convergence and Systemic Fragility in AI-Driven Financial Markets An Exploratory Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study relies exclusively on publicly available market data and does not involve human participants, personal data, or clinical experimentation.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was independently conducted and self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
The proliferation of large language models (LLMs) across financial markets may represent a source of systemic pressure not yet captured by existing risk frameworks: output-level convergence among AI interpretive systems. As AI systems trained on overlapping datasets progressively interpret identical market information in correlated ways, financial ecosystems may transition from healthy interpretive diversity toward representational monoculture-highly efficient locally, potentially fragile globally. 
This paper proposes ergonitive finance as an exploratory experimental framework studying this possible mechanism. The framework rests on three contributions: (1) the cognitive convergence hypothesis-AI interpretive convergence as a possible hidden layer of systemic fragility not captured by traditional volatility metrics; (2) an entropy-based synchronization proxy centered on CC(t); and (3) the adaptive 1 disagreement principle-the conjecture that preserving interpretive heterogeneity may function as a systemic stabilizing mechanism. 
Three retrospective case studies (GameStop 2021, SVB 2023, AI Rally 2023) are offered as qualitative illustrations. Two prospectively specified hypotheses (H1, H2) structure the empirical validation agenda at n_min = 194 trades per group, horizon October-December 2026. The framework is explicitly experimental: it does not claim deterministic prediction, universal applicability, or superiority over existing risk models.

title: The Offtake-Commitment Mechanism: Sigma-Channel Identification via Cross-Sectoral Heterogeneity in Clean-Hydrogen Investment

detail.title: The Offtake-Commitment Mechanism: Sigma-Channel Identification via Cross-Sectoral Heterogeneity in Clean-Hydrogen Investment
detail.abstract:
Pre-financial-investment-decision (pre-FID) offtake commitments in clean-hydrogen projects reduce the cumulative cancellation probability by 11.3 to 13.2 percentage points across five convergent matching estimators (IPWRA, OLS-adjusted, regression-adjusted matching, doubly-robust IPTW, naive IPW), using a project-level panel of 1,354 announced developments from the S&P Global Hydrogen Project Database (2010-2026). The estimate is exceptionally robust to unobserved-confounder bias: the Oster delta_null = 20.23 implies that for unobservables to explain the effect, they would need to be twenty times more influential than the maximally-included set of observable controls. This is the largest and most identification-secure treatment effect in the related dissertation work. 

The substantive interpretation invokes the sigma-channel of the real-options framework: offtake commitments reduce revenue volatility and counterparty risk simultaneously. The sigma-channel comparative statics predict that revenue-volatility-reducing instruments should produce larger effects in high-volatility sectors than in low-volatility sectors. We test this prediction directly via cross-sectoral heterogeneity: the offtake-commitment ATT is concentrated in power and heat (-0.30 pp) and transport (-0.27 pp), and substantially smaller or null in chemical (-0.04 pp) and refinery (-0.02 pp). The pattern matches the sigma-channel prediction in sign and approximate magnitude, providing direct mechanism-identifying empirical evidence that complements the average-treatment-effect identification. 

The methodological contribution is a cross-sectoral heterogeneity test as a direct mechanism-identifying strategy, supplementing the conventional partial-identification sensitivity analysis (Oster bounds). The policy implication is that capex-grant programmes such as the EU Innovation Fund should incorporate demonstrable pre-FID offtake-commitment eligibility requirements, jointly addressing the financing-constraint friction (the Innovation Fund's current target) and the counterparty-risk friction (the Innovation Fund currently leaves unaddressed). offtake commitment, counterparty risk, revenue volatility, real options, sectoral heterogeneity, matching estimators, Oster sensitivity, clean hydrogen

title: Vibe Warfare Architecture: A Natural Language-Driven Multi-Agent Framework for Virtual Staff Operations in Military Command and Control
affiliations: Hanwha Systems Co., Ltd

detail.title: Vibe Warfare Architecture: A Natural Language-Driven Multi-Agent Framework for Virtual Staff Operations in Military Command and Control

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed by Hanwha Systems Co., Ltd. This research was conducted independently, outside the author's professional duties, and was not directed, funded, or commissioned by any organization. All sources cited are publicly available.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper presents a conceptual architecture framework and does not involve human participants, patient data, or empirical experiments.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract:
The modern battlefield has evolved into an environment of extraordinary complexity, where drones, cyber operations, electronic warfare, and AI-driven strike systems operate simultaneously. A fundamental structural gap persists across military echelons: tactical units lack dedicated staff organizations, forcing individual commanders to simultaneously manage personnel, intelligence, operations, and logistics decisions — functions distributed across dedicated staff officers at higher echelons; even at operational and strategic echelons, staff vacancies can critically impair advisory functions during time-sensitive situations. This Staff Gap is a pervasive structural challenge in contemporary warfare.

This paper proposes the Vibe Warfare Architecture (VWA): a virtual staff framework in which an ensemble of specialized AI agents — mapped to the U.S. Joint Staff J-series structure — executes staff functions in parallel and applies mutual checks and balances, orchestrated by the commander's natural language intent ('Vibe'). A core architectural innovation is the Inter-Agent Checks and Balances (IACB) mechanism, which addresses the rubber-stamp failure mode documented in reported accounts of single-function AI targeting systems through an independent JAG Agent with veto authority and an immutable audit trail for IHL compliance.

Drawing on declassified case studies from the Battle of Mosul (2016-2017), the Russia-Ukraine War (2022-present), and reported AI targeting practices in the Gaza conflict, this paper demonstrates VWA's structural applicability across tactical, operational, and strategic echelons.

This paper is a conceptual architecture and position paper. It does not present empirical experiments. Its contribution is architectural: a formally specified framework, a new vocabulary, and a structured argument for inter-agent oversight in military AI. Prototype implementation and empirical validation are designated as future work.

title: Digital Transformation of Clean Energy Sector (Solar Energy)
affiliations: Kanzi Business Consultation

detail.title: Digital Transformation of Clean Energy Sector (Solar Energy)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
This master thesis evaluates the feasibility and strategic implementation of establishing a solar photovoltaic (PV) module manufacturing facility in Saudi Arabia under the Photocell for Energy project. The research is based on a supplied project file dated 2022, which proposes a factory located in King Salman Energy Park (SPARK) in the Eastern Province with an annual production capacity of 300 MW, a total investment requirement of approximately SAR 70,730,600, a 25 percent equity and 75 percent external-finance capital structure, and a phased roadmap for industrial operations, digital transformation, R&D, and innovation. The thesis expands the original project into an academic and professional feasibility study by integrating current renewable-energy policy, global PV supply-chain evidence, Industry 4.0 literature, desert-climate PV performance research, technical manufacturing requirements, and project-finance evaluation.

The study adopts a case-study methodology supported by document analysis, secondary-source analysis, strategic management frameworks, technical feasibility modelling, and financial appraisal. PESTEL, Porter Five Forces, SWOT, Business Model Canvas, risk mapping, and sensitivity testing are applied to assess the commercial attractiveness and strategic robustness of the proposed project. The technical study analyses crystalline-silicon PV module production, quality control, facility layout, supply-chain risk, standards compliance, environmental and occupational-health requirements, and operational-readiness conditions. The digital-transformation plan examines cloud computing, industrial internet of things, robotics, simulation, augmented reality, cybersecurity, systems integration, big data analytics, and intelligent automation as staged capabilities rather than isolated technologies.

The financial analysis uses the core project data supplied in the original file. Under the five-year operating cash-flow schedule provided, and excluding terminal value, the project generates a calculated internal rate of return of approximately 18.9 percent, a net present value of about SAR 19,378,093 at a 10 percent discount rate, and a simple payback period of approximately 3.36 years. These indicators suggest promising feasibility, although the thesis emphasizes that an investment decision should be subject to updated supplier quotations, independent technical due diligence, verified offtake assumptions, local-content incentives, debt-term confirmation, tax treatment, working-capital validation, and risk-adjusted scenario testing.

The thesis concludes that the project is strategically aligned with Saudi Arabia's renewable-energy transition, industrial localization goals, and the need for more resilient PV supply chains. Its success depends on credible certification, bankable demand development, disciplined cash conversion, phased technology investment, strong R&D partnerships, and governance mechanisms that convert the country's desert conditions from a risk into a differentiated product-development advantage. The proposed factory should position itself not only as a module assembler, but as a desert-ready PV manufacturing and innovation platform for Saudi Arabia, the GCC, and wider export markets.

title: Electoral System and Spatial Inequality: Theory and Quantitative Analysis
affiliations: National University of Kaohsiung

detail.title: Electoral System and Spatial Inequality: Theory and Quantitative Analysis
detail.abstract: This paper examines the implications of electoral systems for public-good provision and regional inequality in a spatial economy. We develop a stylized quantitative spatial generalequilibrium model with migration, public goods, and elections. Individuals can move across regions and vote on the allocation of the national budget between local and national public goods, while political representation depends on whether voter registration follows migration and, when it does not, whether migrants can vote remotely. We calibrate the model to Taiwanese migration and public-spending data and evaluate a precinct-voting benchmark system in which voter registration is sticky and ballots must be cast on site. Relative to this benchmark, counterfactual simulations show that introducing absentee voting shifts spending toward the national public good and yields relatively uniform welfare gains across regions. By contrast, when registration follows current residence, local public goods provision and welfare gains become more dispersed across regions. These differences grow with interregional mobility, and when the mobility is sufficiently high, residence-based registration eventually outperforms absentee voting in welfare terms, particularly when preferences for the national public good are weak.

title: Strategic Camouflage and Zombie Cartels: Endogenous Detection in Dynamic Cournot Competition

detail.title: Strategic Camouflage and Zombie Cartels: Endogenous Detection in Dynamic Cournot Competition
detail.abstract:
Competition authorities increasingly rely on empirical screening tools based on observable market signals, such as price anomalies and statistical indicators, to detect collusion. This raises the question of how firms adapt their behaviour in response to such detection mechanisms. 
      We develop an infinitely repeated Cournot model with endogenous detection, in which a Competition Authority allocates enforcement effort based on observed price distortions. Anticipating this response, cartel members have incentives to avoid generating conspicuous signals that could trigger investigation. In equilibrium, firms expand output relative to the monopoly benchmark in order to compress observable price distortions, leading to interior collusion. We refer to this mechanism as strategic camouflage. 
     We then introduce retroactive private damages in the form of a liability stock that accumulates over time. As exposure builds up, the expected cost of detection increases, inducing firms to place greater weight on avoiding detection rather than maximizing short-run profits. The model predicts a gradual compression of observable price distortions even as collusion persists. We refer to this outcome as a zombie cartel. While such behaviour is difficult to observe directly, the mechanism highlights how stock-based liability may induce firms to operate with relatively small observable distortions while remaining coordinated. 
     Overall, enforcement based on observable price signals may transform cartel behaviour rather than eliminate it: collusion becomes less visible but potentially more persistent.

title: Determinants of Implementation of the Circular Economy in the Food Processing Sector on the Example of the Dairy Industry
affiliations: Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute, National Research Institute (PIB) - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI) and Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics – National Research Institute

detail.title: Determinants of Implementation of the Circular Economy in the Food Processing Sector on the Example of the Dairy Industry
detail.abstract: The aim of the study is to present the determinants of the potential application of the circular economy model in the food processing sector on the example the dairy industry. The first part of the article analyzes various factors that stimulate and limit the transformation of the dairy industry towards the circular economy. The second part presents the examples of solutions corresponding to the idea of a circular economy that have been implemented or are planned to be implemented in dairy enterprises. This paper is an overview. It uses strategic EU and national documents, literature on the circular economy in agri- -food systems, as well as reports from the trade press presenting specific examples of the implementation of circular economy solutions in dairies. The analysis shows that in the dairy industry there are great opportunities to implement the circular economy model, but it is a complex process under the influence of stimulating and limiting factors. It requires systemic changes at various levels of the economy, significant financial resources, and above all, adaptation investments in the field of innovative technologies, energy systems, and water and wastewater management. Successful activities supporting the transformation towards the circular economy implemented in dairy enterprises include in particular solutions consisting in: reducing the amount of waste produced and reusing it, direct use of by-products, using renewable energy sources (in heating and cooling systems), reducing consumption of water and reusing it, using eco-friendly packaging and sustainable transportation. In conclusion, it should be stated that the actions taken by the food processing sector, including the dairy industry, aimed at transformation towards the circular economy are necessary, especially in the context of the challenges related to the European Green Deal and the Farm to Fork Strategy.

title: Environmental, Organizational, and Economic Implications for Agriculture in Areas with Different Share of the Natura 2000 Network
affiliations: National Research Institute - Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute (IAFE-NRI)

detail.title: Environmental, Organizational, and Economic Implications for Agriculture in Areas with Different Share of the Natura 2000 Network
detail.abstract: The aim of the study is to assess environmental, organizational, and economic implications for agriculture in municipalities with different share of the Natura 2000 network in Poland. Data on the distribution of Natura 2000 sites and natural management conditions in municipalities are derived from the General Directorate for Environmental Protection and the Institute of Soil Science and Plant Cultivation State Research Institute for 2018. Data on the features of the organizational potential of agriculture across municipalities were collected from the Agency for Restructuring and Modernisation of Agriculture. They were generated on the basis of applications for direct payments under the 2016 and 2021 campaigns submitted by 1345.2 and 1269.5 thousand farms, i.e., the beneficiaries of the 2014-2020 common agricultural policy (CAP), respectively. It was found that municipalities with a large and particularly large share of Natura 2000 areas, as compared to municipalities without such areas, were characterized by significantly worse management conditions and a more diverse landscape, as well as a larger share in agricultural area with extensive production characteristic of high nature value farmlands (HNVf) designated in Poland under the 2014-2020 CAP. Farms located in Natura 2000 areas, as compared to other farms, were characterized by a larger average agricultural area, as well as by lower labor inputs per 1 ha of agricultural area. They were characterized by lower total costs, including direct costs, which resulted in lower factor productivity and income per 1 ha of agricultural area. The conclusion was that they had less development opportunities.

title: Effect of Foreign Farmers’ Presence on Poverty Status of Rural Farming Households in Nigeria
affiliations: University of Ilorin and University of Ilorin

detail.title: Effect of Foreign Farmers’ Presence on Poverty Status of Rural Farming Households in Nigeria
detail.abstract: In pursuing the government's goal of socioeconomic development and poverty reduction, some commercial foreign farmers were invited. Part of the expectation from this collaboration was to boost food production, create jobs for youth, and alleviate rural poverty. The aim of this study was to consider the spillover effect of the foreign farmers' presence on the poverty status of farming households in Kwara State, Nigeria. The population for the study comprises of all the farming households in Edu local government area. There was a random selection of 20 villages and 12 farming households from each village, summing 240 respondents. Analytical methods used were descriptive statistics and structural equation modeling (SEM). Results have shown that adoption index and household size are positively related to total revenue at a 1% level of significance, which indicated a strong influence of the adoption of foreign farmers' technology on the income of local farmers. It was concluded that it is a positive spillover effect of the presence of foreign farmers concerning the technological transfer, increased output with its positive effect on poverty far outweighs the displacement of farmlands. This should preferably be enhanced for better productivity.

title: Tendencies for Usage of Rapeseed Oil and Maize for Biocomponent Production in Poland Between 2015 and 2020
affiliations: Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute

detail.title: Tendencies for Usage of Rapeseed Oil and Maize for Biocomponent Production in Poland Between 2015 and 2020

keywords: Usage of Rapeseed Oil and Maize for Fuel Purposes

detail.abstract: The aim of the article is to present the supply and demand situation on the market of rapeseed oil and maize used for fuel purposes in Poland, as well as analyze the relationship between their prices and production, as well as the consumption of gasoline and diesel fuel. The analysis covered the 2015-2020 period and was based on data from statistics Poland, the National support Center for agriculture, and the Polish Oil industry and Trade Organization. statistical analysis showed that between 2015 and 2020 the dynamics of the usage of raw materials to produce biofuels exceeded the growth rate of their production and harvest. The assessment of the relationship between production and consumption of fuels in Poland showed that the demand from the fuel sector had a dominant influence on the prices of rapeseed oil and maize during the period under consideration, and fuel production had a less significant share in shaping wholesale prices of rapeseed oil and purchase prices of maize. Biofuels are an important and topical issue both in the context of the new energy policy of the european union (eu) and Poland until 2040 and Russia's invasion of ukraine, with one of the consequences being the energy crisis and the announcement of the eu becoming independent from Russian energy. in such a situation, biofuels and raw materials for their production may turn out to be an important element of improving energy security.

title: Should We End the Fed? Can We?
affiliations: University of Mississippi and

detail.title: Should We End the Fed? Can We?
detail.abstract: Should we end the Fed? If so, can we? The first question is largely verboten among academic economists. We discuss the Fed's consequences for U.S. macroeconomic performance and its compatibility with basic democratic norms. The Fed's failure to improve macroeconomic outcomes and its tendency to exceed its legislative mandate suggest that economists are far too quick to dismiss the question of alternative monetary institutions. The second question is insufficiently examined by the Fed's critics. The key constraints are not domestic and economic but international and political. For decades, U.S. policy has promoted and maintained dollar dominance within the international monetary system. The Fed is a crucial institutional support for geopolitical goals. Eliminating the Fed would likely be inconsistent with those goals. Hence, major fiscal and strategic changes must precede any attempt to end the Fed.

title: Culture, Risk-taking, and Public Leadership: Evidence from Chinese Villages

detail.title: Culture, Risk-taking, and Public Leadership: Evidence from Chinese Villages
detail.abstract: Many societies preserve traditional culture tied to risk-taking. This paper shows the substantial impact of traditional risk-taking culture on public leadership and governance, leveraging widely-held zodiac beliefs about risk-avoidance in rural China, which follow an exogenous 12-year cycle tied to a person's birth year. Using a representative village panel, I find that village heads in their risk-avoidant zodiac years follow governance processes more and enhance villagers' perception about responsiveness. I also observe consistent expenditure changes, with higher public good spending and a comparable decline in administration spending that is prone to misuse. However, treated leaders are also less likely to promote policy innovation. These results can be most easily reconciled with a shift in village heads' risk-taking, which may yield a potential trade-off between accountability and public entrepreneurship.

title: Assessment of the Effectiveness of the School Fruit Scheme and School Fruit and Vegetables Scheme in Poland
affiliations: Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute and Institute of Agricultural and Food Economics - National Research Institute

detail.title: Assessment of the Effectiveness of the School Fruit Scheme and School Fruit and Vegetables Scheme in Poland
detail.abstract: The growing health problems of the world's population related to inadequate nutrition have prompted many countries to take measures to develop healthy eating habits. One of the activities in the EU was the implementation of the School Fruit Scheme between 2009/10 and 2016/17, and School Fruit and Vegetables Scheme since 2017/18, in which fruit and vegetables have been one of the two components (the second component is milk and milk products). The aim of the article was to evaluate their effectiveness in terms of the consumption of fruit and vegetables in Polish families. The article was based on: EU legal acts, evaluations of the functioning and implementation of the schemes made by EU and Polish institutions, statistical data from Statistics Poland, and a review of the literature on the consumption of fruit and vegetables. It was found that despite the greater number of schools and children participating in the scheme and the growing expenses for its implementation, in most EU countries, including Poland, there is no increase in the consumption of horticultural products covered by the scheme (Pearson's correlation coefficient between the number of children participating in the scheme and consumption in households between 2009/10 and 2020/21 amounted to-0.77). The reasons may be the weaknesses of the scheme (i.e., generally poor quality of products, too short duration of the scheme, and also insufficient involvement of parents in its implementation) on the one hand and the influence of other factors determining the consumption of fruit and vegetables under the scheme being difficult to statistically confirm (greater availability of other products, ineffective advertising) on the other.

title: Explaining versus Predicting Mutual Fund Returns: Machine Learning, Factor Attribution, and Market Efficiency
affiliations: University of Dundee

detail.title: Explaining versus Predicting Mutual Fund Returns: Machine Learning, Factor Attribution, and Market Efficiency
detail.abstract: Machine learning decomposes mutual fund returns with high fidelity but extracts no forward return signal-a boundary predicted by semi-strong market efficiency that no prior study has tested at this scale. Using 1,100 actively managed U.S. equity funds from January 2000 through December 2025, we evaluate fourteen model architectures on 54 publicly traded factor indices spanning equities, fixed income, commodities, and international assets. ElasticNet achieves 77.57% contemporaneous out-of-sample R², exceeding a Ridge OLS benchmark by 3.81 percentage points. Yet nine one-periodahead trading strategies produce an average annual return of 3.03% (average t-statistic = 1.41), with no strategy surviving multiple-testing adjustment. A contemporaneous quintile sort delivers a 64.69% annualized long-short spread that collapses to 2.41% in forward prediction-economically negligible and statistically indistinguishable from zero (t = 1.10). SHAP-based attribution further reveals that Morningstar style categories explain only 6.0% of cross-sectional factor-exposure variation, with 94.0% attributable to fund-specific heterogeneity, demonstrating that fund-level factor analysis materially dominates categorical classification for risk monitoring purposes.

title: Agriculture in the Peripheries – The Kingdom of Bhutan
affiliations: Warsaw University of Life Sciences and Warsaw University of Life Sciences

detail.title: Agriculture in the Peripheries – The Kingdom of Bhutan
detail.abstract: The main aim of the paper is to familiarize the readers with the economy, and above all the agricultural sector of the kingdom of Bhutan. The direct inspiration for this paper was the ban on cage breeding of laying hens introduced in this country in 2012, which brings to mind an important event, which happened in 1972, when the king of Bhutan announced the concept of the Gross National happiness index (GNh). Figures and graphics presented in the article were prepared on the basis of Bhutan's national statistics and available publications. The structure of Bhutan's economy is dominated by the industrial and services sectors. the share of agriculture in generating GdP has ranged from 14 to 22% in the last twenty years, with employment in agriculture reaching almost 60% of the total workforce. the agricultural sector is highly fragmented, and at the same time vulnerable to threats resulting from difficult natural conditions and climate change. Bhutan is not achieving food self-sufficiency, despite strong support from Bhutanese authorities for the sector and increasing productivity. The changes taking place in agriculture and the entire economy of Bhutan are strongly oriented towards the implementation of the sustainable development paradigm.

title: What Cadastral Tax Rate Should be Imposed on Farm Assets
affiliations: National Research Institute (PIB)

detail.title: What Cadastral Tax Rate Should be Imposed on Farm Assets
detail.abstract: The aim of the study was to determine cadastral tax rate calculated on farm assets, which would allow for replacing the current wealth taxes without increasing the tax burden for farms. The research was based on data from FADN (Farm Accountancy Data Network) farms. The method of financial analysis simulation was used. The research shows that the total wealth tax burden related to farm income is small. The taxes are the greatest burden to the income of very small farms whose economic size is between EUR 2,000 and 8,000 annually (7.37%) and farms dealing with field crops (4.36%). Meanwhile, farms dealing with horticulture (0.69%) and poultry production (0.54%), as well as large farms with an annual economic size of EUR 100,000–500,000 (1.93%) and very large farms with an economic size of more than EUR 500,000 (1.13%) currently pay relatively lower taxes. It was also found that significant changes occurred in the structure of farm assets. While in the 1970s the largest share (approx. 84%) of the assets of individual farms at that time concerned buildings, currently the share of buildings in assets decreased to approx. 19%. There is a relatively larger share of buildings in assets among farms specialized in horticulture and poultry amounting to 43.2 and 37.8%, respectively. The research allowed for determining the rate of a possible cadastral tax, while maintaining the current tax burden for farms. The tax rate may not exceed 0.22%. Relating it to the value of buildings, permanent crops, and land, it will not increase the current tax burden for farms.

title: Calibration-Aware Pneumonia Evaluation: A Reproducible Framework for Threshold Optimization, Reliability Assessment, and Structured Workflow Support
affiliations: Université de Moncton, Alfaisal University, University of Hail and National College Of Business Administration & Economics

detail.title: Calibration-Aware Pneumonia Evaluation: A Reproducible Framework for Threshold Optimization, Reliability Assessment, and Structured Workflow Support
detail.abstract: Chest X-ray pneumonia detection has been widely studied using deep learning, yet many evaluation pipelines remain focused mainly on discrimination metrics such as accuracy, sensitivity, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. These metrics are important but insufficient for decision-support settings in which predicted probabilities should be calibrated, uncertainty should be recognized, and uncertain or high-risk cases should be routed toward appropriate workflow actions. This paper introduces a reproducible calibration-aware pneumonia evaluation framework that integrates predictive modeling, validation-optimized threshold selection, probability calibration, Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty estimation, and constrained multi-criteria workflow evaluation. The objective is not to propose a new state-of-the-art chest X-ray architecture, but to provide a reliability-oriented evaluation pipeline that connects model probabilities with calibrated confidence, threshold-sensitive behavior, uncertainty-aware safety analysis, and structured workflow support. The framework is evaluated on PneumoniaMNIST and further examined under external chest X-ray transferability validation. Temperature scaling preserved discrimination performance and ranking behaviour, but it did not reduce the reported test ECE relative to the raw model; this motivates interpreting calibration jointly with ranking preservation, NLL, MCE, and reliability plots rather than as a single-metric improvement.  A constrained multi-criteria decision-support layer translated calibrated pneumonia probability and predictive uncertainty into four workflow actions: low-risk monitoring, additional evidence acquisition, clinician-confirmed treatment, and escalation for high-risk uncertain cases.The proposed framework provides a transparent and reproducible route for evaluating pneumonia detection models beyond binary classification. By integrating calibration, uncertainty, threshold analysis, safety auditing, and workflowlevel interpretation, it supports more cautious and operationally meaningful assessment of chest X-ray AI decisionsupport systems.

title: The Costs of Leader Biases: Evidence from Superstitious Chinese Mayors
affiliations: and Renmin University of China - School of Applied Economics

detail.title: The Costs of Leader Biases: Evidence from Superstitious Chinese Mayors
detail.abstract: Throughout history, political leaders have not been immune to their subjective beliefs — ranging from denialism to superstitions — yet we lack systematic evidence on their economic consequences.  This paper documents the substantial impact of leaders' non-factual beliefs, leveraging enduring traditional Chinese superstitions about spaces, which enables us to link quasi-random, leader-specific variation to regional development in their cities. We find that municipal zones perceived as unfavorable to mayors have an average 2 percent lower GDP compared to other zones. Exploiting mayoral reports and administrative micro-data, we show greater disruption in local public investment as a key driver. Downstream changes in firms and households further amplify the loss, with a 6% decrease in firm entry, a 4% reduction in the productivity of remaining firms, and a small population decline. While better institutional environments mitigate these effects, campaign-style ideological training does not. Our back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests such non-factual beliefs of Chinese mayors are associated with at least a 0.1% annual GDP loss over the past two decades. Overall, our findings highlight leaders' subjective beliefs as a quantitatively important determinant of economic performance.

title: Towards a Digital Knowledge Act: Mapping Policy Options for Legal Risk Mitigation
affiliations: Institute for Information Law (IViR), University of Amsterdam,  and

detail.title: Towards a Digital Knowledge Act: Mapping Policy Options for Legal Risk Mitigation

declarations.funderStatement: Research conducted between February 2025 and April 2026, carried out jointly by Dr. Kacper Szkalej, Etienne Valk and Prof. Dr. Martin Senftleben, Institute for Information Law (IViR), University of Amsterdam. Funding for this project was secured from COMMUNIA Association. The authors have conducted this study in complete academic independence.

detail.abstract:
Drawing on desk research, stakeholder interviews, and policy analysis, this report identifies and analyses the principal sources of copyright-related uncertainty in the EU copyright system and their implications for knowledge institutions. It considers both the legal framework and ways in which copyright may be strategically leveraged against institutions. Subsequently, the report identifies and evaluates legal mechanisms that may reduce copyright-related uncertainty and create a more predictable environment for knowledge institutions. These mechanisms are: (i) best-practice guidelines; (ii) an advisory and dispute settlement body; (iii) a liability privilege for diligent staff acting in good faith; (v) a country-of-origin rules for cross-border research; and (vi) measures against unfair contract terms. Each mechanism addresses a distinct source of legal uncertainty, yet together they may allow knowledge institutions to move away from a culture of defensive overcompliance towards a position of confident, lawful use of copyright flexibilities.


The report ultimately advances a reform agenda that builds on the existing copyright acquis, emphasising the importance of certainty, fairness, and equitable access to knowledge. Reforms should reaffirm copyright’s role as a facilitator of research and innovation and as a protector of the public interest. Without a coherent, enabling regulatory framework that explicitly recognises and mitigates legal risks, the work of the very institutions designed to drive educational and scientific advancement may be impeded. This, in turn, undermines the fundamental purpose of EU copyright law itself.


As the analysis shows, the plethora of conditions and limiting factors that accompany copyright provisions seeking to support teaching, research and the work of cultural heritage institutions casts doubt upon the effectiveness of these provisions in practice. The minimal degree of legal certainty offered by the provisions for knowledge institutions in EU copyright law raises serious doubts about the potential of the current rules to reconcile the competing fundamental rights at stake. In other words: without appropriate countermeasures, as proposed at the end of this report, the current EU copyright acquis in the field of teaching, research and cultural heritage may be unconstitutional.

title: Too Negative to Believe? How Headline Sentiment Shapes Truth Judgments About Misinformation
affiliations: London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE) - Department of Psychological and Behavioural Science,  and London School of Economics

detail.title: Too Negative to Believe? How Headline Sentiment Shapes Truth Judgments About Misinformation

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval statement This study involved human participants and received ethics approval from the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) Research Ethics Committee. All participants provided informed consent prior to taking part in the study. Participation was voluntary, and respondents were informed of the purpose of the research, their right to withdraw, and the treatment of their data in accordance with applicable ethical and data protection requirements.

detail.abstract: Misinformation on social media is disproportionately negative in tone, yet whether the emotional framing of a headline causally affects belief remains an open question. We address this using a choice-based conjoint experiment in which 500 US respondents evaluated real headlines about Donald Trump's 2023indictment, formatted as Facebook posts. Headlines were randomly assigned values on four attributes: veracity, lexical sentiment, partisan bias, and social endorsement cues. We find that moderately negative sentiment increases belief in false claims by 11 percentage points with no comparable effect on true news, indicating that negativity functions as a credibility cue specific to misinformation. This effect is non-linear: extreme negativity reverses direction and triggers skepticism. Partisan framing uniformly reduces credibility, but the penalty falls disproportionately on outgroup-aligned headlines, consistent with information avoidance rather than concordanceseeking. Finally, likes attributed to friends increase belief in false headlines while decreasing belief in true ones. These findings establish that the words used to frame a claim, not only its factual content or source, shape truth judgments, with direct implications for platform design and media literacy interventions.

title: The Absence of Consensus and Restraint in US Trade Policy: Implications for the World Trading System
affiliations: Brooklyn Law School

detail.title: The Absence of Consensus and Restraint in US Trade Policy: Implications for the World Trading System
detail.abstract: The problem with US trade policy – for both the world trading system and the US itself – is the absence of consensus paired with a lack of meaningful legal restraint.  There is no political consensus on the aims of international trade.  There is limited legal restraint on what trade policies the president in power can pursue.  This combination has led to more than a decade of trade-policy whiplash unmoored from a coherent strategy.  If it endures, it will continue to cause damage to the US economy and alliance system, and to the world trading system itself.

title: Quantifying Tax-Drag Shelter Benefits in Roth Conversions: RMD Reduction and the Hidden Roth Contribution
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Quantifying Tax-Drag Shelter Benefits in Roth Conversions: RMD Reduction and the Hidden Roth Contribution
detail.abstract: Roth conversions generate alpha by sheltering assets from the tax drag inherent in taxable accounts, Tax-Drag Shelter (TDS). A Roth conversion involves two distinct planning decisions: whether to convert, and conditional on converting, whether conversion tax should be paid from Inside or Outside assets. These decisions generate two distinct tax-drag shelter alphas: RMD-reduction alpha (Conversion decision) and Synthetic Roth Contribution (SRC) alpha (Outside-settlement decision only).  Both alphas reduce to the valuation identity, 𝛼 = 𝑃 ⋅ 𝜇, where 𝑃 is sheltered principal and 𝜇 is the per-dollar present value of the yearly sheltered-vs-taxable distribution gap.  Embedding SECURE 2.0'S bounded owner-life and beneficiary distribution structure is the critical addition that closes the stream and admits closed-form present-value measurement of both alphas.

title: Mechanism Design over Magnitude: A Multi-Jurisdiction Evaluation of Carrot-Policy Effectiveness in Clean-Hydrogen Implementation

detail.title: Mechanism Design over Magnitude: A Multi-Jurisdiction Evaluation of Carrot-Policy Effectiveness in Clean-Hydrogen Implementation
detail.abstract:
We evaluate six major clean-hydrogen policy interventions across four jurisdictions (US 45Q, US 45V three-pillars NPRM, EU Innovation Fund, EU CBAM, UK Track-1, China 14th Five-Year Plan) using a project-level panel of 1,354 announced hydrogen developments from the S&P Global Hydrogen Project Database (2010– 2026). Treatment effects on cumulative cancellation probability are estimated using modern difference-in-differences estimators (Sun–Abraham IW, Borusyak–Jaravel– Spiess imputation, IPWRA matching, Synthetic DiD, Causal Forests, and Deaner– Ku hazard DiD) and accompanied by Rambachan–Roth honest-sensitivity bounds. 
Three substantive findings emerge. First, the magnitude ranking of policy effects (China 14th FYP > US 45Q > UK Track-1 ≫ EU Innovation Fund) systematically follows the number of economic frictions each instrument addresses, not the perunit monetary value of the subsidy. The China FYP estimate of −4.5 percentage points (honest-DiD breakdown M∗ = 1.5) exceeds the US 45Q estimate of −3.4 percentage points (M∗ = 0.2) despite comparable per-unit subsidy value, consistent with multi-friction mechanism dominance. Second, two informative nulls are identified: the EU Innovation Fund produces a precise null across six convergent estimators, and the EU CBAM produces a precise null across eight convergent estimators. The substantive interpretation is that the financing-constraint friction is not binding in the contemporary capital-abundant hydrogen environment, and that border-adjustment transmission to project-level investment decisions is weak in the early-implementation phase. Third, the US 45V three-pillars NPRM tripledifference estimate of +0.285 on US-Green cancellation hazard identifies friction amplification by policy design — the cleanest empirical test of perverse-direction κ-channel effects in the sample.
