declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was conducted in accordance with ethical research principles. Informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to data collection. Respondents were informed that participation was voluntary, that responses were anonymous, and that data would be used solely for academic research purposes. No personal identifiers were collected. The study targeted adult professional employees of Lamu County Government in their official capacity. Ethical clearance was obtained through Tsinghua University's academic supervisory framework under which the original Master of Public Administration thesis research was conducted (May 2023).
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no dedicated external funding. The author is supported by the Chinese Government Scholarship Programme (CSC) administered through the Institute of South-South Cooperation and Development (ISSCAD), National School of Development, Peking University, Beijing, China.

detail.abstract: Despite decades of procurement reform in Kenya's devolved government system, the relationship between procurement ethics and functional performance in county government entities remains empirically underexplored. This paper investigates the association between five core ethical constructs -- accountability, confidentiality, transparency, professionalism, and integrity-and the performance of the procurement function at Lamu County Government, Kenya. Drawing on primary survey data from 53 procurement and finance employees and employing ordinary least squares regression with a combined ethical practice index, the study finds that procurement ethical practices are strongly and positively associated with procurement performance (R-squared = 0.923, p < 0.001). Each of the five ethical constructs exhibits a statistically significant positive coefficient. The combined ethical practice index yields a coefficient of 2.178, indicating that a unit improvement in ethical practices is associated with a 2.178-unit increase in procurement performance. These findings align with principal-agent and institutional theoretical frameworks and carry direct policy implications for Kenya's county procurement governance. The study recommends that Lamu County Government and analogous devolved entities institutionalise ethical codes, embed ethics in performance management frameworks, and invest in regular professional training for procurement staff.

title: Who Pays for Natural Disasters? Firm Exit, Market Power, and Consumer Prices
affiliations: Stockholm School of Economics, Copenhagen Business School and ShanghaiTech University, School of Entrepreneurship and Management

detail.title: Who Pays for Natural Disasters? Firm Exit, Market Power, and Consumer Prices
detail.abstract: Using establishment-level data and scanner-based retail prices, we show that the number of firms declines and local retail prices rise in counties affected by natural disasters. Price increases are particularly pronounced for essential goods and low-priced products, as well as in counties with fewer bank branches per capita, where fewer firms enter following natural disasters. The effects extend beyond retailers: large producers raise prices following disasters, especially when many of their competitors are also affected, while smaller producers do not. Consistent with these pricing patterns, large firms experience increases in sales and profits following natural disasters. Our results suggest that the costs of climate-related disasters, which are increasingly frequent negative realizations of physical risk, are ultimately borne by consumers, while large firms benefit from the redistribution of market shares.

title: Tax Salience: How Requiring Transparency Affects the Price of Equality
affiliations: Australian National University (ANU) and University of Massachusetts Amherst

detail.title: Tax Salience: How Requiring Transparency Affects the Price of Equality
detail.abstract: Less-salient taxes can ease the classic equality-efficiency trade-off by making people respond less to taxation. But deliberately obscuring taxes may be viewed as dishonest. This creates a three-way trade-off between equality, efficiency, and honesty. We analyze this trade-off in a simple setting with a linear income tax. We define and characterize the morally efficient frontier, trading off utilitarian welfare against honesty or transparency. Complete honesty is Pareto inefficient but not morally inefficient. More generally, any increase in honesty reduces utilitarian welfare. When utilitarian welfare is decomposed into equality and efficiency, the cost of honesty falls most robustly on equality: higher salience always reduces equality, while the effect on efficiency is ambiguous. This asymmetry is explained by the fact that salience increases the price of equality, which is the efficiency cost of a marginal increase in equality. Our approach could be applied to other settings in which utilitarian and procedural or deontological values conflict.

title:
Trade Wars on the Income Statement: 
The Effects of Tariffs on Firms
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, Federal Reserve Bank of Boston and Federal Reserve Bank of Boston

detail.title:
Trade Wars on the Income Statement: 
The Effects of Tariffs on Firms
detail.abstract: We study the firm-level effects of the 2018 and 2025 US tariff episodes. Combining bill-of-lading, supply chain, and financial data, we construct exposure measures across three channels: direct import costs, upstream suppliers' costs, and retaliatory tariffs on exports, validated using stock returns and earnings calls. We provide new evidence that, in 2025, cost exposure reduced sales and variable costs by about 1 percentage point for firms with average tariff exposure, with no margin or investment effects, consistent with demand-driven contractions under constant markups.

title: Cycle-Anchored Optimization of Immunotherapy Duration in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Multicenter Real-World Study
affiliations: China Medical University, China Medical University, Southern Medical University, Zhengzhou University, China Medical University, China Medical University, China Medical University and China Medical University

detail.title: Cycle-Anchored Optimization of Immunotherapy Duration in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Multicenter Real-World Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors declare no financial or non-financial competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board of Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital, The First Hospital of China Medical University, Nanfang Hospital of Southern Medical University, The First Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University, The First Affiliated Hospital of University of Science and Technology of China, and Shengjing Hospital of China Medical University, (KY2025-473-02, AF‐SOP‐07‐1, 2023‐RE‐113, NFEC-2024-423, and 2025-KT-145). For the local retrospective cohorts, the requirement for written informed consent was waived because all patient data were retrospectively collected and anonymized. For external cohorts, a systematic search of PubMed and Web of Science to identify studies of immunotherapy in patients with NSCLC were conducted. Full texts and associated data sources were then manually reviewed to identify studies that provided publicly accessible patient-level data, including the above-mentioned demographic and survival data. For the enrolled external cohorts, ethics approvals and patient consent were obtained in the original studies, as reported in each study.
declarations.funderStatement: This study received funding from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (92259104).

detail.abstract:
Purpose: The optimal treatment duration of immunotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains uncertain. Under current guideline recommendations, patients in routine clinical practice may be exposed to either premature discontinuation or unnecessary prolonged therapy.

Methods: We analyzed 2,952 patients with NSCLC treated with immunotherapy across six Chinese tertiary hospitals and 22 international cohorts. Landmark cohorts included patients who had reached immunotherapy cycles 6, 12, 14, 18, or 24. Continuation and discontinuation at each time-point were compared using cycle-anchored landmark analyses with clone-censor-weight estimation and stabilized inverse probability weighting. Optimal treatment duration for individual was evaluated using progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS), assessed with weighted Cox models and restricted mean survival time (RMST). In an exploratory safety analysis, immune-related adverse events (irAEs) were assessed across the predefined cycle landmarks.

Results: Among 2,952 patients (median OS: 23·50 months, IQR: 13·95–34·62). Continuation was associated with better PFS and OS benefit at early and mid-course (cycle 6 to 18) landmarks. At cycle 14, continuation showed the strongest association with reduced mortality and progression, remaining robust with overlap weighting for OS (HR, 0·50; 95% CI, 0·38–0·66; P < 0·001) and PFS (HR, 0·34; 95% CI, 0·25–0·46; P < 0·001), whereas benefits attenuated thereafter. RMST-based change-point analyses identified inflection points at cycle 14 and 13 for OS and PFS. Consistent patterns across regions, clinical stage, and treatment regimens analysis support the main finding. Greater survival benefit from continuation beyond cycle 14 was observed in selected subgroups, including women, patients with stage IV disease, and pretreated patients. Cycle 14 showed the highest proportion of grade 1–2 irAEs and the lowest proportion of grade ≥3 irAEs in the safety analyses.

Conclusion: Cycle 14 represents the treatment landmark at which continued ICI therapy showed the greatest survival benefit. The accompanying irAE profile supports this landmark as a clinically relevant point for reassessing benefit and toxicity.

title: On the Fuzzification of Projectile Motion Equation
affiliations: Texas A&M International University

detail.title: On the Fuzzification of Projectile Motion Equation
detail.abstract: Due to the extension of the concept of interval arithmetic, fuzzy numbers, which are a specific category of fuzzy sets, are often favored for representing real-world phenomena that involve uncertainty. This paper deals with the fuzzification of projectile motion, a classical physical phenomenon observed in the real world, that leads in the construction of a triangular parabolic fuzzy number, referred as a projectile fuzzy number (PFN), whose properties are analyzed and discussed in detail. The discussion also covers the arithmetic operations involving two PFNs, not only with the established alpha-cut method but also an approximation method is presented, that preserve the shape after the operations. The fuzzification of projectile motion is utilized once more to construct a fuzzy equivalence relation, known as a projectile fuzzy equivalence relation. It has been shown that the dissimilarity of the projectile fuzzy equivalence relation constitutes a metric, the formula for which is presented explicitly. The application part of the study illustrates the qualitative fuzzy data clustering of the Iris dataset, the Cancer dataset, and the Crude Oil dataset by employing the established projectile fuzzy equivalence relation as a similarity measure among the data points.

title: Does the Nikkei Quanto Spread Contain a Monetizable Risk Premium?

detail.title: Does the Nikkei Quanto Spread Contain a Monetizable Risk Premium?
detail.abstract: The quanto-adjusted risk premium is the difference between the return of a quanto futures contract and that of the conventional futures contract with the same underlying. It is shown to be the sum of the realized covariance of the return of the underlying with the exchange rate and the return of a market neutral spread between the contracts. As such, this risk premium can be monetized only insofar as the market prices of the contracts imply a mispricing of the forward covariance. For if this premium, as given by the return difference, prices the forward covariance correctly, then the market-neutral spread from which we can extract profit will return zero. An analysis of the historical prices of the Nikkei 225 quanto USD Index futures versus the conventional Nikkei 225 index futures confirms this relationship and shows that the mispricing is small, but persistent. Further, the premium is found to be strongly dependent on the realized covariance from the recent past, which is itself mean reverting. Thus, the mispricing results from the premium not pricing in the mean reversion. However, since it is small, a simple implementation of the famous Nikkei quanto "correlation trade" to capture it may not work after transaction costs. Better implementations are discussed.

title: Aging, Credentials, and Replacement Risk in the U.S. Public-Sector Workforce: A Multi-State Analysis

detail.title: Aging, Credentials, and Replacement Risk in the U.S. Public-Sector Workforce: A Multi-State Analysis
detail.abstract: Public-sector workforce planning is dominated by headcount, yet the count is silent about composition, and two workforces of identical size can face very different replacement risk depending on who their employees are. This study uses a cross-sectional analysis of person-level microdata from the 2024 American Community Survey Public Use Microdata Sample for five large and diverse states (California, Florida, Minnesota, New York, and Texas), comprising 544,563 employed records of which 83,809 are government workers representing approximately 8.3 million weighted employees. All estimates are accompanied by margins of error computed from the eighty ACS replicate weights. The government workforce is older than the private workforce (25.0 percent against 20.8 percent aged 55 or older) and more credentialed (54.6 against 37.6 percent with a bachelor's degree or higher), and these gaps hold in every state. Because government is concentrated in older, more credentialed occupations, we test whether the gaps survive adjustment for occupational mix: standardizing the government workforce to the private-sector occupational distribution leaves the age gap intact (27.2 against 20.8 percent) and a smaller but real credential gap (41.1 against 37.6 percent), and government workers are older than private workers within nineteen of twenty-one major occupations, so the age gap is a sector effect rather than a composition artifact. A replacement-risk ratio of employees aged 55 and over per employee under 35 is higher in government (0.90 against 0.54). The most distinctive results are the consistency of these patterns across five diverse states and the joint occupational distribution of aging and credential intensity, which locates the sharpest exposure in credentialed occupations with thin younger pipelines such as management and legal. We argue that workforce monitoring should report workforce composition by age, credential, and occupation rather than headcount alone.

title: Judicial Reform and Breakthrough Innovation: Evidence from China

detail.title: Judicial Reform and Breakthrough Innovation: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: China's 2020 complex-simple civil case diversion reform increased breakthrough patents by 24.9 percent, while leaving total and incremental patents statistically unchanged. The paper uses the reform as a quasi-natural experiment that improved the speed of civil dispute resolution in 20 pilot cities. The evidence points to a financial-enforcement channel: treated courts resolve debt-related civil cases faster, exposed firms receive more trade credit, face lower financing constraints, and raise R&D spending. The effect is larger in technologically specialized city-industry cells and in industries with higher litigation intensity. The results show that procedural judicial efficiency matters for innovation because firms need enforceable contracts to finance and organize risky research.

title: Importing Fragility: When Do Capital Inflows Destabilize Banks? *
affiliations: European University Institute - Economics Department (ECO) and University of International Business and Economics (UIBE)

detail.title: Importing Fragility: When Do Capital Inflows Destabilize Banks? *

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no conflicts of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: not needed
declarations.funderStatement: There was no external finance for this project.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how household indebtedness mediates the relationship between international capital flows and bank stability. We develop an open-economy banking model in which capital inflows initially improve bank liquidity but fuel increases in household leverage, creating a non-monotonic relationship: foreign funding enhances stability at low leverage but becomes destabilizing beyond a critical threshold. Using panel data for 105 economies from 1995-2024, we find that capital inflows improve bank stability when household debt-to-GDP remains below approximately 80%, but significantly increase crisis likelihood at higher leverage levels. Capital controls mitigate this fragility, particularly in fixed exchange rate regimes. Our findings highlight household balance sheets as a critical transmission mechanism for international financial shocks, with direct implications for macro-prudential policy and capital account management.

title: Geographic Variation in the Performance of Public Sector Hospitals in Seven Latin American Countries
affiliations: Inter-American Development Bank, Inter-American Development Bank, Universidad del Rosario - Faculty of Economics, Blutitude, Blutitude and Inter-American Development Bank

detail.title: Geographic Variation in the Performance of Public Sector Hospitals in Seven Latin American Countries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study used de-identified data on hospital discharges that were provided by national statistical offices or Ministries of Health and arise from the delivery of routine public services. No individual-level or identifiable patient information was accessed.
declarations.funderStatement: This study received financial support from the Inter-American Development Bank.

detail.abstract:
Background: Geographic variation in hospital quality and efficiency is well documented and often reflects unwarranted variation. Documenting such variation is relevant since it allows to identify performance gaps and design policies to reduce it and improve quality, equity, and efficiency while lowering costs. This issue is particularly pressing in Latin America and the Caribbean, where hospitals account for a large share of health expenditure, yet evidence on hospital performance remains limited and fragmented.

Methods: We analyzed administrative hospital discharge and birth records (18.9 million discharges and 5.3 million births on average yearly) from public sector hospitals in Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, El Salvador, Mexico, Paraguay, and Peru between 2015 and 2019. We constructed standardized indicators of hospital effectiveness (intra-hospital mortality), efficiency (length of stay), and appropriateness of care (cesarean section rates) at the national and subnational level. We summarized the subnational variation using the interquartile ratio and estimated potential gains of reducing this variation.

Findings: There is substantial variation in all standardized indicators between and within countries. On average, states at the 75th percentile outperform those at the 25th percentile by roughly 40%, even after adjusting for demographics and disease profiles. Potential gains in a conservative scenario could avert around 3.9% of C-sections, 7.1% of intra-hospital deaths and 7.4% of hospital days of stay.

Interpretation: The region needs to strengthen hospital performance monitoring systems and target unwarranted variation to improve quality and efficiency in health care.

title: Academic Staff Welfare and Job Performance in Federal Universities in South-South Geopolitical Zone of Nigeria

detail.title: Academic Staff Welfare and Job Performance in Federal Universities in South-South Geopolitical Zone of Nigeria

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declared no conflicting interest
declarations.funderStatement: No funding or this study

detail.abstract: The study investigated the relationship between academic staff welfare and their job performance in federal universities in South-South, geopolitical zone of Nigeria. The welfare of academic staff is a critical factor in determining their job satisfaction, motivation and overall performance. However, from the literature reviewed so far it was observed that the relationship between academic staff welfare and their job performance has not been given adequate attention in the context of incentive package, office accommodation, internet facilities, electricity, and healthcare system in federal universities in South-South. This study aimed to bridge this gap by examining the relationship between these variables. Five specific purpose, five research questions and five null hypotheses were formulated to guide the study. Two motivational theories directed the study Herzberg’s motivation two-factor theory 1959 and Maslow’s Hierarchy of needs 1943. And correlational research design was adopted, while the population of the study consists of 7,506 academic staff in the six federal universities in South-South. The sample size was 245 respondents. Two research instruments validated by three research experts were used to elicit data for the study. Pearson product moment correlation was used in answering the research questions and testing of the five null hypotheses at 0.05 level of significance. The findings of the study revealed that there is significant relationship between academic staff welfare and their job performance in federal universities in South-South, though with some of the variables showing a weak relationship. It was recommended among others that, federal government should develop and implement a competitive incentive packages to motivate academic staff in federal universities in South-South, focusing on monetary and non-monetary rewards.

title: Environmental Intensity Across Economic Sectors
affiliations: KU Leuven

detail.title: Environmental Intensity Across Economic Sectors
detail.abstract: This note introduces a dataset that provides sector-level environmental intensity rankings derived from EXIOBASE 3 environmental satellite accounts. Economic sectors were evaluated across multiple environmental indicators such as GHG emissions, air pollution, water toxicity, land use, water use, and material extraction. The dataset ranks sectors in a general environmental intensity indicator based on how they rank across individual indicators. The resulting rankings offer a comparative overview of the environmental intensities of economic sectors per unit of economic output. The dataset is designed to support degrowth research and advocacy by identifying environmentally intensive sectors. The framework is not without limitations though; it should not be taken as a call to degrow any high-intensity sectors as it does not account for the social necessity of sectors, or that many 'clean' sectors often drive heavy upstream extraction or intensive downstream processing. Additionally, spikes in volatile commodity prices can lower the environmental intensity per monetary unit of the related sectors rendering them 'clean' without real changes in the environmental impact of its production.

title: Option Pricing under Stochastic Volatility and Jumps: A PIDE Framework with Empirical Evidence
affiliations: Texas Tech University, Texas Tech University, Texas Tech University, Texas Tech University, Texas Tech University and Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School

detail.title: Option Pricing under Stochastic Volatility and Jumps: A PIDE Framework with Empirical Evidence
detail.abstract: We develop a partial integro-differential equation (PIDE) framework for option pricing under joint stochastic volatility and jump dynamics, and evaluate its empirical content using the S&P 500 index option contracts across three maturities. The framework is derived from the infinitesimal generator of an affine Lévy-type process and implemented via finite-difference discretization with FFT-based treatment of the nonlocal jump operator. Calibration via GMM reveals that stochastic volatility accounts for the dominant share of pricing improvement, where relative to Black-Scholes, the Heston specification reduces implied-volatility RMSE by 39%. Jump augmentation via either Merton or CGMY specifications yields marginal improvements concentrated at short maturities and in the deep out-of-the-money region. The calibrated CGMY activity index supports a compound-Poisson structure, consistent with high-frequency evidence on S&P 500 index returns.

title: Comments on the PTO’s Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance, Docket No. PTO-P-2022-0026
affiliations: Bi-Level Technologies

detail.title: Comments on the PTO’s Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance, Docket No. PTO-P-2022-0026
detail.abstract: These comments focus on the very first step in the examiners’ action under 35 U.S.C. § 101—the determination whether the claim is “directed to” a patent-ineligible subject matter. Examiners often make these determinations on a whim, finding “abstract ideas” in claims regardless of what the claims are actually “directed to.” This causes substantial harm to patent applicants by improperly rejecting their claims as patent-ineligible. The comments show that the PTO’s incorrect and arbitrary guidance, both in the PEG and in the MPEP, wrongly instruct examiners to “identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim … that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea.” This contravenes the legal standard enunciated by the Federal Circuit for determining what the claim is “directed to” based on the Claim’s asserted advance over the prior art.

title: Rectified Linear Unit Regression
affiliations: Keio University

detail.title: Rectified Linear Unit Regression
detail.abstract: This paper develops a regression framework for the direct estimation of integrated functionals of conditional outcome distributions. The proposed method, termed rectified linear unit (ReLU) regression, projects the ReLU-transformed outcome onto covariates and admits a closed-form estimator. Its population regression function coincides with the integrated conditional distribution function of the outcome, and its convex conjugate, obtained via the Legendre-Fenchel transformation, recovers the integrated conditional quantile function. Both the regression and its conjugate require only mild distributional assumptions and accommodate non-continuous outcomes. We establish the uniform asymptotic distribution of the estimator and develop inference for the conjugate functional via the delta method for Hadamard directionally differentiable maps. Building on these results, we establish identification and inference for average quantile treatment effects over arbitrary subintervals of probability levels. This broadens the set of distributional parameters available to empirical work.

title: Magnifica Humanitas as the Constitution of Human Supremacy in the Digital Age
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Magnifica Humanitas as the Constitution of Human Supremacy in the Digital Age

declarations.funderStatement: No funder

detail.abstract:
Read most often as a moral commentary on artificial intelligence, Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas (2026), is better understood as something more consequential: the first large-scale theological and constitutional response to the emergence of algorithmic sovereignty. This essay reconstructs the encyclical along that axis. Its governing claim is that the governance failures the document diagnoses are not, at root, ethical failures-failures of intention, virtue, or regulatory compliance-but constitutional failures: failures in the architecture of authority itself. Where the dominant policy literature treats artificial intelligence as a powerful instrument to be used well or badly, the encyclical's deeper logic treats it as an emergent infrastructure of sovereignty that reorganizes who decides, on what basis, and with what possibility of appeal. 
Beginning from the founding opposition between Babel and Jerusalem-recast here as the opposition between centralized informational sovereignty and a plural, subsidiary technological order-the argument develops, in turn, the ontology of simulation without consciousness, the metricization of human dignity, the rise of digital neocolonialism and algorithmic sovereignty, the internal separation of algorithmic powers, the transformation of labor under cognitive-extractive capitalism, the displacement of liberal neutrality by predictive governance, the mechanization of moral agency in autonomous weapons, and the recovery of subsidiarity through decentralized architecture. 
Throughout, the encyclical's anthropology is taken as the foundation for a jurisprudence of human supremacy whose institutional instruments-among them an internal separation of algorithmic powers, hardware-level containment of irreversible action, and an enforceable right to reconstruct automated decisions-are presented not as the heart of the argument but as the architecture that the encyclical's own principles require.

title: Quantifying the Determinants of the U. S. Treasury Term Premium -Theory and Empirical Results
affiliations: Adelphi University - School of Business and University of Texas at Austin - Department of Finance

detail.title: Quantifying the Determinants of the U. S. Treasury Term Premium -Theory and Empirical Results
detail.abstract: When considering the trade-off between equities and Govt securities in active or passive investment management, important inputs are the expected rates of return on equity and Treasury bonds of differing maturities, the volatilities of these assets, and the correlation of their returns. This research considers the theoretical determinants of the Treasury Term Premium, the excess rate of return on the U. S. Treasury portfolio relative to the expected average of the three-month T-Bill short-term riskless rate of interest over the term of the analysis. The theoretical component presents the term premium as the result of an asset pricing model where the asset portfolio is a weighted combination of the equity and Gov't debt markets. In the empirical realm, we explore how both bond volatility and the diversification benefit of holding Treasury bonds, as measured by the relevant correlation, affect the term premium, both in sign and magnitude. Beyond the relevance to investment management, a better understanding of the drivers of the term premium will help guide macroeconomic policy decisions.

title: Beyond disease prevention: rotavirus vaccine rollout and child stunting in Tanzania
affiliations: Institute of Rural Development Planning, Stellenbosch University and Stellenbosch University

detail.title: Beyond disease prevention: rotavirus vaccine rollout and child stunting in Tanzania
detail.abstract: BackgroundTanzania introduced the rotavirus vaccine in January 2013 to reduce the burden of diarrheal disease, a driver of malnutrition. While the vaccine’s effect on diarrheal morbidity and mortality is well established, limited evidence exists on its broader effect on child growth outcomes, particularly stunting which affects about 30% of Tanzanian children under five.MethodsUsing data from the 2015/16 Tanzania Demographic and Health Survey (TDHS) with a sample of 8949 children, this study applies a reduced-form Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) exploiting the vaccine eligibility cutoff (children born ≥ November 2012) and Interrupted Time Series Analysis (ITSA) to estimate both immediate and sustained effects of the vaccine rollout on height-for-age z-score (HAZ).ResultsRDD estimates suggest statistically significant improvements in HAZ for vaccine-eligible children. ITSA results show both immediate gains in child growth and a sustained upward trend in HAZ post-vaccine rollout. Robustness checks using placebo cutoffs and falsification outcomes suggest that the effects are not driven by confounding factors.ConclusionThe introduction of the rotavirus vaccine in Tanzania is associated with reductions in stunting by improving long-term growth outcomes. These findings suggest that vaccination provides benefits beyond infection prevention, serving as an investment in human capital. Policy implications include continuing to prioritise zero-dose and under-vaccinated children, integrating vaccination with maternal and nutrition services and strengthening sustainable financing for vaccination.

title: AM-XGAF: An Adaptive Multi-Agent Explainable AI Governance Framework For Enterprise Digital Banking Ecosystems

detail.title: AM-XGAF: An Adaptive Multi-Agent Explainable AI Governance Framework For Enterprise Digital Banking Ecosystems
detail.abstract: The deployment of interconnected artificial intelligence systems in financial institutions has introduced a governance risk class that existing frameworks do not address: the propagation of governance failures across networked AI agents that share data environments and influence each other's decisions. Current enterprise AI governance frameworks including NIST AI RMF (2023), ISO/IEC 42001 (2023), and the Federal Reserve's SR 11-7 model risk guidance, address governance at the level of individual models. None specifies how governance states should be communicated between AI agents, how governance failures in one agent should be detected before propagating to dependent agents, or how a governance system should coordinate adaptive responses across an agent network in real time. The Financial Stability Board (2022) has identified this multi-agent governance gap as a source of systemic risk in financial AI deployment. This paper introduces AM-XGAF, a design model artefact specifying how adaptive governance coordination mechanisms can detect, contain, and remediate governance failure propagation in enterprise digital banking ecosystems. Developed through Design Science Research (DSR) methodology and grounded primarily in Dynamic Capabilities Theory (Teece et al., 1997), AM-XGAF comprises six-layer governance architecture, a formally specified Agent Communication Protocol enabling governance-aware inter-agent messaging, and a nine-stage adaptive governance feedback engine. The paper introduces governance drift contagion as a formally defined construct identifying inter-agent failure propagation as a distinct systemic risk class requiring dedicated architectural response. Artefact evaluation proceeds through regulatory compliance mapping against GDPR Article 22, EU AI Act Articles 9-14, SR 11-7 model risk management requirements, and MAS Technology Risk Management guidelines, and through two scenario walkthroughs demonstrating the framework's governance response to drift contagion and regulatory change propagation. Five generalizable design principles for adaptive enterprise AI governance are derived in prescriptive form. The paper contributes to Design Science Research in information systems, enterprise AI governance theory, and financial services technology governance practice.

title: Neural Implants: The Promise, Peril, and Regulatory Challenges
affiliations: University of North Carolina School of Law and

detail.title: Neural Implants: The Promise, Peril, and Regulatory Challenges

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None,
declarations.funderStatement: Funded by home institution (UNC) through faculty research support.

detail.abstract:
Neural implants generate considerable enthusiasm. Next generation brain-computer interfaces have particularly captivated the public. This technology translates thoughts into external actions on computers and other devices, offering possible treatments for stroke, spinal cord injury, and other severe afflictions. This Article explores the considerable promise offered by neural implants. But some degree of problematic hype exists. Indeed, much work remains before comprehensive brain-computer interfaces become ready for widespread clinical use. As use of neural implants rapidly expands, the suitability of current regulation takes on increased importance. Yet several dynamics pose thorny challenges for regulating neural implants, such as complicated risk-benefit assessments, difficulty in reversing course after implantation, and uncertain, variable long-term impacts.

This Article further analyzes downsides associated with neural implants. Of particular concern are the abandonment hazards that participants face when unable to maintain effective use of the device because manufacturers and providers no longer support the technology’s continued use or it otherwise becomes obsolete. At the same time, we caution against excessive neuro-exceptionalism. Singling out neural implants for special regulatory requirements may lead to overdeterrence. This Article concludes with some modest recommendations for improving the testing, approval, and clinical use of neural implants.

title: Beyond Recipients: Sibling Spillovers of College Financial Aid
affiliations: and Universidad de los Andes, Colombia - Department of Economics

detail.title: Beyond Recipients: Sibling Spillovers of College Financial Aid
detail.abstract: This paper studies the spillover effects of college financial aid on younger siblings. We exploit the eligibility rules of Ser Pilo Paga (SPP), a large-scale merit- and need-based scholarship program in Colombia, to estimate how having a college-going older sibling affects younger siblings' educational, labor market, and criminal outcomes. When an older sibling qualifies for SPP, younger siblings are more likely to enroll in higher education and in higher-quality institutions, experience temporary declines in formal employment consistent with increased educational investment, and are less likely to be convicted of a crime. The probability that younger siblings themselves qualify for an SPP scholarship rises by 42 percent. Younger siblings of students who narrowly missed the eligibility threshold, and whose families therefore received no financial transfer from the program, also show significant gains in enrollment and reductions in criminal convictions. This pattern is consistent with aspirational and motivational spillovers that operate independently of household resource relief. Spillover effects on enrollment and test scores emerge only when the older sibling performs well in college, are largest in first-generation college families and among siblings close in age, and are present in standardized test scores as early as age eight or nine. The evidence points to aspirations, motivation, and revised beliefs about the returns to education as the primary channels through which college access for one child reshapes the trajectories of others in the same household.

title: The Updated Helm: A Bayesian Style Qualifying Update Specification of Kumar’s Helm for Formula One Race Prediction, 1980 to 2024

detail.title: The Updated Helm: A Bayesian Style Qualifying Update Specification of Kumar’s Helm for Formula One Race Prediction, 1980 to 2024

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I, The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently, without any financial relationship or sponsorship from Formula One, any Formula One constructor, any sports analytics company, any betting or gaming operator, or any other organisation with a stake in the empirical findings of this study. The author holds no shares or financial positions in any company referenced in this paper and has no consulting or advisory relationships with any team, league, or commercial sports analytics provider.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses only publicly available historical Formula One race results data, comprising aggregate race outcomes (finishing position, grid position, constructor identifier, driver identifier, etc.) for races held between 1950 and 2024. No human subjects participated in this study. No personal, biometric, medical, or otherwise sensitive information about individuals was collected, analysed, or stored. The dataset contains only public-domain professional sporting results that are routinely published in newspapers, official race classifications, and sports databases. Ethics committee approval was not required for the use of this publicly available data.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The author conducted this study as an independent researcher. All data sources used in this study (the jolpi.ca mirror of the Ergast Developer API) are publicly available at no cost. All software used in the analysis is open source. The author bore no direct financial cost for the conduct of this research beyond ordinary computing resources.

detail.abstract: Kumar’s Helm is a five facet multiplicative model of two agent competitive outcomes, with facets named Vessel, Experience, Mindset at the moment, Opportunity, and Discernment. In the Standard Helm specification, predictions use only historical pre weekend features. The Updated Helm proposed in this paper treats Saturday qualifying observations not as a sixth independent feature but as Bayesian style updates to two of the existing facets. The driver’s Mindset is multiplicatively adjusted by the qualifying surprise relative to expected grid given prior facets, and the Opportunity facet is replaced by a function of the actual grid position. Across 280,477 pairwise driver matchups in 1,125 Formula One races from 1950 through 2024, the Updated Helm with cross validated qualifying update parameters achieved the highest mean out of sample AUC in both the full era (0.7479) and the modern qualifying era (0.7887), exceeding XGBoost gradient boosting with the same information at AUC 0.7878. The Updated Helm beat the Standard Helm in 96.6 percent of modern era test years and matched feature augmented gradient boosting within 0.001 AUC. A within race teammate decomposition (same constructor) reduced AUC from 0.84 to 0.65, supporting the structural claim that approximately three quarters of F1 predictive signal derives from the vessel and one quarter from driver side facets. The Helm’s empirical purchase in Formula One now sits at the AUC ceiling of feature augmented machine learning, achieved through a structurally cleaner specification.

title: Epidemics in Space: Control, Targeting and Delegation
affiliations: University of Cambridge and Cambridge University

detail.title: Epidemics in Space: Control, Targeting and Delegation
detail.abstract: We analyze optimal disease mitigation in a spatial model where an epidemic disease spreads within and between interconnected regions. We describe optimal strategies and emphasize the role of inter-regional coordination and policy targeting. Delegation of policy to regional planners achieves targeting without coordination, while a centrally determined uniform policy achieves coordination without targeting; both induce inefficiencies. For strongly connected regions, policy coordination is paramount, while for weakly connected regions, targeting becomes more important. Last, we analyze the value of reductions in integration, such as travel restrictions. We show that these may be non-monotone and sensitive to the underlying mitigation policy in place.

title: Who the Safety Net Catches: Trade Shocks, Program Design, and Welfare Take-Up After NAFTA

detail.title: Who the Safety Net Catches: Trade Shocks, Program Design, and Welfare Take-Up After NAFTA
detail.abstract: NAFTA's 1994 tariff phase-out generated a large negative labor-market shock concentrated in the southeastern apparel and textile belt. I examine how the US federal safety net responded, combining a county-level shift-share exposure measure with administrative transfer data on ten federal programs over 1986-2010. Supplemental Security Income transfers fall 6.1 percent per standard deviation of exposure, concentrated in apparel-belt counties at-8.2 percent per standard deviation of apparel-specific exposure. The decline survives a saturated controls stack and seven stricter-identification specifications, with coefficients ranging from-3.4 to-9.9 percent and significant at the 1 percent level in every case. The pattern is consistent with substitution into Social Security Disability Insurance: SSDI administers the same disability standard as SSI but imposes no asset test, and NAFTA-displaced workers' long covered work histories and accumulated assets above SSI's $2,000 threshold route the disability claim to the contributory side. Disability Insurance plus retirement, Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), and Medicaid dollars rise 3.2, 5.9, and 3.7 percent in the baseline and survive the controls stack but are absorbed by state-level policy variation under stricter geographic-by-year fixed effects. The federal safety net's response to NAFTA was a substitution within the disability system rather than a uniform expansion, and the mechanism (a means-tested program paired with a contributory alternative) is portable to any labor-market shock that creates eligibility for both at once.

title: Disrupting Delivery: Why America's AI Infrastructure Build Will Fall Short - and What the Industry Can Do to Save It.

detail.title: Disrupting Delivery: Why America's AI Infrastructure Build Will Fall Short - and What the Industry Can Do to Save It.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests. The author holds no financial position in any company named in this paper and receives no compensation from any vendor, investor, or policy organization referenced. The work was not funded or sponsored by any external party.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This research did not involve human participants, human data, or animals. It is based on analysis of publicly available documents, financial disclosures, and the author's professional experience, and therefore did not require ethics committee approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The work was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: In 2026 the four largest U.S. hyperscalers-Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta-committed combined capital expenditure exceeding $700 billion in a single year, with cumulative AI data center investment projected to reach roughly $8.2 trillion through 2032. This paper argues that the binding constraint on that buildout is not capital, demand, or technology, but construction execution capacity: a physical delivery system constrained by equipment lead times, grid interconnection backlogs, a structural skilled-labor shortage, and a contracting regime that systematically suppresses accurate schedule information. Drawing on public financial disclosures, federal filings, satellite construction analysis, insurance-market data, and the author's thirty-five years of field experience as a contractor, general contractor, and subcontractor, the paper assembles nine independently sourced indicators and models a nine-step contagion through which a single distressed project propagates upward through surety, lending, special-purpose-vehicle, securitization, and private-credit layers. It documents the recent shift by hyperscalers toward behind-the-meter ("bring-your-own-grid") generation as a response to interconnection delay, and argues that this strategy compounds rather than relieves the underlying labor and supply-chain constraints by requiring two megaprojects-a data center and a power plant-drawn from the same depleted resource pools. The paper situates the buildout within the historical pattern of infrastructure and financial overbuilds (the Savings & Loan crisis, the telecom fiber overbuild, the 2008 mortgage crisis, and the V.C. Summer and Three Mile Island nuclear projects), estimates an actionable window of twelve to thirty-six months, and proposes a set of interventions-relational contracting, workforce-pipeline investment, operations-science-based production management, and, centrally, a mandatory Independent Technical Advisor regime modeled on standard practice in other categories of project finance. The contribution is a practitioner-grounded translation of construction-execution risk into terms the capital markets can price.

title: #Me Too Torts
affiliations: Washington University in St. Louis - Washington University in St. Louis - School of Law

detail.title: #Me Too Torts
detail.abstract: #MeToo has demanded greater legal liability for instances of sexual misconduct. At the same time, progressive advocates are increasingly disenchanted with the criminal system and carceral solutions. In this context, tort law has emerged as an attractive venue for interventions to address sexual harm. Courts and the American Law Institute have been gradually expanding negligence and vicarious liability doctrines to enable more victims of sexual misconduct to seek redress. Some courts have allowed plaintiffs to bring negligence claims for rape allegations—until recently adjudicated only as intentional torts. The American Law Institute has approved a section of the Restatement (Third) of Torts that recognizes claims against the wrongdoer’s employer under a theory of respondeat superior, even though courts have traditionally considered sexual misconduct not to fall within the scope of employment and, therefore, not suitable for vicarious liability claims. This Article critiques these incipient judicial developments. It casts doubt on whether these legal innovations would enhance women’s agency and safety and argues that they might instead further disempower women, and create hyper-surveilled spaces in which the danger of sexual violence is felt at every turn. The Article concludes by situating these arguments within a broader critique of tort law as a mechanism for producing gender justice in sex regulation.

title: Twin-Domain Convergence Identity: A Framework for Institutional Namespace Standards in Regulated Digital Asset Infrastructure

detail.title: Twin-Domain Convergence Identity: A Framework for Institutional Namespace Standards in Regulated Digital Asset Infrastructure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of PillarsX, a domain namespace portfolio that holds Twin-Domain pairs (.com/.eth) for regulated digital asset infrastructure terms. The empirical case studies in Section 6 are drawn from the author's own portfolio. This conflict of interest is explicitly acknowledged in Section 6.5 of the paper.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Twin-Domain Convergence Identity framework — a systematic approach to institutional namespace architecture that pairs .com DNS domains with .eth ENS domains as the dual-layer identity standard for regulated digital asset infrastructure.

The framework addresses a structural problem that existing namespace standards have not solved: regulated digital asset infrastructure must simultaneously satisfy two incompatible audiences operating on two incompatible rails. Compliance teams, regulators, and General Counsel operate on the Web2 DNS rail — requiring human-readable, legally referenceable identity. Software architects, protocol engineers, and autonomous AI agents operate on the Web3 ENS rail — requiring machine-readable, cryptographically resolvable identity that executes without DNS intermediary.

Drawing on Ian Grigg's Ricardian Contract framework (1996–2015), the W3C Decentralized Identifiers and Verifiable Credentials specifications, the UK Property (Digital Assets etc) Act 2025, and the US GENIUS Act and CLARITY Act legislative frameworks, this paper demonstrates that the Two-Rail Problem has been independently identified by legal theorists, technical standards bodies, and legislative authorities across four jurisdictions — but has not been resolved by any existing namespace standard.

The Twin-Domain Convergence Identity framework resolves this gap by pairing .com as the Ricardian Contract layer — human-readable, legally referenceable, institutionally brandable — with .eth as the W3C DID-compliant programmable routing layer — machine-readable, on-chain resolvable, protocol-embeddable.

Market demand validation is provided through three case studies demonstrating independent institutional adoption of identical namespace terms, primary source recognition in institutional search contexts, and thematic authority exceeding established high-authority reference domains.

title: Evolutionarily Stable Benchmarks: Endogenous Information Production, Manipulation, and Focal Points *
affiliations: Chapman University - The George L. Argyros College of Business and Economics,  and

detail.title: Evolutionarily Stable Benchmarks: Endogenous Information Production, Manipulation, and Focal Points *
detail.abstract: Reducing a continuous signal to pass/fail is conventionally understood as destroying information. This paper argues that thresholds concentrate an endogenous information ecosystem at the decision boundary, generating a selfreinforcing loop between evaluator coordination and information investment, and that the concentration produces more decision-relevant information than continuous evaluation would. The stochastically stable benchmark maximizes induced screening quality-the sum of raw screening quality and the average information premium along the adoption path-so a benchmark with mediocre intrinsic properties but a rich ecosystem defeats one with superior properties but a thin ecosystem. Stochastic stability and population-game risk dominance both select this benchmark, and a global-games argument under the noise-vanishing limit of Frankel, Morris, and Pauzner (2003) is sketched for the two-benchmark case (Online Appendix). Goodhart's Law, the proposition that a measure used as a target ceases to be a good measure once agents optimize against it, is moderated rather than overturned, because endogenous information production partially offsets manipulation-induced degradation.

title: The Dark Side of Human Decision-Making: A Review of Behavior in the Joy-of-Destruction Experiments
affiliations: University of Richmond - E. Claiborne Robins School of Business and University of Reading

detail.title: The Dark Side of Human Decision-Making: A Review of Behavior in the Joy-of-Destruction Experiments
detail.abstract: Despite extensive evidence on cooperation and prosocial behavior, individuals frequently engage in costly destructive actions that yield no material benefit. This paper surveys experimental literature on the Joy-of-Destruction game, a canonical framework designed to isolate such antisocial behavior. We review evidence across a range of experimental designs, treatment conditions, and subject populations, and show that destruction persists even when standard strategic, distributive, and reciprocity-based motives are eliminated. The findings suggest that such behavior is driven by a combination of intrinsic utility from harming others, belief-driven preemptive responses, and contextual pressures. Psychological traits, group identity, and environmental factors further shape destructive choices. We also examine institutional interventions that have been shown to mitigate such behavior. Finally, we compare the Joy-of-Destruction framework to related money-burning games to clarify how differences in experimental design shape the interpretation of destructive behavior-whether as intrinsically motivated or as a response to inequality and procedural concerns.

title: Wealth and Well-being: The Foundations of a Truly Successful Retirement
affiliations: PGIM

detail.title: Wealth and Well-being: The Foundations of a Truly Successful Retirement
detail.abstract: Roughly one half of American retirees describe their retirement as "very satisfying." Drawing on data from the 2022 RAND Health and Retirement Study, this research explores how two aspects of wealth, total savings and lifetime income, and two aspects of well-being, subjective health and social connectivity, are related to retirement satisfaction. The analysis demonstrates that retirement satisfaction varies significantly across (and within) the factors considered, suggesting that a truly "successful" retirement requires holistic guidance that extends beyond common retirement income considerations, such as e icient portfolio construction. Strategies and solutions that can address multiple factors simultaneously, such as lifetime income overlays (for wealth) and engaging activities like pickleball (for well-being), could be especially attractive for retirees.

title: Information Design and Pricing Strategy in New Product Capacity Investment
affiliations: Hong Kong Polytechnic University, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) and City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Management Sciences

detail.title: Information Design and Pricing Strategy in New Product Capacity Investment
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) often focus on new product development and sales while outsourcing production to contract manufacturers (CMs). Because demand for innovative new products is highly volatile, the CM faces significant risk when investing in capacity prior to demand realization. To incentivize the CM's capacity investment, the OEM commits to an information design strategy conducted via market testing and shares the test outcome with the CM without manipulation. We investigate how the OEM jointly leverages the information design and wholesale pricing to influence the CM's capacity investment. Methodology/results: We model this as a Bayesian persuasion game and analyze the OEM's joint optimization of its market testing strategy and wholesale pricing. We show that as the market price of the new product increases, the OEM raises the wholesale price and adjusts its information strategy, shifting from full disclosure to partial disclosure, then to non-disclosure, and last back to full disclosure. Pricing and information provision act as substitutes when the market price is low but become complements when it is sufficiently high. Market testing does not necessarily benefit the CM. It can lead to a win-win outcome for both the OEM and the CM only when the market price is moderately high. We further extend our model to consider the OEM's capacity subsidy provision. We find that the wholesale price plays a moderating role: when it is low, the OEM offers a generous subsidy and adopts full disclosure; as it increases, the subsidy decreases and the information strategy shifts toward partial or non-disclosure. Managerial implications: Our findings provide actionable implications for firms to adopt pricing and information strategies to align the incentives of supply chain parties.

title: Versatility, Specialisation and Career Development in the Football Labour Market
affiliations: Maastricht University

detail.title: Versatility, Specialisation and Career Development in the Football Labour Market
detail.abstract: Positional versatility is widely valued in modern football, but it is unclear whether player markets price versatility itself or the type of player who becomes versatile. This paper studies that distinction using Transfermarkt market values linked to match-level position data for 15,907 players across fourteen European first divisions from 2013 to 2025. Career-versatile players have higher market values in the cross-section, and market value rises around the season in which a player changes primary position group. However, this pattern is concentrated among young players and among switchers whose values were already increasing before the position change. A within-club event-study design shows positive average effects in the full treated sample, but the estimate becomes small and statistically insignificant once switchers are required to have sufficient pre-switch histories. Players acquired into a new position also command no higher transfer fee and experience no larger value gain than players acquired for a familiar role. The evidence is therefore more consistent with developmental selection than with a direct return to positional versatility. Versatility appears to be a useful signal of young players on an upward trajectory, but not a separately priced skill in the transfer market.

title: Accidental Architects: Self-Effacing Objectives in International Relations
affiliations: University of Oxford

detail.title: Accidental Architects: Self-Effacing Objectives in International Relations
detail.abstract: International relations scholarship typically assumes that states achieve their objectives through deliberate, strategic action. This article develops an alternative account: many state objectives are self-effacing-they cannot be attained directly, but only as byproducts of other pursuits. I argue that this dynamic is especially likely under interdependence, where networks emerge through the voluntary participation of new entrants. Under such conditions, overt bids for future leverage provoke resistance, hedging, and duplication. Where durable structural advantage does materialize, it tends to arise indirectly, as the unintended result of principled state commitments, or of non-state actors pursuing goals unrelated to geopolitics. I illustrate the argument through cases in global finance and global supply chains, showing how leverage repeatedly emerges from processes no state intended. Finally, I turn to foreign influence campaigns to demonstrate how states can nonetheless design conditions conducive to 'welcome byproducts.' Yet doing so requires relinquishing some control. The result is a reframing of strategy in international relations: dominance proves most likely when it is not openly pursued.

title: The Directional Anatomy of Demand Elasticity
affiliations: Reichman University - Interdisciplinary Center (IDC) Herzliyah and Syracuse University - Department of Finance

detail.title: The Directional Anatomy of Demand Elasticity
detail.abstract: This paper develops and estimates the directional anatomy of demand elasticity. In a delegated-management equilibrium, mandates constrain characteristic-based reallocations and costly information acquisition shapes uncertainty about future payoffs. Market clearing yields the aggregate demand Jacobian and its inverse price-impact matrix, making elasticity a property of portfolio directions. Using U.S. institutional equity holdings from 1999 to 2022, we show that price-impact capacity is highly concentrated: the top ten directions account for one quarter of price-impact capacity, and the most fragile directions load especially on valuation and profitability. Directional variation reflects differences in institutional constraints, payoff uncertainty, and price informativeness.

title: The Relevance and Impact of ESG Factors for Sustainable Investment Strategies
affiliations: University of Hamburg, , affiliation not provided to SSRN and Invesco

detail.title: The Relevance and Impact of ESG Factors for Sustainable Investment Strategies
detail.abstract: This paper examines the financial relevance of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors within a systematic, factor-based investment framework. Usingglobal equity data from 2007 to 2022, we analyze the role of ESG as a potentialdriver of return and risk, and its interaction with traditional style factors such as value, momentum, and quality. The empirical results show that ESG characteristics do not constitute a persistent source of excess return. This is consistent with thetheoretical expectation that sustainability preferences influence valuations via discount rate effects rather than cash flow changes. However, ESG attributes modestly improve risk modeling and attribution, as higher-rated firms exhibit lower idiosyncratic volatility and slightly better forecast precision. From a portfolio construction perspective, ESG objectives can be efficiently integrated through constraint-based optimization without compromising diversification or exposure to rewarded risk premia. Moderate improvements in portfolio ESG scores entail limited active risk and negligible performance trade-offs. Overall, ESG integration functions more as a riskmanagement and alignment tool than a return engine, enabling investors to pursue sustainability goals within the discipline of modern portfolio theory.

title: The Institutional Approach to Tokenized Money: Japan's Stablecoin Strategy in Comparative Perspective
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The Institutional Approach to Tokenized Money: Japan's Stablecoin Strategy in Comparative Perspective
detail.abstract: Japan is pursuing a distinctive institutional approach to tokenized money, characterized by centralized coordination among the nation's three megabanks and active regulatory oversight by the Financial Services Agency (FSA). In June 2026, Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG), Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group (SMBC), and Mizuho announced plans to jointly issue a yendenominated stablecoin by March 2027, utilizing a trust-based legal structure with a separate trustee to ensure bankruptcy remoteness. This initiative seeks to modernize Japan's cash-heavy economy and preserve the yen's role in regional settlement across Asia. Unlike the fragmented consortium model emerging in the United States, where JPMorgan, HSBC, and The Clearing House pursue overlapping but not fully compatible tokenized deposit solutions, Japan's strategy prioritizes coordination over competition. Similarly, the European Union's Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) framework pursues regulatory comprehensiveness across 27 member states, imposing uniform licensing and disclosure requirements. These three approaches reflect different strategic rationales: monetary sovereignty in Japan, defense of commercial bank money in the United States, and regulatory harmonization as competitive advantage in the European Union. The Japanese model offers lessons in centralized coordination but depends on conditions unique to the country's concentrated banking sector.

reference: Unsung Heroes of the Market: The 24 Underrated Economists You Need to Know, eds. R. Whaples, C. Coyne, G. Robson, and D. Thomas. Oakland, CA: Independent Institute.
title: Frank Fetter: The Fortunes of Subjectivism

detail.title: Frank Fetter: The Fortunes of Subjectivism

publicationDetails.detailsText: Unsung Heroes of the Market: The 24 Underrated Economists You Need to Know, eds. R. Whaples, C. Coyne, G. Robson, and D. Thomas. Oakland, CA: Independent Institute.

detail.abstract: Frank Fetter’s central contribution to economics was to develop a consistently subjectivist theoretical system based squarely on the work of the Austrian economists and their American sympathizers. This involved a complete reconstruction of the theories of value, price, and distribution, with a particular focus on the themes of capital, interest, and rent. In this chapter, I explore an area of Fetter’s thought that has yet to receive much attention: his work in the history of economic thought. Specifically, I consider his account of the transformation of economics following the “marginalist revolution,” and of the role of subjectivist Austrian economics in that transformation. This topic increasingly occupied Fetter’s attention in the later decades of his career, as he witnessed the theoretical revolution falter and give way to what eventually became anti-subjectivist currents in economics. In Fetter’s view, the promise of the revolution was never fulfilled, and was eventually undermined because subjectivism was never completely or consistently adopted in economics. This led to both conflicts between classical and subjectivist theories, but also to internal disputes among economists who all nominally embraced the new value theory. These difficulties were often overlooked, leading to a false sense of agreement and unity among economists that masked substantial differences that would eventually undermine the accomplishments and prestige of the subjectivists like the Austrians. It became a widespread belief, even among their own ranks, that their insights had been completely integrated into economics, which had at last achieved the goal of becoming a unified, rigorous social science. Yet as Fetter showed, this view was inaccurate and failed to account for the uniquely valuable and revolutionary character of the work done by Menger and his followers.

title: The Expertise Paradox in Algorithmic Decision Support: Evidence from AI-enabled Medical Prescribing
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management, University of Science and Technology Beijing, University of Science and Technology Beijing and University of Toronto

detail.title: The Expertise Paradox in Algorithmic Decision Support: Evidence from AI-enabled Medical Prescribing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study utilizes observational data regarding physician prescribing behavior and algorithm adherence. As it does not involve experimental interventions or direct interaction with human subjects, formal ethics committee approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research is supported by the following funding: National Natural Science Foundation of China (grant no. 72542010 and 72394372)

detail.abstract: We examine the tension between professional expertise and acceptance of algorithmic advice among knowledge workers. Drawing on the cognitive entrenchment perspective, we argue that domain experience fosters highly efficient yet cognitively entrenched schemas that may constrain receptivity to external algorithmic input. Using data from an AI-enabled prescription monitoring system that flags medical prescribing risks such as overdosage, underdosage, and drug interaction under random patient–physician assignment, we find that experienced physicians are significantly less likely to follow AI recommendations. This experience-induced resistance is particularly pronounced among physicians with low openness to experience, high neuroticism, greater work fatigue, and more complex patient cases. Further, adherence to AI warnings significantly reduces patient revisit rates, ruling out inferior algorithm quality as an explanation for experience-driven AI resistance. These patterns suggest that AI resistance among experts emerges not from low algorithm quality but from expertise-induced cognitive rigidity that alters trust calibration toward algorithmic systems.

title: Learning From False Stories
affiliations: Bonn Graduate School of Economics, University of Cologne and

detail.title: Learning From False Stories

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: False information often shapes beliefs even after retraction or correction. Using incentivized online experiments, we document a qualitative residue in learning from false information: False quantitative signals generate little to no belief updating, whereas false stories lead to substantial residual belief impact. This effect is robust across a range of design variants. Replacing evaluative stories with more neutral variants eliminates the residue, indicating that the valence of the qualitative information plays a central role. We provide direct evidence that false stories increase mental simulation, measured via self-reports and valence extracted from speech recordings. Respondents are also more confident in beliefs formed after false stories than after false quantitative information, despite being further from the rational benchmark. Additional experiments suggest that the effect also appears among respondents who report not being influenced by the story, consistent with stories partly shaping beliefs below conscious awareness.

title: What Happens in Paris, Does Not Stay in Paris: Trade Fairs and Search and Matching Frictions
affiliations: , Central European University and Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU)

detail.title: What Happens in Paris, Does Not Stay in Paris: Trade Fairs and Search and Matching Frictions

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Search and matching frictions prevent firms from forming international trade linkages. Despite trade fairs being a common and often subsidized tool to overcome these frictions, we lack causal evidence on how they facilitate link formation. We exploit a unique feature of Hungarian firms' participation in the 1900 Paris World Exhibition, where a trial exhibition revealed firms' ex-ante export potential category to develop a novel bounding strategy that compares treated firms to control groups from "above" and "below" in export potential. To implement our empirical strategy, we constructed a novel panel dataset of approximately 3,600 Hungarian manufacturing firms for the 1896–1906 period by digitizing, parsing and linking over 12,000 records across eleven historical sources, including exhibition catalogs, government surveys, commercial directories, official gazettes and patenting directories. We find that participation increases export probability by 4-10 percentage points, patenting probability by 4-6 percentage points and employment by 16–23% over eight years. Effects are larger when firms face fewer domestic competitors and more potential international buyers. This highlights both matching benefits and congestion effects when search and matching frictions are reduced.

title: Tax Salience: How Requiring Transparency Affects the Price of Equality
affiliations: Australian National University (ANU) and

detail.title: Tax Salience: How Requiring Transparency Affects the Price of Equality

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Less-salient taxes can ease the classic equality-efficiency trade-off by making people respond less to taxation. But deliberately obscuring taxes may be viewed as dishonest. This creates a three-way trade-off between equality, efficiency, and honesty. We analyze this trade-off in a simple setting with a linear income tax. We define and characterize the morally efficient frontier, trading off utilitarian welfare against honesty or transparency. Complete honesty is Pareto inefficient but not morally inefficient. More generally, any increase in honesty reduces utilitarian welfare. When utilitarian welfare is decomposed into equality and efficiency, the cost of honesty falls most robustly on equality: higher salience always reduces equality, while the effect on efficiency is ambiguous. This asymmetry is explained by the fact that salience increases the price of equality, which is the efficiency cost of a marginal increase in equality. Our approach could be applied to other settings in which utilitarian and procedural or deontological values conflict.

title: Macro Theory with Measured Expectations
affiliations: University Tuebingen, University of Cologne, Institut d'Etudes Politiques de Paris (Sciences Po) and University of Cologne

detail.title: Macro Theory with Measured Expectations

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The Lucas critique holds that policy evaluations based on historical correlations can fail because policy changes alter expectation formation. We develop a new approach to monetary policy evaluation that addresses this concern: we elicit expectations under alternative policy scenarios from household surveys and feed these measured expectations into a heterogeneous agent model. The surveys reveal that the response of income and inflation expectations to interest rate changes is state-dependent. Incorporating these expectation differences into the model yields estimates of the effects of policy on aggregate consumption that are state-dependent, varying with economic conditions at the time of the policy change.

title: The Smarter State? Artificial Intelligence and Modern State and Local Public Finance
affiliations: and University of Tennessee, Knoxville - College of Business Administration

detail.title: The Smarter State? Artificial Intelligence and Modern State and Local Public Finance

publicationDetails.journalName: CESifo Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes subnational public finance, largely through familiar channels observed from prior technological change. Although some effects are novel, many issues surrounding the taxation of AI-related income and consumption parallel earlier challenges from e-commerce, digitalization, and remote work. AI shifts income from labor toward capital and reallocates tax bases toward consumption and market-based activity, raising questions such as the sales tax treatment of digital services. For governments, AI relaxes long-standing informational and administrative constraints in taxation, enforcement, budgeting, and service delivery, while strengthening scale economies. Cost reductions depend critically on labor-intensive sectors like K-12 education. However, government AI use may advantage larger jurisdictions with greater data access, raising equity and transparency concerns and increasing the value of interstate cooperation to harness scale economies from more data. Overall, AI reinforces—rather than overturns—the classic trade-offs emphasized in the fiscal federalism literature.
